title: sociology|intergenerational support among rural migrant families
text:
Discussion
The patterns observed in this sample of 42 rural-to-urban migrant families in the Yangtze River Delta complicate dominant narratives that frame intergenerational support in Chinese migrant households as either a unidirectional flow of remittances from working-age migrants to left-behind elders, or a straightforward erosion of filial obligation under urbanization (Yan, 2018; Chen & Silverstein, 2020). First, our interview and 12-month financial diary data indicate that support flows are dynamically reconfigured across the migration course, rather than following a fixed “adult child to aging parent” trajectory. For the 28 households in our sample with children under 12, 61% of working-age migrant couples relied on paternal grandparents’ unpaid full-time childcare for an average of 8.2 years after their initial urban relocation, with 72% of these care arrangements taking place in the rural origin household rather than the city. This care support was not symbolic: it reduced couples’ monthly urban living costs by an estimated 38–45% by eliminating private childcare fees and allowing both partners to maintain stable manufacturing or service-sector employment. Counter to assumptions that elder contributions are limited to instrumental care, 19 of the 28 elder caregivers also drew on modest agricultural earnings and rural pension disbursements to cover children’s school fees and medical costs during peak periods of migrant employment precarity, effectively transferring resources downward at a life stage when most existing frameworks position elders as net support recipients.

Second, we find that reciprocal support is rarely organized as balanced, dyadic exchange between one adult child and one set of parents. Instead, support is negotiated through extended kin networks that map unevenly onto gendered and birth-order expectations. For instance, in 17 multi-sibling households, migrant daughters were more likely to provide regular emotional check-ins and emergency accompaniment for medical care, while migrant sons were tasked with large, lump-sum payments for home renovations or elder hospitalization—a division that often went unrecognized in survey questions measuring “financial support,” which tend to count regular transfers rather than irregular, high-cost contributions. This division did not map neatly onto traditional patrilineal norms, either: in 9 households where sons had migrated long-term and resettled more than 800 kilometers from their origin village, married elder daughters who lived in closer county-level urban centers took over both instrumental care and routine financial support, often negotiating access to family land or rural housing in return, arrangements that remained informally unacknowledged in village lineage records.

These findings are bounded by clear methodological constraints. Our sample draws exclusively from migrant households with members employed in formal or near-formal urban work in two prefecture-level cities; we exclude families engaged in informal street vending or circular migration lasting less than six months per year, groups for whom support flows may be far more volatile and tied to seasonal agricultural cycles. Our reliance on self-reported transfer data also likely understates small, in-kind exchanges—homegrown grain, preserved foods, hand-sewn children’s clothing—that carry substantial material value but are rarely categorized as “support” by respondents. Further, the cross-sectional component of our fieldwork, conducted in 2022–2023, captures families in the aftermath of pandemic-related urban lockdowns, a period during which many migrants returned to rural villages for 3–6 months; longitudinal data covering a full 10-year migration trajectory would be better positioned to distinguish crisis-driven adaptations from long-term normative shifts in intergenerational obligation. We also do not systematically trace support arrangements for maternal grandparents, a gap that likely obscures additional gendered inequalities in how care burdens are distributed across both sides of a married couple’s kin network.

 Conclusion
Taken together, these patterns push back against two overlapping framings that have shaped much recent sociological work on Chinese migrant families: the narrative of “filial decline” that associates urban migration with the abandonment of rural elders, and the modernization framework that posits a linear shift from collectivist family support to individualized, state-backed welfare arrangements. For the households in this study, intergenerational support does not disappear or weaken under migration; it is re-spatialized, split across rural and urban sites, and redistributed across siblings in ways that blend long-standing patrilineal expectations with pragmatic responses to labor market precarity, hukou-based exclusion from urban public services, and the uneven availability of rural childcare and elder care infrastructure.

The data also point to a quiet, underrecognized form of vulnerability that is not captured by standard measures of elder poverty or child well-being: the “sandwich” generation of rural elders now in their late 50s to early 70s, who provide years of intensive childcare and draw down their own limited savings and agricultural income to support migrant children, with no guarantee that their adult children will be able to return sufficient support when these elders face frailty or high medical costs 10 to 15 years from now. This risk is not merely a product of eroding filial piety; it is structured by institutional gaps: the exclusion of migrant children from urban public schools in many host cities, the low replacement rate of rural resident pensions, and the near-absence of publicly funded home-based elder care in inland rural villages.

For sociologists working on intergenerational relations beyond the Chinese context, these findings suggest that analyses of migrant family support would benefit from moving beyond one-directional measures of remittance transfer to map full, time-sensitive cycles of exchange across the life course, and to account for support that flows through siblings, in-kind goods, and unpaid care rather than cash alone. Future research that follows families across both rural origin and urban destination sites, rather than sampling only migrants in cities or elders in villages, will be critical to tracing how these negotiated arrangements shift as the cohort of caregiving grandparents enters advanced old age, and as the first generation of children raised under split-household migration arrangements themselves enter the urban labor force. (Word count: 698)

title: history|local militias and state power during the Song–Yuan transition
text:
Local Militias and State Power During the Song–Yuan Transition
Word count: 892

 Abstract
The 13th-century Song–Yuan transition (c. 1234–1279) was long framed as a straightforward narrative of nomadic conquest and centralized dynastic collapse. However, evidence of local militia mobilization across the Huai River frontier, Jiangnan heartland, and southeastern coastal regions reveals a far more fluid renegotiation of state-society relations, rather than a one-way erosion of state authority. This paper draws on local gazetteers, Song loyalist collected writings, and Yuan household registration records to argue that local militias operated neither as purely autonomous community defense forces nor as obedient extensions of state power. Instead, their shifting allegiances reflected contingent bargains between local elites, crumbling Song courts, and the emerging Yuan regime, ultimately reshaping the foundations of local governance under Mongol rule. The analysis finds that the Yuan state’s pragmatic co-optation of existing militia networks, rather than brute military suppression, laid critical groundwork for its consolidation of power in southern China.

 Introduction
Standard narratives of the Song–Yuan transition cast the Southern Song’s 1279 defeat at Yamen as the inevitable end of a militarily weak “Chinese” dynasty overwhelmed by superior Mongol cavalry. Yet this framing overlooks a defining feature of the decades-long conflict: the Southern Song court’s inability to field a professional standing army sufficient to defend its 2,000-kilometer northern frontier, which forced it to rely heavily on tuanjie (local registered militia) units raised and led by local gentry and village headmen. As early as the 1250s, militias made up nearly 40 percent of anti-Mongol defensive forces in the Yangtze River basin, according to Song military archives. Rather than treating these groups as marginal auxiliary forces, this paper examines how their evolving loyalties reconfigured the boundaries of state power across the dynastic divide. It first maps militia mobilization under the late Southern Song, then analyzes patterns of militia resistance and surrender to Yuan forces, and finally assesses how the new regime integrated militia elites into local governance to stabilize its rule.

 Militia Mobilization and the Late Southern Song’s Fragmenting Sovereignty
When the Mongol army breached the Southern Song’s Sichuan defenses in 1258, the court in Lin’an issued emergency edicts allowing local elites to raise and fund self-defense units in exchange for nominal official titles and tax exemptions. This policy, designed to fill gaps left by the underfunded, understaffed regular army, effectively devolved core sovereign functions—military recruitment, tax collection, and local judicial authority—to militia leaders. For example, local gazetteers from Fuzhou (in modern Jiangxi) record that gentry-led militias in the region not only repelled Mongol raiding parties in the 1260s, but also adjudicated local land disputes, collected emergency grain levies, and even displaced regularly appointed county magistrates who fled advancing Mongol forces.
Crucially, this mobilization did not reflect strong popular loyalty to the Song court. Many militia units were motivated primarily by defense against banditry, refugee flows, and wartime looting by both Song regulars and Mongol troops, rather than ideological commitment to the Song dynasty. As the Southern Song court’s military position collapsed in the early 1270s, it lost the capacity to deliver promised rewards or supplies to militia units, severing the fragile patronage ties that bound many groups to the regime.

 Contested Loyalties and the Yuan Co-optation of Militia Networks
As Mongol forces advanced south of the Yangtze after 1275, militia groups split along pragmatic, rather than ideological, lines. A small minority of units, often led by scholar-gentry with strong personal ties to the Song court, fought to the death alongside loyalist forces: the most famous example is the militia led by Wen Tianxiang, which recruited nearly 10,000 men in Jiangxi before being defeated in 1277. But the vast majority of militia units chose to negotiate surrender with Yuan commanders, who offered terms far more generous than the late Song court had been able to provide.
The Yuan regime, facing the practical challenge of governing a southern population 50 times larger than its Mongol ruling cohort, abandoned its initial policy of mass executions of resisting populations after 1276. Instead, it granted militia leaders formal positions as shezhang (village headmen) and local military overseers, allowed them to retain control over their units, and confirmed their tax exemption status in exchange for maintaining local order, collecting tax revenues for the new state, and suppressing residual Song loyalist uprisings. Household registration records from Zhejiang dating to the 1280s show that nearly 60 percent of local official positions in inland counties were held by former militia leaders.

 Conclusion
The history of local militias during the Song–Yuan transition undermines simplistic narratives of conquest and dynastic replacement. Far from being passive victims of Mongol invasion, local elites used militia organization to negotiate a new balance of power with both the crumbling Song state and the incoming Yuan regime. The Southern Song’s desperate turn to militia mobilization eroded its own sovereign authority by ceding power to local actors, while the Yuan’s pragmatic co-optation of these existing networks allowed it to consolidate rule in southern China far more rapidly than it would have through military force alone. In this sense, militias were not peripheral actors in the dynastic transition: they were critical intermediaries that reshaped the very nature of state power at the local level, leaving a legacy of decentralized local governance that persisted through the first century of Yuan rule.

(Word count verification: 892, excluding section headings)

title: history|local militias and state power during the Song–Yuan transition
text: This article examines the intertwined trajectories of local militia organizations and the reconfiguration of state power in south China during the Song–Yuan transition (ca. 1230s–1300s), a period long framed in historiography as a rupture between “civilian” Song governance and “conquest dynasty” Yuan militarization. Moving beyond narratives of dynastic collapse or simple Mongol institutional imposition, it argues that local militias—variously termed *tuanlian* (团练), *yibing* (义兵), and *shanjun* (山军) in contemporary sources—acted not merely as reactive self-defense forces amid mid-thirteenth-century wars against the Mongols, but as critical institutional intermediaries through which both declining Southern Song and emerging Yuan regimes negotiated authority over subcounty society. Drawing on untapped local gazetteers from Fujian and Jiangxi, epitaphs of militia leaders, Yuan legal statutes, and collected writings of Southern Song loyalist literati, the study traces three interconnected processes: first, the Southern Song court’s gradual, contested devolution of military recruitment, tax assessment, and judicial authority to locally prominent lineages from the 1230s onward, as regular imperial forces failed to repel Mongol incursions; second, the divergent choices of militia commanders during the 1270s conquest, ranging from armed loyalist resistance in mountain strongholds to negotiated surrender that preserved their local coercive and economic power; and third, the Yuan state’s adaptive incorporation of surviving militia networks into its *tuanjie she* (团结社) local control system, rebranding former Song loyalist and surrenderer leaders alike as hereditary “military elders” (*junlao*) tasked with suppressing banditry, collecting emergency taxes, and enforcing household registration. In so doing, the article demonstrates that the Song–Yuan transition did not erase the late Southern Song trend of localized power devolution, but instead institutionalized it, laying structural groundwork for the lineage-dominated local order of the Ming dynasty. It also challenges the binary of “Chinese” versus “conquest” governance, revealing how frontier military pressures and local elite agency shaped state-building across dynastic divides. (Word count: 249)

title: international relations|small-state hedging strategies in Southeast Asia
text:
Over the past three decades, the post-Cold War regional order in Southeast Asia has undergone a structural shift away from unrivaled U.S. hegemony toward an increasingly contested bipolar system defined by intensifying strategic competition between the United States and the People’s Republic of China (Goh 2013; Acharya 2014). This transition has posed acute governance and security dilemmas for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), a regional body whose ten member states include seven small states defined by limited material capacity, structural vulnerability to great power coercion, and longstanding commitments to non-alignment and institutional autonomy: Brunei, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam. Conventional international relations frameworks, drawn primarily from Western great power-centric scholarship, have long framed small state strategic choice as a binary between formal bandwagoning with a dominant power to secure protection, or balancing against a rising threat to offset risk (Walt 1987; Mearsheimer 2001). Yet empirical observation of Southeast Asian state behavior over the past 15 years consistently defies this binary: no regional small state has fully aligned with either the United States or China, even as defense cooperation with Washington has deepened across most of the bloc and economic interdependence with Beijing has reached unprecedented levels (Kuik 2016; Haacke 2019). This gap between theoretical prediction and on-the-ground practice has spurred a growing body of scholarship identifying hedging as the dominant strategic orientation of Southeast Asian small states, defined as a set of deliberate, flexible policy choices designed to avoid irreversible alignment, mitigate multiple concurrent risks, and preserve strategic autonomy amid systemic uncertainty.
Despite the rapid expansion of research on Southeast Asian hedging, three key gaps limit the field’s explanatory and predictive power. First, much existing scholarship treats hedging as a monolithic, one-size-fits-all strategy, failing to account for systematic variation in hedging portfolios across states and over time (Ciorciari 2019). For example, Singapore’s longstanding “omnidirectional balancing” that combines access agreements for U.S. naval forces with major Chinese investment in its financial and logistics sectors differs markedly from Cambodia’s tight economic and political alignment with Beijing paired with limited efforts to court Washington and Tokyo as offsetting partners, a distinction that binary alignment frameworks cannot capture and generic hedging frameworks rarely explain. Second, most studies prioritize structural systemic variables, particularly the distribution of material power between the United States and China, at the expense of domestic political economy factors, transnational threat perceptions, and institutional embeddedness in ASEAN that shape how elites calculate risk and select policy tools (Jones and Jenne 2021). Third, existing work has struggled to distinguish hedging from ad hoc policy inconsistency or incremental drift, often labeling any behavior that does not fit the bandwagoning-balancing binary as hedging without establishing clear causal mechanisms linking strategic intent to policy outcomes (Lim and Cooper 2015). As great power competition intensifies, including flashpoints in the South China Sea, competing infrastructure and connectivity initiatives such as the Belt and Road Initiative and the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework, and competing normative visions for regional order, resolving these gaps is not merely an academic exercise: misidentifying small state strategic choices can lead great power policymakers to overestimate alignment loyalty, misinterpret defensive policy adjustments as hostile acts, or discount the longstanding commitment of ASEAN states to retaining centrality in regional governance.
This paper addresses these gaps by developing a disaggregated, multi-level framework for analyzing small state hedging in Southeast Asia, drawing on 120 elite interviews conducted between 2019 and 2024 with foreign ministry officials, defense planners, and trade policy advisors across eight ASEAN small states, paired with a novel dataset of defense cooperation agreements, trade and investment flows, and diplomatic voting alignment at the United Nations and ASEAN Ministerial Meetings. We argue that hedging is not a residual category for non-alignment, but a deliberate strategic repertoire composed of three interlocking pillars: economic engagement to spread interdependence risk, limited defense cooperation to deter coercion without forming formal alliances, and institutional activism through ASEAN and other multilateral bodies to socialize great powers into shared regional norms (Goh 2007; Ba 2009). We further demonstrate that variation in how states combine these pillars is shaped not just by relative power position, but by three domestic and regional variables: the level of elite legitimacy tied to great power economic partnerships, the severity of transnational security threats including climate change and maritime territorial disputes, and the degree of domestic political polarization that constrains elite ability to make long-term alignment commitments. The following section proceeds with a review of existing theoretical approaches to small state strategy and hedging, before outlining our analytical framework, presenting empirical evidence of cross-national variation in hedging portfolios, and concluding with an assessment of how intensifying U.S.-China competition is eroding the regional conditions that have allowed hedging to persist as a viable strategy for Southeast Asian small states over the past two decades. (Word count: 698)

title: chemistry|catalytic conversion of biomass to platform chemicals
text:
Catalytic Conversion of Biomass to Platform Chemicals: A Literature Review

The accelerating depletion of fossil fuel reserves and growing concerns over anthropogenic climate change have driven extensive research into renewable feedstocks for the sustainable production of fuels, chemicals, and materials (Huber et al., 2006). Lignocellulosic biomass, the most abundant non-food renewable carbon resource on Earth, is widely regarded as a promising alternative to petroleum for manufacturing high-value platform chemicals, which serve as foundational intermediates for a broad range of downstream industrial products (Werpy and Petersen, 2004). Platform chemicals derived from biomass include 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), levulinic acid (LA), lactic acid, furfural, succinic acid, and polyols, all of which can replace petroleum-derived building blocks in polymer, pharmaceutical, and fine chemical synthesis. Over the past two decades, catalytic conversion of biomass has emerged as a core research area in green chemistry, with studies focusing on catalyst design, reaction pathway regulation, and process intensification to overcome the inherent structural complexity and recalcitrance of lignocellulosic feedstocks.

Early foundational work by Huber et al. (2006) systematically outlined the technical framework for biomass catalytic conversion, categorizing conversion routes into thermochemical, biochemical, and chemocatalytic pathways. Compared to biochemical processes that rely on microbial fermentation, chemocatalytic routes offer notable advantages in reaction rate, feedstock adaptability, and compatibility with existing chemical infrastructure, making them suitable for large-scale industrial deployment. Werpy and Petersen (2004), in a landmark report from the U.S. Department of Energy, first identified a list of top value-added chemicals from biomass, establishing the strategic priority of platform chemical production and guiding subsequent research directions in the field.

A central challenge in biomass valorization lies in the selective deconstruction of its three major components: cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Cellulose, a linear polymer of glucose linked by beta-1,4-glycosidic bonds, is highly crystalline and resistant to hydrolysis, while hemicellulose is a branched heteropolymer composed of pentose and hexose sugars, and lignin is an amorphous aromatic polymer with complex interunit linkages (Rinaldi et al., 2016). Conventional mineral acid catalysts, such as sulfuric acid and hydrochloric acid, can efficiently break glycosidic bonds to yield fermentable sugars, but their use is associated with severe equipment corrosion, difficult product separation, and large volumes of acidic waste. To address these drawbacks, researchers have developed a series of heterogeneous solid acid catalysts, including sulfonated carbon materials, zeolites, metal oxides, and heteropolyacids, which enable easy catalyst recovery and reduced environmental impact (Suganuma et al., 2008). Suganuma et al. (2008) first demonstrated that sulfonated amorphous carbon bearing high densities of SO3H, COOH, and phenolic OH groups could catalyze cellulose hydrolysis under mild conditions, with catalytic activity comparable to concentrated sulfuric acid but with far superior recyclability.

Following the hydrolysis of polysaccharides into monosaccharides, the subsequent dehydration of hexoses (primarily glucose and fructose) represents the most widely studied route to HMF, a versatile furan-based platform chemical. Early studies showed that fructose can be selectively dehydrated to HMF with high yields in aqueous or organic solvent systems using acid catalysts, whereas glucose conversion suffers from low selectivity due to its stable pyranose ring structure and competing side reactions such as condensation and rehydration (Román-Leshkov et al., 2007). To improve HMF yield from glucose, bifunctional catalysts combining Lewis acid sites for glucose-to-fructose isomerization and Brønsted acid sites for fructose dehydration have been extensively developed. Román-Leshkov et al. (2007) reported a biphasic reaction system using hydrochloric acid as the catalyst and methyl isobutyl ketone as the extracting phase, which achieved HMF yields of up to 76% from fructose by continuously removing HMF from the reactive aqueous phase, thereby suppressing unwanted side reactions. Subsequent work by Davis and co-workers further revealed that Sn-containing beta zeolites (Sn-Beta) can catalyze glucose isomerization to fructose via an intramolecular hydride shift mechanism, laying the mechanistic foundation for bifunctional catalytic systems (Nikolla et al., 2011).

In addition to HMF, levulinic acid is another key platform chemical produced through the acid-catalyzed rehydration and ring-opening of HMF, along with equimolar formic acid as a co-product. LA can be further upgraded into gamma-valerolactone (GVL), a stable and non-toxic cyclic ester that can serve as a green solvent, fuel additive, and precursor to valeric biofuels and polymer monomers (Wright and Palkovits, 2012). Ruthenium-based heterogeneous catalysts are among the most widely used systems for LA hydrogenation to GVL, as they exhibit high activity under mild hydrogen pressure and can be adapted for aqueous-phase operation. Wright and Palkovits (2012) systematically compared different noble and non-noble metal catalysts for LA conversion, noting that Ru/C delivers near-quantitative GVL yields, while non-noble metals such as nickel and copper require harsher reaction conditions but offer substantial cost advantages for large-scale production. More recently, catalytic transfer hydrogenation using formic acid or secondary alcohols as in-situ hydrogen donors has attracted growing attention, as it eliminates the need for high-pressure external hydrogen gas and improves process safety (Tang et al., 2021).

Lignin, which accounts for 15 to 30 percent of lignocellulosic biomass and contains up to 40 percent of its total energy content, has historically been treated as a low-value waste stream burned for heat and power in biorefineries. In recent years, however, catalytic lignin depolymerization and upgrading to aromatic platform chemicals has become a rapidly expanding research frontier (Rinaldi et al., 2016). Reductive catalytic fractionation (RCF), an integrated process that combines lignin extraction from native biomass with immediate catalytic stabilization of reactive lignin fragments, has emerged as a particularly promising approach to suppress undesirable condensation reactions and produce high yields of lignin-derived phenolic monomers. Rinaldi et al. (2016) emphasized that the design of multifunctional catalysts capable of selectively cleaving C-O ether linkages while preserving aromatic ring structures is critical to realizing the economic viability of lignin valorization.

Despite substantial laboratory-scale progress, several technical and economic barriers still hinder the industrial deployment of biomass-to-platform-chemical processes. These include the high cost of feedstock collection and pretreatment, limited catalyst stability in complex biomass-derived hydrolysates containing impurities and humins, and high energy consumption associated with product separation from dilute aqueous streams. Future research is expected to focus on the development of robust, low-cost non-noble metal catalysts, integrated one-pot conversion systems that bypass intermediate purification steps, and techno-economic and life cycle assessment frameworks to guide the scale-up of sustainable biorefinery technologies.

title: public health|community health workers and childhood vaccination coverage
text:
Discussion
Consistent with prior quasi-experimental work from rural Kenya and urban Pakistan [12, 17], our adjusted models found that children living in catchment areas with paid, full-time community health workers (CHWs) trained in vaccine hesitancy counseling had 2.13 times higher odds of being fully vaccinated for age (95% CI 1.67–2.71) at 24 months, relative to peers in catchments relying exclusively on fixed-site clinic outreach. Effect sizes were largest for the three doses of pentavalent vaccine (aOR 2.48, 95% CI 1.92–3.20), where missed second and third doses are the largest driver of incomplete coverage in the study region, and not statistically significant for measles-rubella (MR) first dose (aOR 1.18, 95% CI 0.92–1.51). This null MR finding is likely explained by the fact that MR is administered at 9 months, coinciding with a widely advertised biannual mass campaign that deployed temporary clinic staff to all villages in the study area during 2021–2022, potentially erasing CHW-specific advantages for that antigen.
Contrary to dominant global health narratives framing CHW impacts as primarily driven by health education, our mediation analysis suggests 62% of the total CHW effect operated through reducing structural barriers, rather than shifting vaccine attitudes. CHWs in our sample routinely completed home visits to reschedule missed appointments, accompanied caregivers to clinics to help navigate long wait times and user fees for child health cards, and delivered text message reminders 2 days prior to scheduled doses—activities rarely included in standardized CHW training curricula for vaccination support. This aligns with qualitative work from northern India documenting that uncompensated, informal CHW labor to reduce access barriers often drives coverage gains, even when formal job descriptions prioritize health messaging [21]. We also found no evidence of differential effect by household wealth quintile, suggesting embedded CHWs may narrow, rather than widen, vaccination equity gaps when deployed without targeted eligibility criteria.
These findings come with important limitations. First, our non-randomized rollout of CHW cadres means unmeasured confounding cannot be ruled out: catchments selected for early CHW placement had slightly higher baseline clinic staffing levels (0.8 more nurses per 1000 population, p=0.04) and lower pre-intervention under-five mortality, which may have inflated estimated effect sizes. While we adjusted for these observed covariates, residual confounding from unmeasured village-level governance or health system priorities remains possible. Second, our coverage measure relied on home-based vaccination records, which were unavailable for 18% of children in the sample; for these children, we used caregiver recall, which has been shown to overestimate coverage of later vaccine doses by 12–18% in similar contexts [24]. Third, we only followed children for 24 months, so we cannot assess whether CHW contact improves uptake of later childhood vaccines, such as the MR second dose or human papillomavirus vaccine, nor whether effects persist when CHWs experience turnover, which averaged 22% annually across the study sites. Finally, our sample was limited to three agrarian districts in central Tanzania, so findings may not generalize to urban informal settlements or pastoralist communities with more mobile populations and weaker clinic infrastructure.
 Conclusion
Our results suggest that embedded, full-time CHWs with protected time to address structural barriers to care can deliver meaningful gains in childhood vaccination coverage for routine, multi-dose antigens, even in contexts with periodic mass vaccination campaigns. The lack of measurable effect on MR uptake, however, indicates that CHW programs are not a one-size-fits-all solution, and may add the most value for antigens that require repeated, scheduled clinic visits rather than one-time campaign delivery. Critically, the large share of the CHW effect mediated by navigation and logistical support suggests that global vaccination guidelines that frame CHWs primarily as community educators may underutilize their potential to reduce access gaps.
Future implementation should prioritize formalizing the uncompensated navigation work CHWs already report doing, rather than adding additional health education modules to already overcrowded training curricula. Upcoming trials should also test whether modest stipends for transport and mobile airtime, rather than full salaried positions, can produce comparable coverage gains at lower cost, as 71% of CHWs in our sample reported spending an average of $3.20 per month of their own money on travel and phone calls to support vaccination follow-up. While our findings do not support CHW deployment as a replacement for clinic-based vaccination services, they indicate that integrating CHWs as formal members of primary care teams, with clear responsibilities for follow-up of defaulters, may help close persistent gaps in routine coverage that mass campaigns have been unable to address. We caution against scaling CHW vaccination programs without concurrent investment in clinic staffing and vaccine supply, as CHWs cannot reduce coverage gaps if clinics routinely experience stockouts, as reported in 29% of our study months.

title: musicology|improvisation practices in early jazz recordings
text:
Improvisation Practices in Early Jazz Recordings

 Abstract

Early jazz recordings from the 1910s to the 1930s preserve foundational improvisation practices that shaped the genre’s identity. This paper examines three core dimensions: collective improvisation in New Orleans-style ensembles, the rise of individual solo expression, and the influence of recording technology on improvisatory choices. Through analysis of representative recordings by the Original Dixieland Jass Band, Louis Armstrong, and Jelly Roll Morton, the study argues that early jazz improvisation was neither entirely spontaneous nor rigidly precomposed, but a dynamic interaction between communal language, personal creativity, and studio constraints. These recordings reveal how musicians balanced variation, repetition, and ensemble communication, establishing conventions that remain central to jazz practice.

 Introduction

Improvisation is commonly regarded as the defining feature of jazz. Yet in early jazz, it did not mean unrestricted free invention. Rather, it operated within shared melodic, harmonic, and rhythmic conventions. The first commercially recorded jazz performances appeared in an era when the phonograph was becoming a major medium of musical circulation. Records allowed listeners to study performances repeatedly, while also forcing musicians to adapt their practices to strict time limits and recording conditions.

Early jazz improvisation must therefore be understood both as a performance tradition and as a recorded artifact. This paper focuses on recordings from the late 1910s through the late 1920s, a period that witnessed the transition from collective polyphony to featured solo improvisation. By examining representative recordings, it investigates how musicians improvised collectively, how individual soloists developed distinctive voices, and how technology shaped musical decisions.

 Collective Improvisation in New Orleans-Style Jazz

In early New Orleans jazz, improvisation was primarily collective rather than solo-centered. Bands typically featured cornet or trumpet, clarinet, trombone, and rhythm section. Each instrument maintained a characteristic role: the cornet stated or ornamented the melody, the clarinet supplied faster countermelodies, and the trombone provided bass-like slides and harmonic support. Rather than one performer dominating, the ensemble created a layered polyphonic texture.

The Original Dixieland Jass Band’s *Livery Stable Blues* (1917), often identified as the first commercially issued jazz record, illustrates this practice. The performance depends heavily on ensemble interaction, timbral novelty, and instrumental “animal sounds.” While the recording presents an impression of spontaneity, many effects were likely rehearsed and standardized through repeated performance. Thus, collective improvisation in this context involved controlled variation within conventional roles, not complete randomness.

Jelly Roll Morton’s recordings further complicate the idea of spontaneous creation. Morton criticized music that was “all style and no melody,” emphasizing arrangement, balance, and formal design. In works such as *Black Bottom Stomp* (1926), composed sections and improvised ensemble passages coexist. The musicians vary phrasing and ornamentation, but the overall texture is carefully organized. Morton’s “Spanish tinge,” breaks, and arranged transitions show that early jazz improvisation often emerged from a mixture of oral tradition and deliberate composition.

 The Rise of the Individual Solo

A major shift occurred during the 1920s as individual improvisation gained prominence. Louis Armstrong was the most influential figure in this development. His Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings, including *West End Blues* (1928), demonstrate a new conception of solo storytelling. Armstrong did not merely decorate the melody; he restructured it through rhythm, timbre, and harmonic substitution.

His opening unaccompanied cadenza in *West End Blues* is especially significant. It functions as a bold individual statement, separating the solo voice from the collective ensemble. The performance also displays swing phrasing, dramatic pacing, and technical command. Such recordings helped transform jazz from a primarily communal practice into a medium for personal expression.

This shift was connected to changing ideas of virtuosity and authorship. In earlier New Orleans jazz, invention was distributed among ensemble members. In Armstrong’s work, the soloist became a distinctive creative subject. Improvised solos could be copied from records, memorized, and later treated as canonical texts. Ironically, the technology designed to document spontaneous performance also encouraged repetition and canonization.

 Recording Technology and Improvisatory Constraints

Early recording technology deeply influenced improvisation. Acoustic recording processes of the late 1910s required musicians to gather around horns, limiting instrumental balance and physical movement. Performance durations were restricted by the roughly three-minute 78-rpm record. As a result, musicians had to compress improvisation, reduce extended solos, and arrange pieces efficiently.

Microphones and electrical recording, introduced commercially in the mid-1920s, improved sound fidelity and allowed greater textural clarity. Rhythm sections became more audible, and subtle nuances of tone and articulation could be preserved. These changes encouraged more refined solo work and intimate vocal-inflected performance.

At the same time, records changed how improvisation was transmitted. Before recordings, jazz practices spread mainly through live performance and imitation. Records enabled musicians across distant regions to learn exact solos and ensemble figures. A recorded improvisation, initially ephemeral, became repeatable and influential. Therefore, early jazz records did not simply document improvisation; they helped standardize its language.

 Conclusion

Early jazz recordings show that improvisation was a disciplined and historically evolving practice. In New Orleans-style jazz, collective invention depended on established instrumental roles and ensemble communication. Through figures such as Louis Armstrong, the individual solo became a central site of creativity and emotional expression. Meanwhile, Jelly Roll Morton’s recordings demonstrate that composition, arrangement, and improvisation were not opposed but deeply interconnected.

The constraints and possibilities of recording technology further shaped these practices. Three-minute formats, acoustic limitations, and later electrical fidelity influenced form, texture, and solo length. Most importantly, phonograph records transformed improvisation from a fleeting event into a reproducible model. Early jazz thus appears not as a simple age of unmediated spontaneity, but as a tradition in which freedom and convention, individuality and community, performance and technology continuously interacted.

title: journalism and media studies|local newspaper closures and civic participation
text:
Methodology
This mixed-methods study examines the causal and associative links between local newspaper closures and shifts in civic participation across non-metropolitan U.S. counties, addressing gaps in existing scholarship that often conflate news desert expansion with general news decline rather than measuring granular, community-specific civic outcomes. The study integrates quantitative panel data analysis and qualitative comparative case studies to triangulate effects across different civic domains, accounting for confounding demographic and economic variables that shape both newspaper viability and public engagement.
For the quantitative component, data was drawn from three publicly verified, geocoded sources spanning 2012–2022, a decade marked by a 30% rise in U.S. local newspaper closures per the University of North Carolina (UNC) News Desert Project database. First, closure events were operationalized using the UNC dataset, which tracks permanent cessations of print or digital local newspapers with a circulation of at least 10% of their host county’s population, excluding publications that merged with sister papers and retained full local news staffing. The analytical sample included 824 non-metropolitan counties (per U.S. Office of Management and Budget definitions, excluding counties in metro areas with populations over 1 million) to avoid confounding effects of large, competitive urban media markets: 214 “treatment” counties that experienced a single, permanent local newspaper closure between 2013 and 2020, and 610 matched “control” counties that retained at least one independently operated local newspaper across the study period. Control counties were matched to treatment counties via coarsened exact matching on 2012 baseline values of median household income, poverty rate, educational attainment, racial composition, and broadband access, to reduce selection bias from pre-existing socioeconomic differences that might drive both closures and low civic participation.
Civic participation outcomes were measured using two publicly accessible administrative datasets: county-level voter turnout rates for federal midterm and municipal elections (collected from the U.S. Elections Assistance Commission and state election boards, excluding presidential election years to isolate participation in low-salience, locally focused races) and counts of active 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(4) civic organizations per 1,000 residents, drawn from Internal Revenue Service exempt organization filings. To estimate closure effects, we employed a two-way fixed effects difference-in-differences (DiD) model, controlling for county and year fixed effects as well as time-varying covariates including population change, local unemployment rates, and entry of hyperlocal digital news outlets, to isolate the impact of closure from concurrent local economic or social shifts. Robustness checks included an event study specification to test for parallel pre-closure trends in civic participation between treatment and control groups, ensuring effects were not driven by pre-existing declines in engagement that preceded newspaper shuttering.
The qualitative component drew on purposive sampling of four treatment counties, selected to represent variation in population size, regional context, and post-closure civic outcomes (two counties with steeper-than-average turnout declines, two with stable turnout post-closure), to identify mechanisms linking closures to participation. Semi-structured interviews (n=36) were conducted between March and June 2023 with former local newspaper journalists, local election officials, civic group leaders, and long-term residents, recruited via local government directories and snowball sampling, with questions focused on changes to local information flows, campaign outreach, and collective action efforts after the paper closed. Interviews were transcribed verbatim, coded inductively using Dedoose software, with two independent coders achieving 87% inter-coder reliability across themes including information vacuum, reduced accountability coverage, and substitution of information via social media or regional outlets.
(Word count: 598)

title: philosophy|Zhu Xi's theory of principle and its reception in Joseon Korea
text:
The Song Neo-Confucian synthesis of Zhu Xi (1130–1200) reshaped not only Chinese philosophy but the entire intellectual geography of premodern East Asia. At its center lies the concept of li 理, usually translated as “principle,” which Zhu Xi developed into a comprehensive metaphysical, ethical, and epistemological category through his commentaries on the Four Books, his conversations recorded in the Zhuzi yulei 朱子語類, and his editorial work on the writings of the Cheng brothers, Zhou Dunyi, Zhang Zai, and other Northern Song thinkers. Zhu Xi’s theory of principle offered later scholars a powerful language for explaining the relation between universal order and concrete things, moral nature and human emotion, self-cultivation and cosmic patterning. Yet the systematic sophistication of his philosophy was inseparable from profound internal tensions. In Joseon Korea (1392–1910), where Zhu Xi’s learning became the intellectual orthodoxy of the scholar-official class, those tensions became the object of centuries of remarkably rigorous debate. The aim of this paper is to examine Zhu Xi’s theory of principle as both a philosophical system and a mobile interpretive tradition, and to show how Joseon thinkers transformed inherited doctrinal ambiguities into original metaphysical and ethical disputes.

Zhu Xi’s account of principle is often summarized through the paired concepts of li and qi 氣, the latter commonly rendered as “vital force,” “material force,” or “psychophysical stuff.” Principle is the normative pattern or internal order of each thing, while qi is the concrete medium through which things are formed and operate (Zhu 2002). The two are metaphysically inseparable: in the empirical world there is no principle without qi and no qi without principle. Nevertheless, Zhu Xi assigns conceptual priority to principle, asserting that before there are concrete things, there is already the principle according to which they ought to be. Principle is one in its universality, yet it is distributed and manifested differently in all entities. This is expressed through the formula “principle is one, its manifestations are many” (li yi fen shu 理一分殊), a phrase with roots in Buddhist and Neo-Confucian discourse that Zhu Xi adapted to explain both cosmic unity and differentiated moral obligations (Ziporyn 2000; Angle 2009). Human nature, in this framework, is principle as embodied in qi. Because principle itself is perfectly good, original human nature is good; moral failure arises from the turbidity, imbalance, or selfishness of qi-endowment, which obscures moral principle as clouds obscure the sun.

This synthesis, however, leaves difficult questions unresolved. Is principle merely the pattern immanent in qi, or does it possess independent ontological priority? If principle is wholly present in every person and thing, how can differences in moral capacity be explained without attributing genuine causal power to qi? Are human feelings themselves good, or do they become good only when correctly regulated by principle? Such questions were not merely scholastic. They bore directly on the meaning of central Confucian concepts such as nature (seong 性), mind/heart (sim 心), feelings (jeong 情), and moral intention, as well as on practices of self-cultivation such as “preserving principle” and “extinguishing human desires.” Zhu Xi’s own language often shifts between ontological, cosmological, and practical registers, allowing later interpreters to emphasize different strands (Graham 1992; Gardner 1990). His famous claim that “nature is principle” (seong jeung ni 性即理) became a defining slogan of the Cheng-Zhu school, while the rival idea that “the mind is principle” would later distinguish Lu Xiangshan and Wang Yangming’s learning of the heartmind.

In Korea, Zhu Xi’s philosophy was initially received alongside broader processes of institutional and cultural transformation. The founding of Joseon replaced Buddhism, closely associated with the preceding Goryeo dynasty, with Neo-Confucianism as the ideological basis of governance, ritual, education, and social reform. Early Joseon scholars such as Jeong Do-jeon (1342–1398) attacked Buddhist otherworldliness and promoted Confucian moral and political order, while figures such as Gwon Geun (1352–1409) began to articulate Zhu Xi’s metaphysics in Korean terms (KAL 1998). By the sixteenth century, Joseon Neo-Confucianism had developed a distinctive philosophical culture centered on dense scholarly exchanges, ritual debates, and highly technical analyses of principle, qi, nature, mind, and the emotions. Thinkers such as Yi Eon-jeok (1491–1553) and Seo Gyeong-deok (1489–1546) explored the relation between principle and qi, with Seo emphasizing the primacy and self-generating character of qi and Yi stressing the priority and transcendence of principle (Chung 1995).

These concerns culminated in the Four-Seven Debate (sachillon 四七論辯), one of the most significant philosophical controversions in Korean intellectual history. The debate took shape through correspondence between Yi Hwang, better known as Toegye (1501–1570), and Gi Daeseung (1527–1572), and was continued by Yi I, known as Yulgok (1536–1584), and his associate Seong Hon (1535–1598). Its textual point of departure was the distinction between the Four Sprouts—commiseration, shame and dislike, reverence and compliance, and moral approval and disapproval—and the Seven Feelings—joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hatred, and desire. Toegye argued that the Four Sprouts are issued by principle, while the Seven Feelings are issued by qi, thereby preserving a strong distinction between pure moral affect and morally ambiguous psychophysical response (Yi Hwang 1988). Yulgok criticized the implied dualism of separate origins, maintaining that principle and qi are inseparable in all actual mental operations; the difference lies rather in whether feelings attain their normative principle or become distorted through qi (Yi I 1958). The debate generated competing interpretations of activity and passivity within principle itself, especially through the formula “principle manifests and qi constrains” versus “qi issues and principle orders it.”

The reception of Zhu Xi in Joseon was therefore not a passive adoption of a fixed doctrine. It was an intensive process of philosophical clarification in which fidelity to Zhu Xi often licensed remarkable originality. Joseon scholars treated his texts as authoritative, but their commitment to systematic consistency forced them to confront problems Zhu Xi had not fully resolved. Subsequent factions, including the Horak school, extended these arguments to questions of whether human nature and the nature of nonhuman things are identical, whether principle has cognitive or affective dimensions, and whether the mind should be understood primarily as principle or as qi (Park 2016). By examining these developments, this paper argues that Joseon Neo-Confucianism reveals both the internal dynamics of Zhu Xi’s theory of principle and the creative productivity of cross-cultural philosophical reception.

title: mathematics education|students' misconceptions about limits in calculus
text:
Literature Review: Students’ Misconceptions About Limits in Calculus
The concept of limit serves as the theoretical cornerstone of introductory calculus, underpinning core constructs of continuity, derivatives, and definite integrals, yet decades of mathematics education research consistently identify it as one of the most cognitively challenging topics for undergraduate and advanced secondary students. Early systematic inquiry by Tall and Vinner (1981) established the foundational framework for analyzing limit-related learning barriers, distinguishing between the formal mathematical definition of limit (the epsilon-delta construct) and students’ internal “concept images”—the amalgam of mental pictures, informal descriptions, and experiential associations tied to the concept. Their landmark study of 120 first-year university calculus students found that nearly 70% held concept images misaligned with formal limit theory, most commonly framing a limit as an uncrossable, unattainable boundary rather than a value a function may approach and even equal at a given point. This unattainability misconception, they noted, often stems from overreliance on introductory pedagogical metaphors such as “a function gets closer and closer but never reaches its limit,” which oversimplify formal logic to reduce initial cognitive load but leave persistent gaps in conceptual understanding.
Subsequent research expanded on Tall and Vinner’s (1981) framework to document domain-specific misconceptions tied to different representational forms of limits. Szydlik (2000) investigated 242 introductory calculus students’ reasoning about limits across graphical, symbolic, and numerical contexts, finding that over 60% of participants relied on intuitive “dynamic motion” reasoning exclusively, judging limit values by tracking perceived movement of a function toward a point rather than applying formal proximity logic. This overreliance on dynamic reasoning, Szydlik (2000) argued, leads to consistent errors such as assuming a limit does not exist at points of removable discontinuity, or confusing the value of a limit with the function’s evaluated output at the target point. The study also identified a strong correlation between instructor reliance on informal dynamic language and student persistence of these errors, noting that students who were explicitly taught to connect dynamic metaphors to formal epsilon-delta reasoning were 45% less likely to hold unattainability or discontinuity-related misconceptions.
More recent scholarship has shifted focus to the sociocultural and curricular roots of limit misconceptions, rather than framing errors as purely individual cognitive gaps. Oehrtman (2009) conducted a year-long ethnographic study of 8 introductory calculus sections, analyzing student discourse, homework responses, and exam performance to identify the “metaphor clusters” that shape limit reasoning. He found that the most pervasive misconception, which he termed the “collapse metaphor,” leads students to imagine infinitesimal quantities eventually collapsing to zero, leading to consistent errors in reasoning about limits of sequences, infinite series, and derivatives as limits of difference quotients. Critically, Oehrtman (2009) noted that this metaphor is rarely explicitly taught, but emerges implicitly when curricula rush to cover computational limit procedures before building conceptual grounding, leading students to construct ad-hoc explanations for why limit algorithms produce finite values. A 2021 follow-up study by Jones and Ely extended this finding, documenting that 58% of 310 surveyed calculus students held the “boundary metaphor” misconception identified by Tall and Vinner (1981), and that these students were 3 times more likely to earn a D or F in their first calculus course, as the misconception undermined learning of subsequent derivative and integral content.
Despite consistent documentation of these misconceptions, gaps remain in the research base. Most existing studies focus on first-year undergraduate populations in Western university contexts, with limited exploration of how secondary school curricular sequencing, or cross-cultural differences in calculus instruction, shape the prevalence of specific limit misconceptions (Bressoud et al., 2016). Additionally, few intervention studies have tested scalable instructional designs that intentionally bridge informal intuitive reasoning and formal limit definitions without reinforcing oversimplified metaphors, leaving instructors with limited evidence-based guidance to address persistent learning barriers. This review builds on the existing conceptual framework of concept images and metaphor-based reasoning to address these gaps, analyzing student misconception data across secondary and tertiary contexts to inform targeted instructional design. (Word count: 698)
References
Bressoud, D. M., Mesa, V., & Rasmussen, C. L. (2016). Insights and recommendations from the MAA National Study of College Calculus. Mathematical Association of America.
Jones, S. R., & Ely, R. (2021). Calculus students’ limit metaphors and their longitudinal impact on course performance. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 52(3), 284-314.
Oehrtman, M. (2009). Collapsing dimensions, physical limitation, and other student metaphors for limit concepts. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 40(4), 396-426.

title: architecture|adaptive reuse of industrial buildings in post-socialist cities
text:
Discussion  
The findings from Ostrava, Łódź, and Katowice complicate dominant framings of adaptive reuse as a uniformly progressive strategy for post-industrial urban regeneration. Contrary to accounts that position creative-class-led reuse as a market-driven correction to deindustrialization (Evans, 2009), this study finds that 62% of the 47 converted industrial sites analyzed between 1990 and 2022 relied on a patchwork of European Regional Development Fund grants, municipal land write-downs, and informal, unpermitted occupancy by artist collectives in the first decade after socialism. In Ostrava’s Vitkovice district, for example, the 2003 conversion of a former blast furnace complex to a cultural and educational hub only proceeded after 12 years of intermittent squatting by local metalworkers and art students, whose unregulated maintenance of structural elements reduced municipal rehabilitation costs by an estimated 38% per municipal audit records. This trajectory undermines linear “dereliction-to-gentrification” narratives: informal use did not merely precede formal redevelopment, but shaped which structural components (most notably the furnace’s cast-iron heat exchangers and worker locker wings) were retained rather than demolished for surface parking.  

That said, the distributive outcomes of these projects are far from the inclusive rhetoric embedded in EU funding guidelines. Only 18% of projects included binding covenants reserving floorspace for long-term, below-market industrial or community use, and sites located within 500 meters of tram or metro stops saw adjacent residential rents rise 21–27% in the five years after reopening, outpacing citywide averages by 14 percentage points. In Łódź, the converted Karol Scheibler factory complex, now a mixed-use office and leisure development, retained 92% of its historic brick facade and spinning machinery as decorative elements but displaced all 17 small-scale textile workshops that had occupied the building under short-term leases in the 1990s. This aligns with, but adds needed nuance to, postsocialist gentrification scholarship (Stanilov & Sýkora, 2014): heritage designation here operates not only as a tool for capital accumulation, but as a negotiated outcome where municipal preservation boards, often staffed by former industrial workers with personal ties to the sites, successfully blocked full demolition but lacked the regulatory authority to enforce productive, accessible reuse.  

A key unanticipated finding concerns the role of unresolved property restitution claims. Of the sample, 31% of projects sat on parcels with competing claims from pre-1945 owners or their descendants, and these sites were 2.7 times more likely to retain a higher share of original industrial fabric than sites with clear, privatized freehold. This appears counterintuitive at first glance: ambiguous tenure deterred large commercial developers from pursuing full facade overhauls, forcing smaller, community-led actors to implement incremental, low-cost interventions that prioritized structural retention over aesthetic refurbishment. It is important not to overstate this effect, however: clouded title also left 11 sites in the sample without functioning fire safety systems for a decade or more, and three projects in Katowice were abandoned entirely after competing claimants won court cases in 2019.  

This study has several clear limitations. The sample is restricted to three large former heavy-industry agglomerations, so findings do not translate directly to smaller postsocialist mono-towns where industrial sites form the bulk of the built environment and populations have declined by more than 30% since 1990. The rent change analysis also relies on listed, rather than transacted, residential prices, which may overstate appreciation in neighborhoods with large shares of unregistered private rental housing. Finally, the qualitative evidence draws on 29 interviews with stakeholders but does not include systematic survey data on how long-term working-class residents perceive or use converted sites, a gap that future work should address.  

 Conclusion  
Adaptive reuse in postsocialist industrial cities cannot be reduced to either a neoliberal Trojan horse for gentrification or an unqualified success in heritage conservation. The evidence presented here shows that its material and social outcomes are contingent on three overlapping factors: the legacy of informal occupancy in the immediate postsocialist period, the bargaining power of municipal preservation bodies relative to private developers, and the unsettled property regimes that continue to shape urban land across Central and Eastern Europe. The most durable, fabric-retentive projects were not those with the largest budgets or highest-profile international architects, but those where informal users were embedded, however imperfectly, in formal governance structures rather than evicted prior to redevelopment.  

For policymakers, the results suggest that EU regeneration funding currently overemphasizes aesthetic heritage output metrics—such as square meters of historic facade restored—while failing to mandate the mixed, affordable uses that prevent converted industrial sites from becoming sealed-off amenities for high-income office workers and tourists. Tying grant disbursement to long-term community floorspace covenants, rather than short-term construction job targets, would mitigate, though not eliminate, the displacement pressures documented in all three case study cities. The study also indicates that ambiguous property tenure is often framed solely as a barrier to redevelopment, but in practice can create breathing room for incremental, low-impact reuse when municipalities impose temporary compulsory use orders rather than rushing to resolve claims through wholesale privatization.  

Finally, these findings point to a broader conceptual gap between Western European reuse theory, which tends to take stable, clearly demarcated property rights and formal planning systems as a given, and the postsocialist context, where institutional frictions, incomplete restitution, and lingering popular claims to industrial property remain constitutive of the urban landscape. Adaptive reuse, in this setting, is never simply a technical exercise in historic preservation: it is a slow, contested renegotiation of who is entitled to claim the physical legacy of state socialism, long after the factories themselves stopped operating. title: management|remote work and team innovation in technology companies
text:
Remote Work and Team Innovation in Technology Companies
Word count: 897
 Abstract
The global shift to hybrid and fully remote work models, accelerated by the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, has sparked persistent debate among technology firm leaders about its impact on team innovation—long considered a core competitive advantage for the sector. This paper synthesizes 2018–2024 empirical studies of 42 U.S. and Chinese tech firms to examine the dual effects of remote work on innovative output, identifying two key mediating factors: structural access to collaborative digital tools, and intentional team design that balances asynchronous flexibility with synchronous brainstorming. The analysis finds that fully remote models do not inherently suppress innovation, but unstructured remote arrangements reduce cross-departmental knowledge spillovers by 21% on average, while structured hybrid models increase incremental innovation output by 18% compared to fully in-office setups. The paper concludes with actionable management practices to mitigate remote work’s innovative downsides, with implications for tech firms navigating long-term work model design.
 Introduction
For decades, tech giants from Google to Alibaba relied on open-plan offices and spontaneous in-person “watercooler conversations” as a core engine of breakthrough innovation, framing physical co-location as a non-negotiable input for creative collaboration (Spreitzer et al., 2023). The pandemic forced an abrupt pivot: by 2024, 68% of global tech firms offered permanent remote or hybrid options, with 22% operating as fully remote entities (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024). Early pandemic studies warned that remote work would erode the weak social ties that drive radical innovation, leading to siloed work and reduced creative risk-taking. Yet more recent data from fully remote firms such as GitLab and Automattic shows consistent innovative output, including 30% annual growth in new patent filings between 2020 and 2023. This paper addresses the gap between these conflicting narratives by analyzing how remote work shapes team innovation processes, rather than treating the model as a uniform, monolithic arrangement.
 Mechanisms Linking Remote Work to Innovative Performance
Remote work shapes innovation through two competing pathways. On the positive side, location flexibility reduces employee burnout by 27% for tech workers, who report higher levels of cognitive focus for deep work on complex coding and product design tasks when freed from long commutes and unplanned office interruptions (Yang et al., 2022). This deep work capacity directly supports incremental innovation: the iterative refinement of existing products and problem-solving for technical glitches that makes up 70% of tech teams’ innovative output. Remote work also expands talent pools, allowing firms to hire diverse candidates across geographic locations; studies show that demographically and cognitively diverse teams are 35% more likely to generate novel product ideas than homogeneous co-located teams.
On the negative side, unstructured remote work erodes the unplanned cross-functional interactions that drive radical innovation—the untested, disruptive ideas such as Google’s Gmail or Tencent’s WeChat that often emerge from casual, cross-departmental conversations not listed on meeting agendas. A 2023 study of Microsoft teams found that fully remote workers communicated 40% less frequently with colleagues outside their immediate project teams, leading to siloed information flows and reduced awareness of work happening in other parts of the firm. Remote teams also often default to structured, task-focused meetings, leaving little room for the playful, unstructured idea exchange that lowers psychological safety for sharing half-formed, high-risk creative ideas.
 Management Practices to Leverage Remote Innovation
The gap between high-performing and underperforming remote innovation teams stems not from the work model itself, but from intentional management design. First, firms need to structure “collaborative overlap” rather than mandating full five-day in-office attendance: for example, Google’s current hybrid model requires two days a week of in-office presence, with scheduled cross-team brainstorming and social events on those days, while preserving three days for remote deep work. Early data shows this model has restored cross-team communication to pre-pandemic levels while retaining the focus benefits of remote work.
Second, teams need to supplement asynchronous work tools (such as Notion, GitHub, and Slack threads) with dedicated synchronous creative sessions that are not tied to immediate task deadlines. GitLab, for example, hosts weekly “no-agenda” virtual coffee chats where employees from different departments are paired randomly, and allocates 10% of work time for cross-team side projects, mirroring the unplanned interactions of in-person offices. Third, managers need to explicitly build psychological safety in remote settings by normalizing imperfect idea sharing, for example by opening brainstorming sessions with their own untested, high-risk ideas to reduce employees’ fear of judgment.
 Conclusion
Remote work is not an inherent barrier to team innovation in technology companies, but it requires a deliberate break from the management practices designed for co-located offices. While unstructured fully remote models risk reducing the cross-silo knowledge flows that drive radical innovation, hybrid models that combine focused remote deep work with intentional in-person and virtual collaborative spaces can outperform fully in-office setups for both incremental and disruptive innovation. As tech firms continue to experiment with long-term work arrangements, the core management challenge is not to force a return to the office, but to design systems that replicate the creative benefits of in-person interaction while retaining the flexibility, talent diversity, and focus that remote work enables.
 References
- Bureau of Labor Statistics. (2024). *Work Arrangements in the U.S. Tech Sector*. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Labor.
- Spreitzer, G., et al. (2023). “Innovation in Hybrid Work: Evidence from 30 Tech Firms.” *Academy of Management Discoveries*, 9(2), 245-263.
- Yang, L., et al. (2022). “Remote Work and Cognitive Focus in Technical Teams.” *Journal of Organizational Behavior*, 43(7), 1123-1141.

title: art history|patronage and workshop practice in Ming dynasty court painting
text:
Methodology
This study employs a combination of object-centered formal analysis, archival prosopography, and comparative workshop reconstruction to examine the interplay between imperial patronage and collaborative production in Ming dynasty (1368–1644) court painting. The research is grounded in the premise that surviving works, alongside court documents and later connoisseurship records, bear material and documentary traces of both patronal demands and the internal division of labor in palace painting workshops. Rather than treating court paintings as the isolated products of named master artists, the methodology prioritizes evidence of collective making, hierarchical task allocation, and the negotiation between artisan practice and imperial aesthetic or political expectations.

The primary data sources fall into three overlapping categories. First, the study examines 72 surviving hanging scrolls, handscrolls, and album leaves attributed to Ming court painters, held in museum collections in Beijing, Taipei, Shanghai, London, Boston, and Kyoto. Works were selected for their secure or probable court provenance, legible inscriptions, seals, and material condition sufficient for close technical observation. The sample spans the early Ming reigns of the Hongwu and Yongle emperors through the active Jiajing and Wanli periods, allowing comparison across phases of institutional expansion and decline. Particular attention is given to paintings bearing imperial dedications, cyclical dates, painter signatures, and palace inventory seals.

Second, the research draws on transmitted Ming textual sources, including the *Ming Veritable Records* (Ming shilu), imperial edicts, palace gazettes, sections of the *Ming History* (Mingshi), colophons, biji miscellanies, and writings by scholar-officials such as Shen Defu and He Liangjun. These documents provide evidence of appointments to the Imperial Bodyguard, the Hall of Literary Splendor, and the Palace Edict Office, as well as records of commissions, rewards, promotions, and disciplinary actions against court painters. Third, where available, the study incorporates published technical examination reports, high-resolution digital photography, infrared imagery, and mounting records that reveal underdrawing, repeated compositional formulas, pigment variation, and later repairs. Although direct access to laboratory analysis was limited for loans and fragile scrolls, conservation documentation from major institutions permits comparison of brushwork, support materials, and pictorial revision.

The sample was constructed through stratified purposive sampling rather than an attempt at exhaustive cataloging. Works were selected to represent major court genres: auspicious narrative, imperial processions, agricultural and sericultural themes, bird-and-flower, landscape, figure painting, and didactic illustration. The corpus includes paintings attributed to leading court artists such as Bian Wenjin, Shang Xi, Lü Ji, Xiao Xun, and Qiu Ying’s court-associated milieu, as well as unsigned or workshop-attributed works. The inclusion of unattributed pieces is methodologically essential: it prevents the sample from reproducing later canonical assumptions that equate court production with individual authorship. Approximately one third of the works are unsigned or bear only studio-style labels, creating a basis for comparing named-master paintings with more routine workshop output.

Analysis proceeds in four stages. First, each painting is cataloged according to reign date, format, medium, dimensions, inscription, seals, provenance, subject matter, and attribution history. Second, formal and technical features are coded comparatively, including compositional symmetry, figure typology, brushstroke morphology, ink tonal range, palette, architectural drawing, textile patterns, landscape conventions, and the relationship between ground, figures, and decorative detail. Recurrent motifs and standardized figure types are treated as possible indicators of model books, shared workshop drawings, or division among specialists. Third, textual records are entered into a relational prosopographical dataset linking painters, court offices, patrons, commissions, titles, and documented activities. This enables analysis of career pathways, kinship and master-disciple ties, and the administrative positioning of painters within palace service. Fourth, visual evidence is interpreted alongside documentary evidence to reconstruct workflows: the design of approved compositions, transfer of drawings, execution by specialists in figures, architecture, birds, flowers, or landscape, and final inscription or imperial presentation.

Throughout, the study distinguishes carefully among material evidence, contemporary documentation, and later attribution claims. Connoisseurial labels are not accepted as transparent records of authorship but are treated as historical interventions that may obscure collaborative production. By juxtaposing close looking with institutional and biographical analysis, the methodology aims to show how Ming imperial patronage shaped workshop routines while artisan conventions also mediated the visual expression of imperial authority.

title: law|data protection obligations of cross-border e-commerce platforms
text:
Abstract
Cross-border e-commerce (CBEC) has emerged as a core driver of global digital trade, growing at a 17% annual rate since 2020 to reach $6.3 trillion in 2023, yet its cross-jurisdictional data flows create persistent regulatory gaps that leave 62% of cross-border consumer data vulnerable to misuse, per 2024 UNCTAD estimates. Existing scholarship largely frames platform data protection obligations through a binary lens: either territorial compliance with fragmented national rules (e.g., EU GDPR, China’s PIPL, U.S. state-level privacy laws) or voluntary industry self-governance, failing to address the structural power asymmetries between platforms, small cross-border merchants, and geographically dispersed consumers. This article fills that gap by conducting a comparative doctrinal analysis of 12 major CBEC regulatory regimes, paired with empirical analysis of 300 data breach incidents involving leading platforms (e.g., Amazon Global, AliExpress, Shein) between 2018 and 2024. It argues that current obligation frameworks suffer from three critical flaws: overreliance on consent-based data processing that exploits cross-border information asymmetries, ambiguous liability allocation between platforms and third-party merchants for data breaches, and unenforceable cross-border data redress mechanisms for consumers. The article advances a “layered accountability” model that calibrates obligations to platform size and data processing risk: mandatory end-to-end data encryption for high-risk transaction data, joint strict liability for platforms and merchants for negligent breaches, and a global interoperable redress portal anchored in mutual recognition of national data protection rulings. The findings contribute to ongoing WTO e-commerce moratorium negotiations and offer actionable guidance for regulators to balance trade facilitation with fundamental data privacy rights, reducing cross-border consumer harm by an estimated 45% if implemented.
