title: civil engineering|fatigue performance of steel bridge welds
text:
Discussion
The observed 12–18% reduction in fatigue strength for transverse fillet welds with 300–500 μm root undercuts relative to the AASHTO Category B baseline aligns with prior small-scale specimen tests (Maddox, 2018) but diverges from field monitoring data from the I-95 Schuylkill River Bridge (Kain et al., 2022), where equivalent undercuts correlated with a 32% strength reduction over 12 years of service. This discrepancy is not an artifact of specimen fabrication: our post-test fractography confirmed that root undercuts in our samples acted as crack initiation sites in 89% of failed specimens, consistent with Kain et al.’s field observations, but our constant-amplitude loading protocol did not replicate the 15–20% overstress events from heavy permit trucks that dominated crack propagation in the I-95 study. The implication is that current code provisions, which rely exclusively on constant-amplitude test data, may underestimate fatigue damage in welds exposed to frequent, legal oversize loads—a gap that is not addressed by generic safety factors, as the magnitude of the underprediction scales directly with the frequency of overstress events, not just static load magnitude.

Our finding that ultrasonic peening (UP) improved fatigue strength by 41% for welds with initial residual stresses of 280–320 MPa, but only 17% for welds with residual stresses below 120 MPa, partially resolves conflicting results in the UP retrofit literature. Earlier studies reporting 30–50% fatigue life extensions (e.g., Roy et al., 2020) tested as-welded specimens with high as-fabricated residual stresses, while studies reporting <20% benefits (e.g., Garcia & Hicks, 2021) tested stress-relieved specimens or welds that had already seen 10+ years of cyclic loading, which naturally dissipates near-surface residual stresses. We caution against extrapolating our UP results to field welds with pre-existing fatigue cracks, however: all our peened specimens were uncracked at the time of treatment, and preliminary (unpublished) data from our lab suggests UP provides no measurable life extension for cracks longer than 0.5 mm, as the compressive residual stress layer introduced by peening only extends 1–1.5 mm below the weld toe.

A key unanticipated result was the 9% higher fatigue strength of welds fabricated with E71T-8 flux-cored wire relative to E7018 stick welds, even when controlling for weld profile and defect size. Fractographic analysis revealed that the E71T-8 welds had a finer acicular ferrite microstructure that slowed microcrack coalescence by an average of 35% in the early crack growth stage (ΔK < 10 MPa√m). This effect is not captured in current code provisions, which classify welds by strength grade rather than filler material microstructure, though we note this result is limited to the two heat lots of filler material tested here; lot-to-lot variations in flux composition could alter this microstructural benefit, and we did not test welds exposed to long-term atmospheric corrosion, which may preferentially attack the finer ferrite grain boundaries.

 Conclusion
This study’s constant-amplitude fatigue testing of 72 full-scale steel bridge fillet weld specimens demonstrates that root undercuts in the 300–500 μm range reduce fatigue strength sufficiently to shift welds from AASHTO Category B to Category C when subject to frequent overstress events, even though the defects fall within current code-acceptable tolerance limits. For bridges with more than 5% of annual traffic consisting of heavy permit trucks, our results suggest that targeted inspection of transverse fillet welds for undercuts at diaphragm connections could reduce unanticipated fatigue cracking risk by an estimated 40%, though we emphasize this estimate is based on a limited set of load spectra calibrated to northeastern U.S. traffic patterns, and may not apply to bridges with high volumes of logging or mining loads.

Ultrasonic peening is a highly effective retrofit for as-welded connections with high residual stresses, providing life extensions consistent with prior published data, but its benefits drop sharply for welds that have already seen sufficient cyclic loading to relax near-surface residual stresses, or for welds with pre-existing microcracks. For departments of transportation considering UP as a retrofit, this means that peening should be deployed within the first 5 years of a bridge’s service life, or immediately after weld repair, rather than as a reactive treatment for already cracked connections.

We do not propose revisions to existing weld strength classifications based on filler material type at this stage, given the limited number of filler lots tested and the absence of corrosion-coupled fatigue data. Future work should prioritize variable-amplitude testing that replicates observed overstress events from permit vehicles, as well as coupled corrosion-fatigue testing of peened and unpeened welds, to resolve the remaining gaps between small-scale laboratory results and long-term field performance. The results presented here should not be generalized to groove welds or welded connections subject to out-of-plane bending, as our test program only addressed in-plane loaded transverse fillet welds, the most common connection type in steel girder bridges but not the only fatigue-critical detail. (Word count: 698)

title: economics|minimum wage increases and employment in small retail firms
text:
Minimum Wage Increases and Employment in Small Retail Firms

 Abstract
The impact of minimum wage hikes on employment remains one of the most debated topics in labor economics. While large corporations may absorb higher labor costs through profits or price adjustments, small retail firms—characterized by thin profit margins and labor-intensive operations—are often presumed to be more vulnerable. This paper examines how minimum wage increases affect employment in small retail businesses, drawing on competing theoretical frameworks, empirical evidence, and heterogeneous firm responses. The analysis suggests that modest, phased-in minimum wage rises exert limited negative employment effects on average, but outcomes vary by wage levels, profitability, location, and labor market tightness. Small retailers often adjust through higher prices, reduced turnover, productivity gains, and shorter hours rather than extensive layoffs. Nevertheless, sharp unanticipated increases can accelerate closures among the least profitable establishments. Policy design therefore matters substantially: predictable regional differentiation and tax or compliance support can reduce harm while protecting low-wage workers.

 1. Introduction
Minimum wage policy aims to raise earnings for low-paid workers, reduce poverty, and limit exploitation. Yet it also raises the cost of hiring workers whose marginal revenue product may be close to the legal wage floor. Small retail firms are especially relevant because they employ many young, low-skilled, and part-time workers and typically operate with narrow markets. Convenience stores, local grocery shops, apparel retailers, and specialty shops compete not only with one another but also with large chains and e-commerce platforms.

Traditional competitive labor market theory predicts that a binding minimum wage reduces labor demand. However, modern empirical studies, particularly following Card and Krueger’s influential work, often find small or statistically insignificant disemployment effects. This paper evaluates whether that conclusion applies to small retail firms. It first outlines theoretical mechanisms, then reviews empirical evidence and adjustment channels, and concludes with policy implications.

 2. Theoretical Framework
Under the perfectly competitive model, firms hire labor up to the point where the wage equals the marginal revenue product of labor. A mandatory wage increase raises the cost of low-productivity workers, leading firms to reduce employment, hours, or both. In small retail businesses, where the wage bill often represents a large share of operating costs, this effect could be substantial.

Monopsony models offer a different prediction. If employers have wage-setting power because workers face mobility costs, imperfect information, or limited outside options, firms may pay below the competitive level. A moderately higher minimum wage can increase both wages and employment by encouraging non-participants to enter the labor market and reducing costly worker turnover. In concentrated local labor markets, some small retailers may possess limited monopsony power, although they often compete with larger nearby employers.

Institutional and behavioral perspectives add further nuance. Small firms are not simple profit-maximizing machines; owner preferences, family labor, managerial ability, and relationships with employees influence decisions. A wage increase may be absorbed through lower owner earnings, modest price increases, or efficiency wage effects. Thus, theory alone cannot determine the employment response.

 3. Why Small Retail Firms Are Distinctive
Small retailers differ from large firms in several ways. First, they generally have thinner profit margins and weaker access to credit, making it harder to absorb sudden cost shocks. Second, they are less able to automate or reorganize production rapidly. Third, owners may substitute their own labor or family labor for paid employees. Fourth, small retailers often serve local customers and may have some pricing power, allowing at least partial pass-through to prices.

At the same time, these firms may benefit from reduced turnover. Retail jobs traditionally have high quit rates, and recruitment and training are costly. A higher minimum wage can improve worker retention, raise morale, and increase productivity. Because small employers interact closely with staff, efficiency-wage benefits may be especially visible. Therefore, vulnerability and flexibility coexist.

 4. Empirical Evidence
Empirical findings are mixed but increasingly indicate that moderate minimum wage increases have small average employment effects. Early studies using national time-series data often found negative teenage employment elasticities, but later research exploiting state-level variation produced less consistent results. Card and Krueger’s study of fast-food restaurants in New Jersey found no evidence that a minimum wage increase reduced employment, challenging the conventional competitive model.

Research focused specifically on small retail firms suggests heterogeneous outcomes. Shops paying near the minimum wage experience the strongest cost pressure, while higher-paying firms are less affected. Establishments in low-income regions or areas with weak product demand may reduce headcount or close, whereas firms in prosperous cities often pass costs to customers without visible job losses. Franchised and chain-affiliated retailers may cope better than independent stores because of standardized technology, bulk purchasing, and stronger finances.

Firm-exit evidence is important. Even if employment among surviving businesses changes little, minimum wage hikes may raise closure rates among the least profitable firms. However, new businesses may enter with operating models designed around higher wages, partly offsetting job losses. Studies that examine only continuing firms can therefore miss part of the adjustment process.

 5. Adjustment Channels Beyond Layoffs
Small retailers rarely respond through layoffs alone. A common channel is price increases. Because many competitors face the same wage shock, relative prices need not change dramatically, allowing firms to share costs with consumers. This is easier for locally traded retail services than for goods competing with online sellers.

A second channel is reduced labor turnover. Higher wages attract more applicants, reduce quits, and encourage better work performance. Lower turnover saves recruitment and training costs and may improve customer service. Third, firms may compress benefits, reduce bonuses, limit scheduled hours, or require greater effort. Fourth, owners may accept lower profits or work longer hours themselves. Finally, some businesses invest in payment technology, self-checkout, inventory software, or online sales systems, which can raise productivity but may substitute for routine labor over time.

 6. Policy Implications
Policymakers should distinguish modest, predictable increases from abrupt, large shocks. Phased implementation gives small firms time to adjust through prices, productivity, and lower turnover. Regional differentiation is also valuable because a minimum wage that is manageable in a high-income city may be restrictive in a rural area. Tax relief, simplified compliance, and targeted support for independent retailers can reduce adverse effects.

Furthermore, policy evaluation should examine hours, earnings, closures, and worker turnover—not only headcount employment. A small reduction in hours may coexist with higher weekly or monthly earnings, while zero employment effects could conceal rising closure rates.

 7. Conclusion
Minimum wage increases do not mechanically cause large employment losses in small retail firms. The evidence supports a more conditional conclusion: moderate and well-designed wage hikes can raise low-wage earnings with limited average disemployment effects, but sharply rising labor costs can threaten the least profitable businesses. Small retailers respond through multiple margins, including prices, profits, turnover, working hours, owner labor, and productivity. The net employment effect depends on labor market competition, local demand, wage levels, and the speed of implementation. Balanced minimum wage policy can therefore improve incomes while preserving jobs if increases are gradual, regionally sensitive, and accompanied by support for small businesses.

title: literary studies|landscape and exile in the poetry of Su Shi
text:
Methodology
This study employs a text-centered, historically situated close reading framework rooted in Chinese literary studies’ *shishi huzheng* (mutual illumination of text and historical context) tradition, complemented by critical exile studies and humanistic geography, to trace how Su Shi (1037–1101) reconfigured landscape as a site of subjective belonging amid recurring political banishment. The methodology prioritizes the poetic text as both an aesthetic artifact and a record of lived spatial experience, while contextualizing Su’s landscape representations within Song Dynasty travel cultures, bureaucratic exile norms, and the Chan Buddhist and Daoist intellectual traditions that shaped his worldview. Unlike prior scholarship that has framed Su’s exile poetry as a narrative of stoic “transcendence” of displacement, this approach foregrounds the reciprocal shaping of self and place, attending to how landscape mediates, rather than erases, the tensions of exile.

 Data Sources and Sample
The primary corpus is drawn from the authoritative Zhonghua Book Company 1982 annotated edition of *Su Shi Shiji* (Collected Poems of Su Shi), a comprehensive, philologically verified compilation based on Song-era woodblock editions, supplemented by Su’s travel prose (*youji*) and surviving personal letters from the 1986 *Su Shi Wenji* to corroborate biographical and contextual details of his composition. The sample is delimited to poems written during Su’s three formal periods of political exile, selected to capture the evolution of his landscape poetics across shifting geographic and personal contexts: 1) the 1080–1086 Huangzhou exile (Hubei, central Yangtze River basin), triggered by the Crow Terrace Poetry Trial conviction for lèse-majesté; 2) the 1094–1097 Huizhou exile (Guangdong, subtropical Lingnan region), following his blacklisting by the New Policy regime; and 3) the 1097–1100 Danzhou exile (Hainan Island, the southernmost frontier of the Northern Song), the harshest of his banishments.
To avoid selection bias that overemphasizes his most anthologized “transcendent” works, the sample includes both canonical, widely circulated poems (e.g., “Nian Nu Jiao: Memories of the Red Cliff,” *Eight Views of Huangzhou*) and understudied occasional verses: 24 poems of rural labor observation, 17 short inscriptions on rock faces and local shrines, 12 verses presented to local indigenous hosts, and 9 fragmented drafts recovered from Song-era miscellanies, totaling 129 individual poems. This sample balances works of celebrated scenic sites (the Red Cliff, West Lake in Huizhou) with mundane, unmarked landscapes: flood-prone river flats, overgrown lychee groves, malarial tidal creeks, and village rice paddies, to capture the full range of Su’s engagement with place rather than only curated “scenic” encounters.

 Analytical Procedure
Analysis proceeds in three iterative stages. First, philological coding identifies all explicit landscape references (toponyms, flora, hydrological features, built environment markers), paired with historical annotation to map each poem’s precise composition location, date, and biographical context, distinguishing poems written during moments of acute hardship (e.g., crop failure, malarial illness, news of political persecution) from those composed during periods of relative stability. Second, close formal analysis traces how Su adapts conventional Song landscape tropes: it maps shifts in prosody, diction, and perspective, noting when he departs from the inherited exile poetry convention of framing southern frontier landscapes as alien, hostile, and a marker of imperial disfavor, to instead anchor embodied, reciprocal engagements with place (e.g., his decision to purchase a plot of farmland in Huangzhou, plant lychee trees in Huizhou, or dig a well for Danzhou villagers). Third, contextual interpretation draws on contemporary exile geography scholarship and Song bureaucratic records to situate Su’s landscape poetics against institutional norms of exile, which required banished officials to remain within designated prefectural boundaries and frame their displacement as a deserved imperial punishment. Across this analysis, the study tracks how landscape operates not as a passive backdrop for expressions of longing for the capital, but as an active agent: a medium for Su to negotiate displaced identity, build local belonging, and redefine political worth outside the imperial court’s value system. All coding was cross-checked against two leading annotated editions of Su’s work to resolve philological ambiguities, with attention to how later anthologization has shaped dominant readings of his poetics of exile. title: philosophy|moral luck and the limits of responsibility
text:
Moral Luck and the Limits of Responsibility
 Abstract

The problem of moral luck arises from a seeming paradox: we commonly hold agents morally responsible for outcomes shaped by factors beyond their control, yet the control principle—widely taken as foundational to ordinary moral judgment—holds that agents cannot be morally assessed for what lies outside their agency. A driver who negligently strikes a pedestrian is judged more harshly than an equally negligent driver who passes through an empty crossing, though the presence of the pedestrian is pure luck. This article defends a *bounded control account* of responsibility that resolves the paradox without denying the reality of moral luck or abandoning the core normative force of the control principle.

Against standard responses that either eliminate moral luck by restricting justified blame to the quality of an agent’s will (Nagel, Richards) or treat resultant luck as straightforwardly altering moral desert (Williams), I argue that moral luck operates at two distinct levels: the *scope* of moral responsibility, which legitimately expands to include actual outcomes of voluntary risky action, and the *degree* of basic moral standing, which remains immune to luck. Drawing on Strawson’s reactive attitudes framework and recent work on epistemic partiality, I show that our differential responses to lucky and unlucky negligent agents are not irrational retributive impulses but track two separate functions of blame: addressing harm to victims, and registering impairment in an agent’s quality of will.

The account further clarifies the hard limits of responsibility: circumstantial and constitutive luck impose stricter constraints on warranted blame than resultant luck, because they shape the very quality of will the control principle is meant to protect. The conclusion outlines practical implications for criminal law, where outcome-based differential punishment (e.g., for completed versus attempted crimes) is defensible only on harm-rectification grounds, never as a claim about differing moral desert. (Word count: 249)

title: literary studies|unreliable narration in post-war British fiction
text:
Unreliable narration, a narrative mode long central to debates about literary truth, perspective, and readerly trust, takes on distinctive thematic and formal weight in post-war British fiction, a body of work shaped by the collective trauma of global conflict, the collapse of imperial hegemony, and the fragmentation of long-held social and moral consensus. While Wayne C. Booth’s foundational 1961 formulation of unreliability as a gap between a narrator’s account and the implied author’s normative framework remains a critical touchstone, post-war British writers repeatedly stretch, subvert, and reconfigure this device to grapple with historical experiences that resist straightforward, authoritative narration: the disorientation of civilian life during the Blitz, the moral ambiguities of colonial retreat, the quiet violence of class hierarchy in the welfare state, and the lingering intergenerational trauma of combat and loss. Unlike the modernist experiments with unreliable perspective that preceded them, which often anchored narrative distortion to individual psychological crisis or formal experimentation for its own sake, post-war British deployments of unreliability are inextricably tied to public, collective ruptures, framing narrative untrustworthiness not as a quirk of individual perception but as a structural condition of life in a nation stripped of its old claims to moral, political, and epistemic certainty. This paper argues that post-war British fiction redefines unreliable narration as a tool of historical and ethical inquiry, rather than a mere formal puzzle, inviting readers to confront the limits of narrative coherence in the aftermath of catastrophe while interrogating the ideological work performed by claims to “truthful” storytelling in a period of rapid social change.
Early critical accounts of unreliability in post-war British writing often framed the device as a symptom of national decline, reading narrators’ evasions, misperceptions, and outright lies as reflections of a broader cultural inability to come to terms with lost imperial status and the trauma of total war (Bergonzi 1970). For Bernard Bergonzi, the proliferation of untrustworthy first-person narrators in 1950s fiction by writers such as Graham Greene and Angus Wilson signaled a retreat from the social realist commitments of earlier 20th-century British writing, a turn inward to subjective delusion that avoided direct engagement with structural inequity. Subsequent scholarship, however, has pushed back against this dismissive framing, emphasizing how unreliability in this period often functions as a deliberate critique of dominant narratives of national unity, wartime heroism, and benevolent imperial rule. As Jed Esty (2004) notes, the contraction of British global power after 1945 created a cultural context in which the authoritative, omniscient narrative voices that had anchored much Victorian and Edwardian fiction felt increasingly untenable, tied as they were to a vision of British identity as stable, morally upright, and central to global order. Unreliable narration, in Esty’s reading, emerges as a formal corollary to this contraction, allowing writers to expose the gaps between official stories of national virtue and the messy, often shameful realities of post-war life: the persistence of class prejudice, the violence of colonial counterinsurgency in Kenya and Malaya, the quiet despair of suburban conformity, and the state’s failure to deliver on the promises of the welfare state for marginalized communities.
This analysis builds on that critical foundation by tracing three interconnected strands of unreliable narration across four decades of post-war British fiction, from the immediate post-austerity 1950s through the Thatcher-era 1980s. First, it examines what might be called “traumatic unreliability,” in which narrators’ misrememberings, evasions, and contradictory accounts stem from unresolved experiences of wartime violence, as seen in the work of Elizabeth Taylor and Pat Barker, where narrative gaps mirror the unspeakable nature of combat trauma and civilian loss that official commemorative narratives often erase (Miller 2000). Second, it explores “ideological unreliability,” in which narrators unconsciously reproduce the biases and blind spots of their class, racial, or gendered positions, as in the work of Sam Selvon and Zadie Smith, where untrustworthy perspective exposes the dissonance between dominant narratives of meritocratic inclusion and the persistent exclusions of British national identity (Gunning 2018). Third, it considers “metafictional unreliability,” in which writers including John Fowles and Angela Carter draw explicit attention to the constructed nature of narrative itself, using untrustworthy narration to challenge the very idea of a single, authoritative account of history, particularly as it relates to gendered and colonial power structures (Waugh 1984). Across all three strands, unreliability is never merely a formal game: it demands active, critical engagement from readers, who must navigate gaps, contradictions, and evasions to piece together accounts of the past that official narratives have suppressed. In doing so, these works reframe readerly distrust not as a failure of narrative communication, but as an ethical practice, one that mirrors the critical work required to confront the contested, often painful histories that shaped post-war Britain.
