title: agronomy|intercropping maize and soybean under drought stress
text:
Discussion
The consistent 13–22% yield advantage of maize-soybean intercropping over monoculture maize under moderate drought stress (soil water content 40–55% of field capacity) observed across two growing seasons aligns with complementary resource use frameworks, though the magnitude of benefit was lower than the 28–35% reported in well-watered intercropping systems in the North China Plain (Li et al., 2021). This discrepancy likely stems from drought-induced suppression of soybean nodulation: we measured a 41% reduction in nodule dry weight per plant in intercropped soybean under severe drought (<40% field capacity), which eroded the nitrogen facilitation effect that typically supports intercropped maize performance. Notably, land equivalent ratio (LER) remained above 1.1 under all drought treatments, indicating intercropping still delivered modest land use efficiency even when soybean yields declined by 37% relative to monoculture soybean under severe stress.

Root niche partitioning appeared to mediate drought resilience more strongly than aboveground light interception in our study. Minirhizotron imaging showed intercropped maize extended 18% deeper into the 40–60 cm soil layer than monoculture maize, while intercropped soybean concentrated 62% of its root biomass in the 0–20 cm layer, reducing overlap for residual soil water. This vertical differentiation was less pronounced in the 2022 season, when a 12-day mid-season heatwave coincided with peak tasseling, raising the possibility that high vapor pressure deficit limits the expression of root plasticity under combined heat and drought stress. We also found that intercropped maize maintained 9–14% higher leaf relative water content at silking than monoculture maize, but only in plots with 2:2 maize-to-soybean row ratio; the 1:1 row arrangement showed no significant difference, likely because closer proximity intensified early-season water competition before soybean canopy closure.

Our finding that intercropping did not improve water use efficiency (WUE) under severe drought contrasts with recent meta-analyses reporting 17% higher WUE in cereal-legume intercropping under water limitation (Zhang et al., 2023). One plausible explanation is that our rainout shelter design excluded small, frequent rainfall events that often support surface-rooted soybean in field conditions; under natural drought, sporadic light showers may sustain soybean nitrogen fixation and reduce net water use in ways our controlled treatment could not replicate. Additionally, we did not quantify root exudate-mediated rhizosphere processes, which have been linked to improved soil water retention in intercropped systems, representing an unmeasured pathway that may have contributed to the yield gaps between treatments.

Several limitations constrain the generalizability of these results. First, all measurements were conducted on a loam soil with high organic carbon content (14.2 g kg⁻¹); on sandy soils with lower water-holding capacity, interspecific competition may outweigh complementary benefits even under moderate drought. Second, we used a single late-maturing maize cultivar and early-maturing soybean cultivar; cultivar phenology matching is a core driver of intercropping performance, and different maturity combinations could alter both resource partitioning and drought response. Third, our rainout shelters reduced photosynthetically active radiation by 11–15%, which may have suppressed soybean biomass independently of drought treatment, though the uniform shelter setup across all plots should minimize relative bias between planting patterns. Finally, we only assessed two years of data, and interannual precipitation variability across a longer time series would be needed to quantify risk profiles for farmer decision-making.

 Conclusion
Across two rainout shelter field seasons, 2:2 row ratio maize-soybean intercropping maintained LER values of 1.12–1.27 under moderate drought, supported by vertical root niche separation and partial retention of soybean nitrogen facilitation, but yield and WUE benefits disappeared under severe drought when soybean nodulation and biomass were strongly suppressed. The 1:1 row arrangement offered no measurable drought resilience benefit relative to monoculture maize, likely due to intensified early-season water competition. These results suggest that maize-soybean intercropping can serve as a modest drought adaptation strategy for the western Huang-Huai-Hai region, where moderate seasonal drought occurs in 60% of growing years, but should not be promoted as a risk-mitigation practice for areas facing frequent severe drought without supplemental irrigation. Future work should test cultivar mixtures across soil textural gradients under fully open-field conditions, and incorporate rhizosphere trait measurements to disentangle the belowground mechanisms driving interspecific interactions under combined drought and heat stress.

(Word count: 698)

title: environmental science|wetland restoration and carbon sequestration
text:
Wetland Restoration and Carbon Sequestration: Synergies, Trade-offs, and Climate Mitigation Potential
(Word count: 892, excluding references)

 Abstract
Wetlands are among the most carbon-dense ecosystems on Earth, storing an estimated 30% of global soil carbon despite covering less than 6% of terrestrial land area. Widespread wetland drainage and degradation over the past century have converted these carbon sinks into significant greenhouse gas (GHG) sources, accounting for roughly 10% of annual anthropogenic land-use emissions. This paper synthesizes peer-reviewed evidence on the carbon sequestration co-benefits of wetland restoration, analyzes biophysical mechanisms driving carbon accumulation, and identifies key trade-offs that can undermine net climate gains. We find that restored coastal and inland wetlands can sequester 2–5 times more carbon per unit area than upland forests, but poorly designed projects risk elevated methane emissions or failed carbon storage if hydrological regimes are not matched to native vegetation communities. The paper concludes that wetland restoration is a cost-effective natural climate solution, but requires site-specific monitoring and long-term stewardship to deliver sustained carbon and biodiversity benefits.

 Introduction
Global efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C require rapid, scalable removal of atmospheric carbon dioxide alongside deep emissions cuts. Natural climate solutions (NCS)—conservation, restoration, and improved management of ecosystems—have emerged as a low-cost, high-co-benefit strategy to close the emissions gap, but wetland carbon sequestration has long been underprioritized relative to forest-based NCS. Since 1900, 64% of global wetlands have been lost to agricultural conversion, urban development, and hydrological modification, releasing an estimated 450 Gt of stored soil carbon to the atmosphere. Recent policy frameworks, including the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, have set targets to restore 30% of degraded wetlands by 2030, but questions remain about how to maximize carbon returns while avoiding unintended ecological consequences. This paper evaluates the climate mitigation potential of wetland restoration, addresses critical biophysical and management constraints, and outlines evidence-based best practices for project design.

 1. Biophysical Basis of Wetland Carbon Sequestration
The exceptional carbon storage capacity of wetlands stems from their unique hydrological conditions: saturated soils create anaerobic environments that slow the decomposition of organic matter by 60–90% relative to aerobic upland soils, allowing plant detritus to accumulate as peat or organic-rich sediment over centuries. Two wetland types deliver outsized sequestration benefits: coastal “blue carbon” ecosystems (mangroves, salt marshes, seagrasses) and inland peatlands. Coastal wetlands sequester carbon at an average rate of 235 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹, 2–5 times the rate of tropical upland forests, because tidal inputs continuously deposit mineral sediment that stabilizes organic carbon, preventing erosion and long-term oxidation. Inland peatlands, meanwhile, store 600 Gt of soil carbon globally—twice the carbon stock of all the world’s forests—with undisturbed bogs sequestering 20–50 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹ over millennial timescales.
Restoration re-establishes these carbon-accumulating conditions by rewetting drained soils, reintroducing native hydrophytic vegetation, and removing tidal or fluvial barriers. A 2023 meta-analysis of 203 wetland restoration projects found that sites recover 75% of their pre-disturbance carbon sequestration rates within 20 years of restoration, with coastal sites reaching full sequestration capacity 10–15 years faster than inland peatlands due to faster vegetation regrowth.

 2. Trade-offs and Implementation Barriers
Despite high sequestration potential, wetland restoration does not automatically deliver net climate benefits, and poorly executed projects can generate net GHG emissions. The most widely documented trade-off is elevated methane (CH₄) emissions from rewetting: CH₄ has a 28-fold higher global warming potential than CO₂ over a 100-year timeframe, and freshwater wetlands restored without appropriate vegetation or hydrological calibration can emit enough CH₄ to offset 30–60% of their CO₂ sequestration gains for the first 10–15 years after rewetting. For example, a 2021 study of restored peatlands in the UK found that sites flooded to overly high water tables produced 3 times more CH₄ than sites with water levels maintained 5–10 cm below the soil surface, with no significant difference in long-term carbon accumulation rates.
Additional barriers include land-use competition and leakage: 60% of degraded global wetlands are currently used for crop production or grazing, and restoration that displaces agricultural activity can drive deforestation or wetland drainage elsewhere, erasing 40–80% of project-level carbon gains. Many restoration projects also fail to account for long-term vulnerability: coastal wetlands restored without accounting for sea-level rise may drown within 30 years, releasing stored carbon back to the atmosphere as vegetation dies and soils erode.

 Conclusion
Wetland restoration is a high-impact natural climate solution that delivers outsized carbon sequestration benefits alongside co-benefits for flood control, biodiversity, and water purification, but its climate value is not guaranteed. Evidence shows that projects designed to match hydrological regimes to native plant communities, maintain water levels that minimize CH₄ emissions, and avoid displacing food production can deliver sustained carbon sequestration at costs 30–50% lower than equivalent forest restoration or technological carbon removal strategies. To unlock this potential, policymakers should integrate wetland carbon accounting into national climate targets, mandate long-term monitoring of both CO₂ and CH₄ fluxes at restoration sites, and prioritize restoration of coastal and peatland sites with the highest pre-disturbance carbon density. As global carbon budgets shrink, wetland restoration offers a rare triple win for climate, biodiversity, and human well-being—if implemented with attention to site-specific ecological constraints.

 References (abbreviated for course submission)
1. Mitsch, W. J., et al. (2013). Wetlands, carbon, and climate change. *Landscape Ecology*, 28(4), 583-597.
2. McLeod, E., et al. (2011). A blueprint for blue carbon: toward an improved understanding of the role of vegetated coastal habitats in sequestering CO₂. *Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment*, 9(10), 552-560.
3. Taillardat, P., et al. (2020). Climate change mitigation potential of wetlands and the cost-effectiveness of their restoration. *Biological Reviews*, 95(6), 1709-1727.

title: nursing|nurse staffing levels and patient falls in acute care
text:
Methodology
This retrospective longitudinal observational study employed a cross-sectional repeated-measures design to examine the association between nurse staffing levels and patient fall events in adult acute care units. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the affiliated academic medical center; given the use of de-identified administrative data, the requirement for written informed consent was waived, and all procedures adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki.

 Data Sources
Three linked, de-identified hospital administrative databases from a 1,200-bed urban academic tertiary care hospital in the Mid-Atlantic United States were used for analysis, covering a 24-month study period from January 2022 to December 2023. First, the electronic health record (EHR) nursing acuity system provided shift-level staffing data, including total daily nursing hours per patient day (NHPPD), registered nurse (RN) hours per patient day (RN-HPPD), unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) hours per patient day, patient-to-RN ratio per shift, and unit-level patient acuity scores (calculated daily using the validated Patient Acuity Classification System, PACS). Second, the hospital’s voluntary incident reporting system, cross-validated with EHR fall-related documentation (e.g., fall risk assessments, post-fall injury notes), captured all confirmed patient fall events, including fall date/time, unit, patient age, fall injury severity (rated per the National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators [NDNQI] classification: none, minor, moderate, major), and whether the fall was assisted or unassisted. Third, the hospital admission-discharge-transfer (ADT) database provided unit-day level covariates: total patient days, average patient age, proportion of patients aged ≥65 years, average length of stay, proportion of patients with documented fall risk on admission (per Morse Fall Scale score ≥45), unit type (medical, surgical, medical-surgical combined, step-down), and monthly hospital occupancy rate. To eliminate reporting bias, falls documented only in incident reports but not corroborated in EHR clinical notes were excluded, and duplicate fall entries for the same patient event were merged via unique medical record number and event timestamp.

 Study Sample
The unit of analysis was the unit-day, to align staffing exposure and fall outcomes at the temporal and operational level where staffing assignments occur. The initial sample included all 32 adult acute care inpatient units, yielding 23,360 unit-day observations across the 24-month period. Exclusion criteria were applied prior to analysis: (1) specialty units with structurally distinct staffing models and fall risk profiles, including intensive care units (ICUs), labor and delivery, pediatric, psychiatric, and rehabilitation units (n=8 units, 5,840 unit-days); (2) unit-days with incomplete staffing or acuity data due to EHR system outages or unit closure for outbreaks (n=722 unit-days); (3) unit-days with fewer than 3 occupied beds, where staffing ratios do not reflect routine operational conditions (n=418 unit-days). The final analytic sample comprised 24 general adult acute care units (10 medical, 8 surgical, 6 mixed medical-surgical/step-down) and 16,380 valid unit-day observations. All falls occurring on included units among admitted adult patients (≥18 years) during the study period were eligible for outcome ascertainment; falls occurring during off-unit diagnostic procedures or patient leave were excluded, as staffing on the home unit was not causally linked to those events.

 Statistical Analysis
Descriptive statistics were first calculated for all staffing, outcome, and covariate variables: continuous variables were reported as means with standard deviations (SD) or medians with interquartile ranges (IQR) based on normality assessed via Shapiro-Wilk tests, while categorical variables were reported as counts and percentages. Bivariate associations between unit-day fall occurrence (binary: any fall vs. no fall) and each staffing measure were evaluated using independent samples t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables, and chi-square tests for categorical covariates.

Given the hierarchical structure of the data (unit-days nested within units, with repeated observations across months), multivariable multilevel logistic regression models (generalized linear mixed models, GLMMs) were constructed to estimate the association between nurse staffing levels and odds of patient falls, with random intercepts for unit and calendar month to account for within-unit correlation and seasonal temporal trends. The primary exposure was daily RN-HPPD, modeled both as a continuous variable and as a categorical variable grouped by NDNQI benchmark quartiles to assess threshold effects. Secondary exposures included total NHPPD, patient-to-RN ratio, and proportion of staffing provided by UAPs.
All models adjusted for prespecified confounders identified via directed aciclic graph (DAG) analysis: unit type, daily average patient acuity, proportion of patients at high fall risk, proportion of patients aged ≥65 years, average length of stay, daily occupancy rate, day of week, and season. Separate subgroup models were run to test whether associations differed by fall injury severity (any injury vs. no injury) and unit acuity type (general medical-surgical vs. step-down). Two-sided p-values <0.05 were considered statistically significant, and odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were reported. All analyses were performed using Stata/SE 17.0 (StataCorp, College Station, TX). (Word count: 597)

title: law|data protection obligations of cross-border e-commerce platforms
text:
Abstract
The exponential growth of cross-border e-commerce (CBEC), which hit $6.3 trillion in global transaction value in 2024, has turned transnational data flows into a core operational backbone for platform operators, while creating fragmented, often conflicting data protection obligations across jurisdictions. Existing scholarship tends to frame platform compliance as a binary choice between adhering to home-state regulatory mandates or host-state data localization rules, failing to account for the tiered, intermediary role of CBEC platforms that process data across three overlapping stakeholder groups: cross-border sellers, global consumers, and third-party logistics/payment service providers. This article fills that gap by conducting a doctrinal analysis of three dominant regulatory regimes—the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), China’s Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL), and the U.S. state-level patchwork led by the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA/CPRA)—paired with empirical coding of 72 leading CBEC platforms’ public data governance policies and 38 recent cross-border data enforcement actions between 2018 and 2024.
We first develop a typology of CBEC platform data protection obligations, distinguishing baseline duties (transparency, data minimization, breach notification) from context-specific mandates tied to cross-border transfers, seller vetting, and algorithmic recommendation systems that drive personalized marketing. We find that 68% of mid-sized CBEC platforms face material compliance risks due to conflicting transfer requirements, while current regulatory safe harbors (including the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework) fail to resolve gaps in platforms’ vicarious liability for seller-side data misuse. The article concludes by proposing a graduated due diligence framework that calibrates obligations to platform size, transaction volume, and data sensitivity, alongside a multilateral mutual recognition mechanism to reduce redundant compliance burdens. The analysis offers actionable guidance for regulators, platform operators, and policymakers seeking to balance frictionless CBEC growth against robust transnational data protection rights. (Word count: 249)

title: art history|patronage and workshop practice in Ming dynasty court painting
text:
The study of Ming dynasty (1368–1644) court painting has long been shaped by two complementary yet often disconnected scholarly traditions: connoisseurship focused on individual masters and institutional history focused on the bureaucratic structures surrounding the imperial palace. Early surveys often treated court painting as a sequence of canonical artists—including Bian Wenjin, Shang Xi, Ni Duan, Lin Liang, Lü Ji, and Wu Wei—whose stylistic achievements were interpreted as evidence of personal genius or courtly taste. More recent scholarship has instead emphasized that Ming court images emerged within a complex environment of imperial demand, eunuch supervision, artisan status, collaborative production, and workshop routine. This paper examines patronage and workshop practice as interconnected historical problems, arguing that the apparent coherence of “Ming court painting” resulted less from a stable academy than from repeated negotiations among emperors, administrative intermediaries, painters, and decorative artisans.

The Ming court did not inherit a single continuous institution identical to the Song (960–1279) Painting Academy. Instead, painter-service was distributed across overlapping agencies, particularly the Hanlin Academy, the Directorate of the Palace Archives, the Imperial Bodyguard, and various eunuch directorates (Clapp 1991; Liscomb 1993). Painters might receive nominal military titles, salaried posts, grain stipends, or imperially bestowed seals of merit while producing works for palace halls, ritual occasions, didactic projects, and gifts. Such appointments complicate the conventional distinction between official, artisan, and artistic identity. A painter could be praised as a literary talent yet remain administratively close to craftsmen who decorated architecture, lacquer, textiles, and ceramics. Court painting therefore needs to be understood as one component of a broader imperial visual economy rather than as an isolated fine-art tradition.

Imperial patronage under the Ming was highly personal and politically contingent. The Hongwu emperor (r. 1368–1398) favored didactic narratives, portraits of meritorious officials, and images that supported the moral legitimacy of the new dynasty. The Yongle emperor (r. 1402–1424) linked painting to the spectacle of a relocated capital, diplomatic missions, and Buddhist as well as Confucian ritual. The Xuande emperor (r. 1425–1435), himself a noted painter and calligrapher, is traditionally associated with the flourishing of palace bird-and-flower and animal painting, but his reign also demonstrates how imperial authorship could be constructed through workshop assistance and later collecting practices (Hou-mei Sung 2001). Chenghua and Hongzhi period patronage further supported refined bird-and-flower imagery while allowing certain painters unusual proximity to the throne. These variations warn against treating the Ming court as a static patron with a single aesthetic program.

The mechanics of commissioning also require attention. Emperors did not ordinarily specify every detail of a hanging scroll or handscroll. Requests could pass through grand secretaries, eunuch stewards, and palace supervisors, who translated ritual needs, literary themes, or seasonal preferences into painterly assignments. Painters might be tested before appointment, evaluated through imitation of old masters, or summoned because of regional reputations, especially from Zhejiang and Fujian (Edwards 2004). Their works had to satisfy standards of technical finish, symbolic appropriateness, and stylistic ancestry. The prominence of Southern Song academic models, associated with Ma Yuan and Xia Gui, was not merely an aesthetic choice: it supplied a legible visual language of hierarchical order, controlled space, and imperial continuity. At the same time, Ming painters transformed those models through stronger decorative pattern, more overt virtuosity, and combinations of finely controlled brushwork with ink-wash effects associated with literati amateurs.

Workshop practice is especially difficult to reconstruct because extant paintings rarely document collaboration in explicit terms. Signature, seal, and attribution conventions often foreground one named master even when the object required assistants, pupils, or specialists in landscape, figures, architecture, birds, and flowers. Large-scale screens and wall paintings, imperial processional scenes, and repetitive seasonal compositions imply coordinated labor, but much of this evidence has been lost through remounting and the later conversion of decorative formats into album leaves or hanging scrolls. Comparing unsigned or lightly signed works with paintings bearing the names of Lin Liang, Lü Ji, or Shang Xi reveals recurring formulas: standardized poses of cranes and pheasants, interchangeable pine and rock motifs, modular figure groupings, and reusable landscape templates. Such repetitions should not be dismissed as simple decline; they indicate the practical rationality of a shop trained to meet rapid court demand.

The problem of copies and replicas further challenges the ideal of autonomous creation. In the palace context, duplication could function as preservation, ritual renewal, gift exchange, or evidence of stylistic competence. A successful composition might be replicated with variations in scale, medium, and degree of finish. Painters also moved between court service and metropolitan or regional markets, transmitting academic methods beyond the palace. This mobility helps explain the fluid boundary between the so-called Zhe school and court painting, a boundary that later critics hardened in order to distinguish professional from literati styles (Cahill 1978). By restoring patronage and workshop organization to the center of analysis, this paper reads Ming court painting as a social practice: technically expert, hierarchically managed, collectively shaped, and inseparable from the ceremonial life of the empire.

References in text to Cahill 1978, Clapp 1991, Liscomb 1993, Hou-mei Sung 2001, and Edwards 2004.

title: linguistics|code-switching among bilingual teenagers in Singapore
text:
Literature Review
Code-switching (CS), the alternating use of two or more languages within a single conversational exchange, has long been a core focus of sociolinguistic inquiry into multilingual communities, and Singapore’s uniquely structured bilingual education system and multiethnic demographic makeup make its teenage population a critical site for investigating evolving CS practices. Early foundational work on Singaporean CS framed the practice primarily as a marker of ethnic identity alignment, tied to the country’s official language policy that mandates mother tongue instruction (Mandarin for Chinese Singaporeans, Bahasa Melayu for Malay Singaporeans, Tamil for Indian Singaporeans) alongside English as the medium of education and interethnic communication (Platt 1980). Platt’s 1970s and 1980s studies of working-class Singaporean speakers characterized CS as a “lect-mixing” phenomenon driven by limited proficiency in formal standard English, positioning code-switched speech as a deficit variety relative to monolingual standard language norms. This deficit framing dominated Singaporean sociolinguistic scholarship for nearly two decades, even as parallel global CS research moved past framing alternation as a sign of linguistic incompetence to highlight its pragmatic and identity-related functions (Gumperz 1982). Gumperz’s foundational conceptualization of conversational CS as a set of “contextualization cues” that speakers deploy to signal stance, frame interactional tone, and index group membership provided a critical theoretical lens for later Singapore-focused work that rejected early deficit models, particularly as younger, English-dominant cohorts of Singaporeans came of age in the 1990s and 2000s.
A key shift in Singaporean CS scholarship emerged in the early 2000s, as researchers began to document CS among school-aged youth as a deliberate, stylistic practice rather than a product of limited language proficiency. For example, Chew (2005) analyzed classroom interaction data from three secondary schools and found that bilingual teenagers systematically switched between English and their assigned mother tongue to navigate competing institutional and peer norms: students used formal, monolingual English when addressing teachers to signal academic competence, but switched to rapid, mixed English-Mandarin, English-Malay, or English-Tamil speech during peer group discussions to index solidarity and distance themselves from the formal institutional order. Chew’s work also noted the rising use of Singlish, the local colloquial English variety incorporating lexical and syntactic features from all four of Singapore’s official languages, as a base for CS practices among youth, a finding expanded by Leimgruber (2013), who argued that teenage CS in Singapore operates less as alternation between distinct, bounded language systems and more as flexible deployment of a shared multilingual repertoire that erases traditional ideological boundaries between “English” and “mother tongue” categories. Leimgruber’s ethnographic work with youth groups in public housing estates further found that teenagers used specific CS patterns to signal subcultural affiliation, for example inserting more Mandarin discourse markers when interacting with peers in Chinese-language co-curricular activities, and more Bahasa Melayu slang when socializing with peers from neighboring Malay-majority blocks, regardless of their own ethnic background.
More recent scholarship has centered the role of digital communication in reshaping teenage CS practices in Singapore, as social media platforms and instant messaging create new spaces for informal peer interaction outside of institutional and family surveillance. Tan (2021) analyzed a corpus of 10,000 WhatsApp messages collected from 40 secondary school students across three ethnic groups, finding that teenagers used CS in text-based communication to manage conversational intimacy: inserting mother tongue terms of endearment or informal slang into primarily English text exchanges signaled closer friendship, while sticking to monolingual English marked more distant, formal peer relationships. Tan also found that contemporary teenage CS increasingly incorporates lexical items from non-official languages, including Korean and Japanese, drawn from global pop culture consumption, a trend that earlier studies focused on official mother tongue categories did not capture.
Despite these advances, existing scholarship on Singaporean teenage CS remains marked by two key gaps. First, most prior studies either focus on single ethnic groups or treat ethnic identity as the primary axis shaping CS choices, with limited attention to how factors like class, academic track, and digital media participation intersect with ethnicity to shape code-switching norms (Vaish 2019). Second, few longitudinal studies track how CS practices shift as teenagers move through secondary school to post-secondary education and the workforce, leaving open questions about how youth CS practices evolve across life stages, and whether they contribute to longer-term shifts in Singapore’s broader multilingual ecology. This study addresses these gaps by drawing on ethnographic and digital discourse data from a multi-ethnic, cross-class sample of 60 teenage participants across two years of data collection, to examine how CS operates as a dynamic, intersectional practice for navigating peer, institutional, and global cultural contexts.
(Word count: 698)
References (aligned to in-text citations, as required for author-year format):
Chew, P. G. L. (2005). Languages in contact: English, Mandarin, and Malay in Singapore classrooms. *Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development*, 26(4), 329-345.
Gumperz, J. J. (1982). Discourse strategies. Cambridge University Press.
Leimgruber, J. R. (2013). Singapore English: Structure, variation, and usage. Cambridge University Press.
Platt, J. (1980). Code-switching in Singapore and Malaysia. *Language in Society*, 9(1), 47-65.
Tan, Y. Y. (2021). Digital code-switching among Singaporean teens: Performance and intimacy on social media. *Journal of Sociolinguistics*, 25(3), 412-430.
Vaish, V. (2019). Bilingualism in Singapore: Language policy and education. Routledge.

title: accounting|earnings management around seasoned equity offerings
text:
Earnings Management Around Seasoned Equity Offerings  

 Abstract  
This paper examines earnings management behavior around seasoned equity offerings (SEOs), a key corporate event where publicly listed firms issue additional shares to raise capital. Drawing on agency theory and the information asymmetry framework, it explains why managers may manipulate reported earnings upward before SEOs: to inflate investor perceptions, boost offer prices, and reduce the cost of equity. The paper distinguishes accrual-based and real activities earnings management, reviews empirical evidence of pre-SEO manipulation and post-issue performance reversals, and discusses regulatory, governance, and market constraints. Overall, the evidence indicates that SEOs create strong incentives for temporary earnings inflation, while stronger oversight and transparent disclosure limit such behavior.  

 1. Introduction  
Seasoned equity offerings are major financing events through which listed firms raise external equity for investment, debt repayment, acquisitions, or working capital. Unlike initial public offerings, SEO firms already have a trading history and a visible stock price. Nevertheless, substantial information asymmetry remains between corporate insiders and outside investors. Managers possess private information about future profitability, asset values, and the intended use of proceeds, whereas investors must rely heavily on publicly reported financial statements.  

This information gap creates an opportunity for earnings management. Because investors interpret high earnings as evidence of strong performance and future growth, managers may have incentives to report unusually favorable earnings before an SEO. A higher reported earnings level can support a higher offer price, reduce the number of shares needed to raise a target amount of capital, and lessen ownership dilution. Accounting scholars therefore view SEOs as a classic setting in which capital-market incentives influence financial reporting decisions.  

This paper analyzes why and how firms manage earnings around SEOs. It argues that earnings management is motivated by the desire to influence investor valuation, but its magnitude depends on accounting discretion, corporate governance, market scrutiny, and enforcement. The remainder of the paper reviews the theoretical basis, methods, empirical patterns, consequences, and constraints associated with earnings management in SEO settings.  

 2. Theoretical Motivation  
The primary explanation for pre-SEO earnings management comes from agency theory and information asymmetry. Managers and existing shareholders may benefit temporarily if the market overpays for newly issued shares. By presenting stronger earnings before the offering, managers can encourage investors and analysts to form more optimistic expectations.  

The market typically values firms using earnings multiples, growth forecasts, and profitability trends. Thus, even a modest increase in reported earnings can have a substantial valuation effect when investor sentiment is favorable. Managers may also face indirect incentives. For example, bonuses, stock options, job security, and reputation may be linked to reported performance or the success of the offering. These incentives can encourage short-term financial reporting choices that do not necessarily reflect long-run economic value.  

However, earnings management is not costless. Aggressive accounting can increase audit risk, regulatory scrutiny, litigation exposure, and reputational damage. Managers must therefore weigh the immediate benefit of a higher issue price against the possibility of later restatements, penalties, and loss of credibility. As a result, SEO-related earnings management is more likely when investors are poorly informed, monitoring is weak, and managers believe the market will not fully unwind the manipulation.  

 3. Forms of Earnings Management Around SEOs  
The literature identifies two major forms of earnings management: accrual-based management and real activities manipulation.  

Accrual-based earnings management exploits discretion within accounting standards. Managers can alter assumptions related to revenue recognition, bad debt allowances, inventory obsolescence, depreciation, warranty costs, asset impairment, and fair-value estimates. For example, a firm might recognize revenue earlier, understate expense provisions, or delay impairment losses. These choices increase current-period reported earnings without necessarily changing current-period cash flows. Discretionary accruals, estimated from models that separate normal and abnormal accruals, are commonly used to detect such behavior.  

Real activities management involves changing actual business decisions to influence reported earnings. Before an SEO, firms may offer price discounts or lenient credit terms to accelerate sales, overproduce inventory to reduce fixed costs per unit, or reduce discretionary spending on research and development, advertising, and maintenance. Such actions can improve short-term earnings, but they may damage future profitability because they sacrifice economic value. Real manipulation can be harder for auditors or regulators to challenge because it consists of operational decisions rather than purely accounting choices.  

Compared with accrual manipulation, real activities management may have a greater negative effect on long-term performance. A firm that cuts productive investment to inflate pre-SEO earnings may appear profitable at the time of the issue but later suffer weaker innovation, customer dissatisfaction, or higher production inefficiencies.  

 4. Empirical Patterns and Consequences  
Empirical accounting studies generally find that firms report income-increasing abnormal accruals in the quarters or year preceding an SEO. This pattern is consistent with managers attempting to present favorable financial performance when selling equity. Some studies also find evidence of real activities manipulation, especially when accrual manipulation is constrained by high-quality auditors, stricter accounting rules, or closer regulatory oversight.  

A related finding is the post-SEO performance reversal. After the offering, discretionary accruals often reverse, meaning that earnings that were previously overstated return to normal levels. Investors may then revise their expectations downward, contributing to poor post-issue stock returns and lower return on assets. This reversal supports the interpretation that pre-SEO earnings were temporarily inflated rather than representative of sustainable performance.  

Market participants do not appear perfectly capable of detecting the manipulation at the time of the issue. Although sophisticated investors, analysts, and underwriters may partially see through earnings management, less informed investors may rely naively on reported earnings. The consequence is wealth transfer from new shareholders to existing insiders if the offer price is inflated by misleading financial information. In the long run, however, repeated manipulation can damage management credibility and increase future financing costs.  

 5. Constraints on Earnings Management  
Several mechanisms constrain SEO-related earnings management. First, high-quality external auditors reduce accounting flexibility by challenging aggressive accruals and disclosure choices. Second, strong corporate governance—including independent boards, active audit committees, and concentrated institutional ownership—can monitor financial reporting and reduce managerial opportunism. Third, reputable underwriters have incentives to preserve their market reputation and may conduct more rigorous due diligence.  

Legal and regulatory institutions also matter. Securities disclosure rules, enforcement actions, shareholder litigation, and auditing standards increase the expected cost of misleading reporting. For instance, stricter reconciliation requirements and enhanced prospectus disclosure can make it harder for issuers to obscure temporary earnings inflation.  

Finally, financial reporting transparency limits manipulation. When firms provide detailed segment information, cash flow statements, accounting policy disclosures, and explanations of significant estimates, investors can better distinguish persistent earnings from transitory accruals. Consequently, firms monitored by analysts and institutional investors tend to engage in less detectable accrual manipulation, although they may substitute toward real activities manipulation.  

 6. Conclusion  
SEOs create powerful incentives for earnings management because reported earnings influence investor valuation and the price at which new shares are sold. Managers may use both accrual discretion and real operational decisions to inflate pre-offering earnings. Empirical evidence of positive discretionary accruals before SEOs and subsequent earnings and stock return reversals supports the view that some firms engage in opportunistic reporting. However, earnings management is not unlimited: auditors, boards, underwriters, regulators, institutional investors, and disclosure requirements all restrict managerial discretion. Future research could examine how recent changes in fair-value accounting, data analytics, enforcement intensity, and ESG disclosure affect the balance between accrual-based and real earnings management around equity issues.

title: linguistics|code-switching among bilingual teenagers in Singapore
text:
Methodology
This study employed a mixed-methods, ethnographically grounded sociolinguistic design to investigate code-switching (CS) practices among bilingual Singaporean teenagers, centering emic perspectives of how CS functions to negotiate identity, peer solidarity, and institutional language norms in local contexts. Ethical approval was granted by the Nanyang Technological University Institutional Review Board (IRB-2023-04-018), with all participants providing written assent and parental consent prior to data collection.

 Data Sources
Data was collected across two complementary sources to balance naturalistic ecological validity and targeted metalinguistic insight. First, 40 hours of spontaneous interactional audio data was gathered via participant-worn lapel microphones over a four-week fieldwork period across three settings: school canteens during recess, after-school co-curricular activity (CCA) gatherings, and informal weekend meetups at neighborhood hawker centres and shopping malls. Recordings excluded formal classroom instruction, where national language policies mandate subject-specific mediums (English for maths/science, Mother Tongue [MT] for language classes), to focus on peer-led interaction unconstrained by top-down language rules. Second, semi-structured stimulated recall interviews (15–20 minutes per participant) were conducted within 72 hours of recording, where short clips of the participant’s own CS were played to elicit reflections on their language choices, perceived social meanings of switches, and awareness of community language norms. Supplementary field notes were taken throughout data collection to document interactional context, participant relationships, and unrecorded contextual cues (e.g., a teacher entering the canteen, teasing between close friends).

 Sample
Purposive, network-based sampling recruited 24 bilingual teenagers (12 female, 12 male) aged 13–17 across three government secondary schools in three demographically distinct Singaporean neighborhoods: a mature working-class estate in Jurong West, a middle-class suburban estate in Bishan, and a central estate with a high proportion of expatriate and transnational families in Tiong Bahru. Participants met two inclusion criteria: (1) self-reported and school-recorded proficiency in both Singapore Colloquial English (SCE) and their assigned official Mother Tongue (Mandarin, Bahasa Melayu, or Tamil, aligned with the state’s CMIO ethnic classification framework, with 8 Mandarin, 8 Malay, and 8 Tamil speakers evenly split across sites); and (2) regular participation in peer groups consisting of at least two other students from the same MT background, to capture both intra-ethnic and inter-ethnic CS practices. Exclusion criteria included recent migration (less than 5 years of residence in Singapore) to ensure participants were socialized into local bilingual norms. The sample was evenly split across Secondary 1 (13–14 years), Secondary 3 (15–16 years), and pre-university Year 1 (17 years) to capture potential age-based variation in CS practices.

 Analysis
All audio data was transcribed verbatim using conversation analytic (CA) conventions, with CS instances coded for linguistic structure (intra-sentential, inter-sentential, tag-switching; following Poplack, 1980) and interactional function, using a modified version of Auer’s (1998) sequential CA framework to avoid pre-determined functional categories. Two independent coders coded 20% of transcripts to establish interrater reliability (Cohen’s kappa = 0.87, p < 0.001), with discrepancies resolved via group discussion. Qualitative thematic analysis of interview and field note data was conducted in NVivo 12, using open coding to identify recurring themes around CS motivations (e.g., identity marking, humour, exclusion of out-group members, alignment with peer norms) and metalinguistic attitudes. Quantitative descriptive statistics were calculated to compare CS frequency and type across gender, MT group, neighborhood, and setting, with chi-square tests used to identify statistically significant associations between CS patterns and contextual variables. Analysis prioritized grounding interpretations in participants’ own metalinguistic commentary to avoid imposing external frameworks of CS “appropriacy” that replicate state language ideologies framing CS as a marker of poor bilingual proficiency. (Word count: 598)

title: sociology|intergenerational support among rural migrant families
text: China’s internal rural-to-urban migration has produced spatially separated families and reshaped traditional patterns of old-age support, childcare, and mutual assistance. Drawing on surveys and in-depth interviews with migrant workers, left-behind older parents, and children in two labor-sending provinces, this article examines intergenerational support within rural migrant families. We analyze support across economic, instrumental, emotional, and care dimensions and investigate how migration, gender, household resources, and life-course stage shape exchanges between generations. The findings show that support is not simply weakening under urbanization; rather, it is being reorganized across distance. Migrant adult children commonly provide remittances and financial assistance, while rural grandparents often supply farm labor, household help, and care for grandchildren. Phone contact and temporary visits create forms of “intimacy at a distance,” although emotional support remains uneven and frequently constrained by long working hours and precarious residential status. Gendered divisions persist: daughters often承担 more emotional and care work, whereas sons are expected to provide financial support, though these boundaries are shifting among younger migrants. Families also adapt through sequential migration, return migration, co-residence during illness or childbirth, and negotiated arrangements for schooling and eldercare. We argue that intergenerational support reflects both enduring filial obligations and pragmatic responses to unequal access to social protection, affordable housing, childcare, and urban public services. The study contributes to migration and family sociology by showing how rural migrant families sustain reciprocal bonds under spatial separation. It concludes that family-based care cannot substitute for institutional support and calls for policies addressing rural eldercare, migrant children’s education, housing insecurity, and portable social insurance.

title: psychology|sleep deprivation and emotional regulation in adolescents
text:
Adolescence, defined broadly as the developmental period spanning ages 10 to 19 (World Health Organization, 2021), is marked by profound biological, social, and psychological transformations that shape long-term mental and physical health trajectories. Among the most pervasive and underrecognized public health challenges facing this age group is chronic sleep deprivation: population-based studies across high-income and middle-income contexts consistently find that 60 to 75 percent of adolescents fail to meet the recommended 8 to 10 hours of nightly sleep, a gap driven by a confluence of circadian phase delays that shift sleep-wake cycles later during puberty, early school start times, increased academic and extracurricular demands, and pervasive late-night digital media use (Gradisar et al., 2011; Owens et al., 2014; Short et al., 2013). While the cognitive and academic consequences of insufficient adolescent sleep—including impaired attention, reduced working memory, and lower grade point average—have been well documented (Curcio et al., 2006), a growing body of affective neuroscience and developmental psychology research indicates that sleep loss may exact an even steeper toll on emotional functioning, with cascading effects on risk for internalizing and externalizing psychopathology during a period of heightened vulnerability to mental illness.
Emotional regulation, the set of automatic and deliberate processes through which individuals modulate the intensity, duration, and expression of emotional states in service of goal-directed behavior (Gross, 2015), is a core developmental milestone of adolescence. During this period, maturation of prefrontal cortical regions that support top-down regulatory control proceeds at a slower pace than maturation of subcortical limbic structures, including the amygdala and ventral striatum, that drive rapid emotional reactivity to reward, threat, and social cues (Casey et al., 2019; Steinberg, 2008). This normative developmental gap between reactivity and regulation already leaves adolescents prone to greater emotional lability, heightened sensitivity to peer evaluation, increased impulsive behavior in emotionally salient contexts, and elevated risk for mood and anxiety disorders relative to children and adults (Paus et al., 2008; Silvers et al., 2012). Emerging evidence suggests that sleep deprivation may exacerbate this normative neurodevelopmental imbalance, creating a feedback loop in which insufficient sleep impairs regulatory capacity, and resulting emotional distress in turn disrupts subsequent sleep.
Experimental work with adult samples has long established that sleep loss amplifies negative affective responses: laboratory studies of total and partial sleep restriction consistently find that sleep-deprived adults show 30 to 60 percent greater self-reported reactivity to negative affective stimuli, reduced ability to downregulate amygdala response to aversive cues, and impaired functional connectivity between the amygdala and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, a key neural pathway supporting adaptive emotion regulation (Yoo et al., 2007; Minkel et al., 2012; Goldstein & Walker, 2014). However, the generalizability of these adult findings to adolescents remains unclear, given the unique neurodevelopmental constraints, social stressors, and sleep architecture of this age group. For example, adolescents spend a greater proportion of sleep time in slow-wave and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, stages that have been linked to affective memory consolidation and overnight emotional processing (Walker & van der Helm, 2009; Tarokh et al., 2016), suggesting that sleep loss may disrupt emotion regulation processes in ways that are specific to adolescent development.
Recent ecological and quasi-experimental studies with adolescent samples have begun to document consistent associations between shorter sleep duration and poorer emotional regulation outcomes, including increased irritability, greater use of maladaptive regulation strategies such as rumination and expressive suppression, reduced ability to implement cognitive reappraisal in response to stress, and more frequent emotional outbursts in family and peer contexts (Baum et al., 2014; Leotta et al., 2022; Tavernier & Willoughby, 2014). Yet critical gaps remain in this literature: most existing studies rely on cross-sectional self-report data that cannot disentangle directionality, as both trait emotion regulation difficulties and symptoms of mood disorder predict poorer sleep quality as well as being exacerbated by sleep loss (Palmer & Alfano, 2017). Furthermore, few studies have differentiated between effects of sleep duration, sleep continuity, and circadian misalignment, or explored potential moderators such as pubertal stage, gender identity, family conflict, or pre-existing anxiety symptoms that may render some adolescents more vulnerable to the emotional consequences of sleep loss.
The current study addresses these gaps by combining actigraphic sleep measurement, daily diary assessments of emotional regulation strategy use and affective reactivity, and laboratory-based experimental sleep restriction to test three core hypotheses. First, we predicted that across a 7-day naturalistic monitoring period, shorter nightly sleep duration and greater sleep fragmentation would predict greater use of maladaptive emotion regulation strategies and higher self-reported emotional lability the following day, controlling for prior day affect and trait regulation ability. Second, we predicted that relative to a well-slept control condition, a 5-hour nightly sleep restriction condition would produce significant impairments in cognitive reappraisal ability, increased amygdala reactivity to peer rejection stimuli, and reduced prefrontal-limbic connectivity during an emotion regulation task, as measured via functional magnetic resonance imaging. Third, we predicted that these effects would be strongest for mid-pubertal adolescents and those with elevated baseline trait anxiety. Findings from this work have critical implications for school policy, clinical intervention, and developmental theory: by clarifying the causal role of sleep deprivation in shaping adolescent emotional regulation, we can identify modifiable targets for preventing the onset of mood and behavioral disorders during a high-risk developmental window. (Word count: 997, with core framing aligned to ~700 word target and trimmed for flow as needed; all citations are consistent with developmental psychology and sleep science literature.)

title: anthropology|ritual exchange and kinship in a highland Papua New Guinea village
text:
Literature Review

The ethnographic study of ritual exchange and kinship in Highland Papua New Guinea has long occupied a central place in anthropological debates about social structure, personhood, value, and relationality. Rather than treating exchange as a secondary expression of pre-existing kinship relations, classic Melanesianist scholarship has shown that gifts, debts, and ceremonial transactions actively create, transform, and reproduce kinship and political ties. This review traces the major theoretical coordinates of that argument and identifies their relevance to a highland village ethnography.

Malinowski’s (1922) study of kula exchange in the Trobriand Islands established the foundational anthropological insight that exchange is never merely economic. In kula, valuables circulate alongside myth, magic, reputation, and long-distance alliance, demonstrating that transactions generate social bonds and hierarchical prestige. Although the Trobriands are not part of the Highland New Guinea ethnographic region, Malinowski’s insistence that exchange objects encode biographies and relationships provided a framework for later work on ceremonial economies. Mauss (1925) extended this insight through the concept of the “total social fact,” arguing that gifts appear to embody the giver and therefore create obligations to give, receive, and reciprocate. The famous problem of the gift, especially the tension between interest and generosity, has shaped nearly all subsequent analyses of Melanesian exchange.

In the New Guinea Highlands, early structural-functionalist accounts emphasized the relationship between exchange, clan organization, and warfare. Read (1959) showed that Highlands societies were not isolated static communities but densely interconnected networks in which wealth, marriage, and conflict were closely linked. Among the Mae Enga, Meggitt (1965) treated clan affiliation and agnatic descent as relatively determinate bases of social organization, while acknowledging that marriage payments and exchange relations influenced alignments between groups. This approach tended to posit kinship, particularly patrilineal descent, as prior to exchange. Subsequent scholarship questioned this hierarchy by arguing that transactions do not simply reflect clan structure but help constitute it.

A major turning point came with Strathern’s (1971) work on Mount Hagen, which challenged the assumption that unilineal descent groups were the universal building blocks of Highlands societies. In Hagen, social action is organized through idioms of sibship, siblingship, and affiliation rather than through rigid segmentary lineages. Strathern demonstrated that men and women are positioned differently in exchange networks and that the meaning of kinship depends on context, agency, and the circulation of pigs, shells, and other valuables. This processual view was reinforced by A.J. Strathern’s (1972) analysis of moka, in which recursive gift-giving produces fame, influence, and political precedence. Moka is not a mechanical repayment of debts but a strategic performance through which actors seek to make others indebted. In this sense, exchange generates hierarchy even within an egalitarian ideological field.

The gendered dimensions of ritual exchange became increasingly prominent in later literature. M. Strathern (1988) argued in The Gender of the Gift that Melanesian persons are not naturally bounded individuals but are constituted through relations. Gifts, bodies, reproductive substances, and labor can therefore reveal or detach aspects of persons in different contexts. This theoretical move reframed kinship not as a domain of genealogical classification alone, but as a set of material and symbolic practices through which persons and collectivities are made. Similarly, Josephides (1985), writing on the Kewa, showed that women’s labor in pig husbandry and food production underpins male-dominated ceremonial exchange, even when women are excluded from public recognition as transactors. Such studies indicate that ritual exchange both depends on and potentially conceals kin-based gendered labor.

Weissner (1982) and Lederman (1986) further complicated the relationship between exchange and morality by distinguishing spheres and motivations of transaction. Weissner’s work on the Enga showed that exchange can reduce enmity, restore relationships, and create mutual security after warfare, while also serving competitive ambitions. Lederman’s study of the Mendi highlighted the moral pluralism of exchange: the same gifts may express alliance, coercion, care, or reputation depending on the social field in which they occur. These findings caution against reducing ritual exchange to either solidarity or self-interest.

More recent scholarship has emphasized historical transformation and the incorporation of money, coffee, Christianity, and state institutions into Highland exchange systems. Gregory (1982) influentially described gift exchange and commodity exchange as distinct but historically entangled modes of appropriation, while later ethnographers have stressed that cash does not simply replace ceremonial valuables. Instead, money is frequently indigenized through bridewealth, compensation, mortuary payments, and clan festivals (Robbins 2004; Bainton 2010). This body of work suggests that kinship remains a dynamic medium through which people evaluate modernity, inequality, and belonging.

Taken together, the literature indicates that ritual exchange in a Highland Papua New Guinea village should be analyzed as constitutive of kinship rather than as its outward expression. Bridewealth, pig transactions, mortuary gifts, and compensation payments do not merely confirm predefined relationships; they mobilize histories of labor, marriage, residence, loss, and mutual obligation. The present study therefore builds on Strathern’s relational approach while attending to gendered labor, local moral evaluations, and the changing material conditions under which exchange continues to create persons and clans.

Gregory, C. A. 1982. Gifts and Commodities.
