title: musicology|improvisation practices in early jazz recordings
text:
Discussion
The close analysis of 112 surviving recordings made in New Orleans, Chicago, and New York between 1917 and 1927 challenges the longstanding popular framing of early jazz as unstructured, collective “free improvisation” untethered to pre-compositional planning. Perhaps most notably, the high degree of consistency across alternate takes of the same number—documented here for the first time for 37 tracks held in the Rodgers and Hammerstein Archives of Recorded Sound—suggests that “improvisation” in this era operated as a set of shared, rule-governed practices rather than unplanned spontaneous invention. For example, across the three surviving takes of King Oliver’s Creole Jazz Band’s 1923 *Dippermouth Blues*, Oliver’s celebrated cornet solo varies by only 12 notes out of 108 across all performances, with the vast majority of deviations consisting of rhythmic anticipations or subtle timbral shifts rather than wholesale melodic reinvention. This finding aligns with Paul Berliner’s earlier work on mid-20th century jazz improvisation as a process of “formulaic variation,” but pushes that framework back 30 years, complicating narratives that frame early jazz as a “primitive” precursor to the more sophisticated solo improvisation of the swing era. It is worth noting, however, that this consistency may be partially an artifact of the recording context: studio time was prohibitively expensive in the 1920s, and bands typically rehearsed arrangements extensively before cutting sides, a constraint that likely discouraged the kind of risky, open-ended improvisation that might have occurred in dance hall or speakeasy sets.

It is also important to push back against the binary that has structured much prior scholarship on early jazz: that of collective improvisation versus individual soloing. The corpus analysis demonstrates that the boundary between these two modes was far more porous than has been acknowledged. In 68% of the recordings sampled, individual “solos” were accompanied by countermelodies improvised by the clarinet or trombone players that did not appear on published stock arrangements of the same tunes, and which also varied across alternate takes. For instance, on the 1926 recording of Louis Armstrong and His Hot Five’s *Heebie Jeebies*, Kid Ory’s trombone line behind Armstrong’s scat vocal shifts from a simple root-movement bass line on the first take to a contrapuntal response to Armstrong’s melodic phrases on the second, even as Armstrong’s vocal remains largely consistent. This suggests that collective improvisation did not disappear with the rise of the star soloist in the mid-1920s, as is often claimed, but rather shifted to a supporting role that has been largely invisible in prior analyses focused on lead lines.

These findings are limited, of course, by the inherent bias of the surviving archival record. The vast majority of early jazz recordings were made by white-owned record companies for predominantly white, middle-class audiences, and many bands were pressured to simplify arrangements or minimize improvised content to fit the three-minute runtime of 78rpm discs, or to align with racist stereotypes of Black jazz as “unruly” or “unrefined.” We have no way of documenting the improvisational practices of the dozens of Black New Orleans bands that never recorded, or the extended improvisations that likely took place in unrecorded live sets that could stretch for 10 minutes or more. Additionally, the reliance on lead sheets and stock arrangements as a point of comparison risks framing deviation from written notation as the sole marker of improvisation, when in fact many early jazz musicians could not read notation, and learned parts by ear; some elements that appear “improvised” on record may in fact have been memorized, collectively worked-out arrangements that were never written down.

 Conclusion
While this study cannot resolve longstanding debates about the “origins” of jazz improvisation, it does offer concrete evidence that the improvisational practices of early recorded jazz were far more systematic, collaborative, and rooted in shared formulae than popular narratives of spontaneous genius have allowed. The close alignment of solo lines across alternate takes, and the persistence of collective contrapuntal improvisation behind high-profile soloists, suggests that early jazz musicians balanced individual creativity with collective accountability to a shared set of melodic, rhythmic, and structural norms that were specific to the recording studio context of the 1920s. There is little evidence here for the claim, common in 1950s jazz criticism, that early jazz was a “raw” or untutored form of expression; instead, the recordings reveal a sophisticated practice of structured variation that required extensive rehearsal and deep familiarity with bandmates’ stylistic vocabularies.

Future work would do well to move beyond the narrow corpus of canonical recordings by Oliver, Armstrong, and the Original Dixieland Jazz Band to analyze the understudied sides recorded by all-Black women’s bands, territory bands, and regional groups that operated outside of the New York-Chicago recording axis, as well as oral history accounts from musicians active in the period that may shed light on unrecorded performance practices. For now, though, this analysis makes clear that the line between composition and improvisation was no more rigid in early jazz than it is in many other oral musical traditions: the “improvised” passages on these landmark recordings were not unplanned, but rather the product of a collective, iterative creative process that unfolded across rehearsals, live performances, and multiple recording takes. To frame them as purely spontaneous is to erase the deliberate craft, and the collaborative labor, that went into making some of the most influential recordings in 20th century popular music. (Word count: 712)

title: accounting|earnings management around seasoned equity offerings
text:
Methodology
 3.1 Data Sources
This study constructs a multi-source merged dataset to examine earnings management behaviors around seasoned equity offerings (SEOs), drawing on three core authoritative databases widely used in capital market accounting research, supplemented by manual verification to ensure data accuracy. First, SEO event data are obtained from the China Stock Market & Accounting Research (CSMAR) Database’s Seasoned Equity Offering Sub-database, which records full details of equity issuance events for A-share listed firms in China, including announcement dates, issuance execution dates, actual raised capital, offering type (public versus private placement), and regulatory approval status. Second, firm-level financial data, corporate governance characteristics, and market trading data are extracted from CSMAR’s Financial Statements Database, Corporate Governance Database, and Stock Market Trading Database, respectively. These data cover core accounting items required to calculate accrual-based and real activity earnings management proxies, as well as control variables such as firm size, leverage, and board structure. Third, industry classification codes (based on the 2012 China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) industry classification) and annual risk-free return rates are sourced from the RESSET Financial Research Database to support industry-level adjustment in empirical calculations.
To mitigate data bias from missing or misclassified records, all SEO events are cross-checked against official issuance announcements published on the CNINFO website (the designated information disclosure platform for Chinese listed firms). Firms with inconsistent event dates or incomplete issuance information across databases are excluded after manual verification. All continuous variables are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles to reduce the impact of extreme outliers, and all financial data are denominated in Chinese yuan (RMB) to eliminate exchange rate interference.

 3.2 Sample Selection
The initial sample includes all non-financial A-share listed firms that completed SEOs between January 2010 and December 2022, a period covering multiple regulatory policy cycles for equity refinancing in China, including the 2014 new refinancing rules and the 2020 registration-based reform for private placements. The sample period is selected to avoid structural breaks from the 2007 accounting standards convergence and the 2008 global financial crisis, while capturing sufficient cross-sectional and time-series variation in SEO activities.
Following standard screening procedures in earnings management and SEO literature (Cohen & Zarowin, 2010; Kothari et al., 2005), the sample is filtered according to the following criteria: (1) Exclude firms operating in the financial and insurance industries (CSRC industry code J) due to their distinct accounting reporting rules and regulatory capital requirements; (2) Exclude firms designated as “special treatment” (ST/*ST) in the two years before or after the SEO, as these firms face delisting pressure and have distorted earnings incentives unrelated to general SEO motivations; (3) Exclude firms with missing core financial data (e.g., total assets, operating revenue, net income) required to calculate earnings management metrics in the three years surrounding the SEO (year t-1, t, t+1, where year t is the SEO issuance year); (4) Exclude firms that conducted multiple SEOs within a three-year window to avoid overlapping event periods that would confound the measurement of pre- and post-issuance earnings management; (5) Exclude initial public offering (IPO) firms with less than 12 months of trading history before the SEO announcement, as their accrual estimation models lack sufficient pre-listing data.
After applying these filters, the final sample consists of 2,147 firm-year observations corresponding to 1,089 unique SEO events, comprising 217 public offerings and 872 private placements. For comparative analysis, a matched control sample of non-SEO firms is constructed via one-to-one propensity score matching (PSM), matching on industry, fiscal year, firm size, and return on assets in the pre-SEO period, to isolate earnings management specifically associated with SEO events rather than common time or industry trends.

 3.3 Empirical Analysis Strategy
The study measures both accrual-based earnings management (AEM) and real activity earnings management (REM), as SEO firms may substitute between the two strategies based on regulatory scrutiny and accounting flexibility. AEM is proxied by performance-matched discretionary accruals calculated using the modified Jones model (Dechow et al., 1995), estimated cross-sectionally for each industry-year with at least 15 observations. Specifically, total accruals are regressed on the change in revenue adjusted for the change in accounts receivable and gross property, plant, and equipment, with all variables scaled by lagged total assets; the residual from the regression represents discretionary accruals, with higher values indicating greater income-increasing AEM.
REM is measured following Roychowdhury (2006) through three individual proxies: abnormal operating cash flow (from aggressive price discounts to boost sales), abnormal production costs (from overproduction to spread fixed costs over more units), and abnormal discretionary expenses (from cutting R&D, advertising, and administrative expenses to inflate short-term earnings). A composite REM index is constructed as the sum of negative abnormal operating cash flow, positive abnormal production costs, and negative abnormal discretionary expenses, with higher values indicating more severe income-increasing real earnings manipulation.
The empirical analysis proceeds in three stages. First, univariate tests compare the mean and median levels of AEM and REM between SEO firms and matched non-SEO firms across the pre-SEO year (t-1), SEO year (t), and post-SEO year (t+1), using t-tests and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests to assess statistical significance. Second, multivariate panel regressions with year and industry fixed effects are estimated to test whether SEO firms exhibit significantly higher earnings management in the pre-issuance period, controlling for standard determinants including firm size, leverage, market-to-book ratio, return on assets, audit quality (Big 4 auditor indicator), ownership concentration, and board independence. Standard errors are clustered at the firm level to address heteroskedasticity and within-firm serial correlation. Third, cross-sectional heterogeneity analyses are conducted by splitting the sample along offering type (public vs. private placement), regulatory regime (approval-based vs. registration-based period), and external monitoring intensity (institutional ownership and analyst coverage), to explore how institutional and firm characteristics moderate the relation between SEOs and earnings management. Robustness checks include alternative earnings management metrics (performance-adjusted Jones model and Stubben’s revenue discretionary model), placebo tests using pseudo-SEO dates, and instrumental variable regression to address potential endogeneity from unobserved firm characteristics. (Word count: 598)

title: journalism and media studies|local newspaper closures and civic participation
text:
Abstract
Over the past two decades, 25% of U.S. local newspapers have closed, leaving more than 2,000 communities as “news deserts” with no dedicated local news outlet. While prior scholarship has documented correlations between newspaper closures and declines in civic engagement, most studies rely on cross-sectional data that fails to disentangle causal direction or capture heterogeneous impacts across demographic and geographic groups. This article addresses that gap by analyzing a 15-year panel dataset (2008–2023) of 3,200 U.S. counties, combining administrative records of newspaper closures, voter turnout data, municipal meeting attendance logs, local election candidate filings, and 42 semi-structured interviews with residents, local officials, and remaining news workers in 12 matched pairs of counties (half with a closure, half without) across rural, suburban, and urban contexts.
We find that newspaper closures reduce municipal election turnout by 3.8 percentage points on average, with effects twice as large in low-income rural counties, and reduce competitive local races by 29%. These impacts are not immediate: they emerge 2–3 years post-closure, as remaining outlets (digital startups, hyperlocal blogs, and regional papers) fail to fill coverage gaps for municipal governance, school board decisions, and local candidate profiles. Interviews reveal that closures erode shared civic information ecosystems, enabling misinformation about local issues and reducing perceived accountability of elected officials. Contrary to assumptions that digital news substitutes for print, we find that digital-only local outlets reach 60% fewer residents in closure-affected counties, particularly among older and low-literacy populations.
These findings advance theories of media ecology and civic infrastructure, demonstrating that local newspapers function as irreplaceable “civic glue” whose loss deepens participatory inequities. We conclude by discussing policy implications, including subsidies for local news and support for community-led news models, to mitigate democratic erosion in news deserts. (Word count: 249)

title: international relations|small-state hedging strategies in Southeast Asia
text:
Small-State Hedging Strategies in Southeast Asia: Navigating Great Power Competition in the 21st Century

The return of great power competition between the United States and China has fundamentally transformed the strategic landscape of Southeast Asia, presenting small and medium-sized states in the region with unprecedented diplomatic, economic, and security challenges. Unlike the bipolar structure of the Cold War, contemporary rivalry unfolds amid deep economic interdependence, creating a strategic environment characterized by what many scholars describe as "complex multipolarity" or "competitive interdependence" (Goh 2019; Kuik 2021). In this context, Southeast Asian states have largely eschewed formal bandwagoning with or balancing against either major power, instead pursuing nuanced approaches that combine elements of cooperation, competition, and risk mitigation. These approaches, broadly categorized as hedging strategies, have become the defining feature of regional foreign policy and represent a significant departure from traditional alliance patterns observed in other regions.

Hedging as a concept in international relations theory emerged in the early 2000s as scholars sought to explain the behavior of secondary states facing uncertainty about future power distributions and intentions. While early formulations by Medeiros (2005) and Goh (2005) focused primarily on East Asian responses to China's rise, subsequent literature has refined the concept to encompass a broader spectrum of strategic behaviors. Kuik (2008, 2016) has provided perhaps the most influential definition, characterizing hedging as behavior that keeps multiple policy options open while cultivating a middle position between opposing powers, thereby avoiding the need to choose sides under conditions of high uncertainty and high stakes. This definition distinguishes hedging from both balancing and bandwagoning, which represent clearer choices to counter or align with a threatening power respectively.

Southeast Asia provides particularly fertile ground for studying hedging due to the region's unique combination of strategic vulnerabilities and diplomatic agency. The ten member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) vary considerably in size, economic development, military capabilities, and historical relationships with external powers, yet they share fundamental characteristics of small states: limited material capabilities relative to major powers, high levels of economic openness, and acute vulnerability to external shocks (Anwar 2020). These structural conditions would traditionally predict either balancing through external alignment or bandwagoning with the dominant power. Instead, Southeast Asian states have demonstrated remarkable strategic creativity in developing policy portfolios that allow them to engage multiple powers simultaneously across different issue areas.

The empirical manifestations of hedging in Southeast Asia are diverse and context-specific. Economically, virtually all regional states have deepened trade and investment ties with China while simultaneously pursuing economic agreements with the United States, Japan, and other partners through frameworks such as the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) and the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF) (Solingen 2021). In the security domain, countries like Singapore and the Philippines maintain security cooperation with Washington while developing varying degrees of defense diplomacy with Beijing, whereas Indonesia and Malaysia have emphasized non-alignment and "independent and active" foreign policies while modernizing their military capabilities (Laksmana 2020). Institutionally, ASEAN centrality serves as a collective hedging mechanism, providing a multilateral framework that socializes major powers into regional norms while preventing either from achieving exclusive dominance (Ba 2009; Eaton & Stubbs 2023).

Despite substantial scholarly attention, significant debates persist regarding the nature, effectiveness, and future trajectory of small-state hedging. Critics argue that the concept has become overly elastic, encompassing virtually any foreign policy behavior short of outright alignment and thereby losing analytical precision (Lim & Cooper 2017). Others question the sustainability of hedging as US-China competition intensifies, suggesting that mounting pressure over issues such as Taiwan, the South China Sea, and technological decoupling may force Southeast Asian states into increasingly difficult choices (Chen 2022). Furthermore, existing studies have been criticized for treating Southeast Asian states as largely reactive to great power dynamics rather than proactive actors with their own regional ambitions and domestic political imperatives (Aspinall & Muhtadi 2022).

This paper contributes to these debates by examining hedging strategies as dynamic, evolving responses shaped by both international structural pressures and domestic political calculations. It argues that Southeast Asian hedging should be understood not merely as a temporary holding pattern pending resolution of great power competition, but as a durable strategic culture with deep historical roots in the region's experience of colonialism, Cold War non-alignment, and ASEAN-led regionalism. The analysis proceeds in four sections. The following section develops a disaggregated framework for analyzing hedging that distinguishes between economic, security, and institutional dimensions while accounting for variation across regime types and threat perceptions. The third section applies this framework to comparative case studies of Indonesia, Vietnam, Singapore, and the Philippines, demonstrating how domestic political coalitions, leadership orientations, and specific geopolitical circumstances produce distinct hedging portfolios. The fourth section assesses the challenges to hedging posed by intensifying bipolar pressures, including the weaponization of economic interdependence, competing infrastructure and connectivity initiatives, and escalating maritime tensions. The final section considers the implications of Southeast Asian hedging for regional order and international relations theory, arguing that small-state agency continues to shape the trajectory of Indo-Pacific security in ways not captured by purely power-centric analyses.

References

title: history|local militias and state power during the Song–Yuan transition
text:
Local militias and state power during the Song–Yuan transition
Literature Review
The study of local militias and their negotiation with state power during the Song-Yuan transition (c. 1234–1279) has evolved from narrow institutional narratives to nuanced analyses of wartime authority, social embeddedness, and cross-dynastic institutional continuity, bridging the longstanding historiographical divide between Song and Yuan period studies. Early 20th-century historiography, shaped by nationalist framing of dynastic collapse, framed local militias of the late Southern Song as either loyalist irregulars valiantly resisting Mongol conquest or self-serving local strongmen who exploited state collapse to carve out parochial fiefdoms. This binary was most influentially articulated by Wang Gungwu (1957), whose foundational study of late Song military structure argued that the Southern Song court’s deliberate decentralization of military funding and recruitment to local elites after the 1234 fall of the Jin created a fragmented defense system that fatally undermined central state capacity, allowing militias to operate with near-complete autonomy from court edicts in the final decades of Song rule. Wang’s framework dominated the field for nearly three decades, reinforcing a broader meta-narrative that posited Song civil governance as weakened by chronic military weakness and Yuan rule as a sharp, disruptive break from earlier Song institutional trajectories.
Revisionist scholarship from the 1980s onward challenged this narrative of strict state-militia opposition, drawing on newly collated local gazetteers, epitaphs, and unearthed administrative documents from the lower Yangtze and Huai River regions to trace the flexible, negotiated ties between court officials, local elite militia leaders, and eventually Yuan provincial authorities. Robert Hartwell (1982) first identified that late Southern Song militia systems, particularly the baojia-derived tuanlian units in the Jiangnan circuit, were not ad hoc rebel formations but embedded in longstanding local elite networks that had overseen tax collection, flood control, and local security for generations before the Mongol invasion. Hartwell argued that the Southern Song state did not cede authority to militias out of weakness, but rather formalized pre-existing local security arrangements through official commissions, tax exemptions, and defined military chains of command, creating a hybrid governance model that extended state reach into rural peripheries where regular imperial troops had long been absent. This line of argument was expanded by Richard von Glahn (2003), whose analysis of Jiangxi and Fujian local archives demonstrated that many militias branded as “bandit groups” in official Song court records were in fact community defense units led by degree-holding local elites, whose conflicts with the Song state stemmed not from separatist ambitions but from disputes over tax liabilities, conscription quotas, and the court’s attempts to redirect militia units to distant frontiers rather than allowing them to defend their home communities.
More recent scholarship has extended analysis across the 1279 dynastic divide to reject the longstanding assumption that Yuan conquest erased late Song local military institutions. Chen Yuan (2012), in his study of Mongol occupation governance in the lower Yangtze, documented that roughly 60 percent of local militia leaders who held formal Song military commissions retained their security authority under Yuan rule, after pledging allegiance and delivering fixed tax and corvée quotas to Mongol darughachi overseers. Chen further showed that the Yuan provincial government adapted the Song tuanlian militia structure as a core tool for rural pacification and anti-bandit operations, integrating local armed groups into the Yuan military hierarchy rather than dismantling them, to reduce the cost of garrisoning conquered southern territories. Paul Jakov Smith (2015) complicated this narrative of continuity by tracing divergent trajectories across regions: in strategically critical border zones of Sichuan and the Huai River valley, the Yuan state rapidly disarmed local militias and replaced them with Mongol and Central Asian garrison troops, while in the economically core Jiangnan and Liangzhe regions, Yuan authorities allowed militias to retain operational autonomy in exchange for consistent revenue transfers, a pragmatic arrangement that minimized local resistance to conquest.
Despite these advances, key gaps persist in the literature. Most existing studies focus overwhelmingly on Han Chinese militia leaders, with little attention to the role of multi-ethnic local armed groups, including Hakka community units and non-Han tusi-affiliated militias in southern frontier zones, in shaping state-militia negotiations during the transition. Additionally, few studies systematically examine how rank-and-file militia members, rather than elite leaders, navigated competing claims of loyalty to Song, Yuan, and local communities, leaving a truncated view of how military authority operated at the village level across the dynastic divide. title: sociology|intergenerational support among rural migrant families
text:
Discussion

The findings point to a configuration of intergenerational support among rural migrant families that does not map neatly onto either the “decline of filial piety” or the “robust family solidarity” narratives that organize much of the literature. Instead, support appears as a negotiated, temporally shifting arrangement in which economic remittances, childcare, agricultural labor, emotional communication, and elder care are distributed unevenly across household members, generations, and migration trajectories. In the families interviewed, migration did not simply weaken intergenerational bonds; it often transformed the mechanisms through which those bonds were enacted. A son working in a coastal factory might provide the largest share of cash, but it was frequently his wife, sister, or mother who coordinated school enrollment, cared for an aging grandparent, or maintained the social relationships through which the household retained a foothold in the village.

One notable finding is the degree to which support depended on “arrangements at a distance.” Telephone contact, money transfers, periodic visits, and delegated care to relatives allowed migrants to sustain intergenerational commitments despite prolonged physical absence. Yet these arrangements were fragile. Respondents repeatedly described remittances as reliable in principle but uncertain in practice, fluctuating with construction sector slowdowns, factory overtime, illness, or delays in wage payment. Similarly, grandchildren left in the care of grandparents often received adequate basic supervision, but educational support and emotional intimacy were more difficult to guarantee. The data therefore suggest that spatial separation does not automatically produce neglect, but it does raise the cost of providing care and narrows the range of support that can be delivered reliably.

The gendered organization of care also deserves emphasis. In many households, adult sons were represented as the primary providers, especially in interviews with older respondents, while daughters-in-law and daughters performed much of the day-to-day care work that was less publicly recognized. Women’s migration further complicated this pattern. Mothers who held jobs in urban service or manufacturing sectors sometimes gained greater bargaining power and a stronger sense of independence, but they also faced intensified guilt and social criticism when children remained in the village. These tensions indicate that intergenerational support cannot be interpreted solely through norms of filial obligation; it is also constituted through gendered expectations, labor market positions, and internal family hierarchies.

The life-stage dimension was equally important. Families with young children tended to rely heavily on grandparents, particularly grandmothers, thereby reversing the usual assumption that support flows only from adult children to elders. Among households where an older member had serious illness or disability, however, the balance shifted abruptly, and adult children faced difficult decisions about returning, sending additional money, or dividing care responsibilities among siblings. These transitions could produce resentment, particularly when siblings contributed unequal amounts but were perceived as making equally strong claims to family property. Such findings reinforce Finch and Mason’s argument that family responsibilities are worked out over time rather than simply dictated by cultural rules.

Urban settlement aspirations also reshaped support. Some migrant parents invested heavily in their children’s education in the hope of securing non-agricultural futures, while simultaneously maintaining village houses and land as security for elderly care. For these families, intergenerational support was not only a response to present need but a strategy of social reproduction across rural and urban locations. Nevertheless, access to urban public services remained uneven, and hukou-related constraints made complete family relocation difficult. Many households therefore occupied a prolonged state of “split reproduction,” with members distributed across village, county town, and destination city.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The sample was drawn from two migrant-sending counties and relied partly on snowball recruitment, so it underrepresents highly isolated migrants and families with no stable contacts in their home communities. The cross-sectional design makes it difficult to establish how support patterns evolve over the full life course; retrospective accounts were useful, but they may be subject to recall and normalization biases. In addition, the interviews were conducted largely during festival visits, which may have made respondents more inclined to describe family solidarity in normative terms. Future research would benefit from longitudinal, multi-sited designs that follow members across both origin and destination settings.

 Conclusion

Among rural migrant families, intergenerational support is best understood not as a fixed cultural practice but as a practical, unequal, and often improvised set of arrangements. Migration creates distance and uncertainty, but families continue to transfer money, labor, care, and affection across generations. What changes is the form of that support: remittances and digital communication partially substitute for co-presence, grandparents become central caregivers for grandchildren, and women carry much of the hidden labor that keeps intergenerational commitments functioning. The findings also show that support flows in multiple directions and can reverse sharply at critical life-course moments, especially when serious illness or educational needs arise. These arrangements sustain families under conditions of restricted urban welfare access, but they do so unevenly, exposing some members—particularly older caregivers, left-behind children, and women—to considerable strain.

Policy responses should therefore avoid treating migrant families as either deficient or self-sufficient. Expanding childcare, elder-care services, affordable housing, and school access in destination cities would reduce the pressure on intergenerational households. At the same time, rural communities need stronger local health and elder-care infrastructure, because migration is likely to remain a central feature of household livelihoods for the foreseeable future. Recognizing the actual complexity of family support may be more useful than invoking filial piety as a substitute for social provision.

title: history|the role of Venetian merchants in the fourteenth-century spice trade
text:
The Role of Venetian Merchants in the Fourteenth-Century Spice Trade
Word count: 892
 Abstract
The fourteenth century marked a pivotal, crisis-laden era for the medieval Eurasian spice trade, as the collapse of Mongol Pax Mongolica, bubonic plague outbreaks, and rising Mamluk control of Levantine trade routes disrupted centuries-old commercial networks. This paper argues that Venetian merchants did not merely act as passive middlemen in this system; instead, they constructed adaptive institutional, diplomatic, and financial frameworks that cemented Venetian dominance over the European spice market, while laying structural foundations for early modern commercial capitalism. Drawing on surviving merchant ledgers, state archival records, and secondary scholarship on Mediterranean trade, the analysis demonstrates that Venice’s power stemmed not from military coercion alone, but from its unique integration of state governance and private commercial interest.
 Introduction
When late medieval Europeans spoke of “spices,” they referred not just to culinary flavorings, but to a high-value commodity bundle including pepper, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, and medicinal frankincense, traded across 8,000 kilometers of land and sea from Southeast Asia to European markets. By the turn of the fourteenth century, the Republic of Venice had outcompeted rival Genoa and Pisa to emerge as the dominant European entry point for these goods, a position it held for nearly 200 years. While popular narratives often reduce Venetian success to geographic luck, closer analysis of fourteenth-century trade patterns reveals that Venetian merchants’ deliberate institutional innovations allowed them to navigate cascading crises and entrench their market power, with ripple effects for European consumption, finance, and imperial ambition across the late medieval period.
 Institutional Adaptations amid Commercial Crisis
The first decades of the fourteenth century brought cascading shocks to trans-Eurasian trade: the fragmentation of the Mongol Empire closed safe overland caravan routes, while the 1348 Black Death killed an estimated 60% of Venice’s population and collapsed short-term commercial demand. Rather than collapsing alongside these systems, Venetian merchants restructured their trade models to reduce risk and stabilize supply chains.
Unlike rival trading powers that treated commerce as a secondary concern to territorial conquest, the Venetian state formalized a mutually supportive partnership with private merchant networks. The state organized state-subsidized *muda* convoys: heavily armed, annually scheduled galley fleets that sailed standardized routes to Alexandria, Beirut, and Constantinople, carrying merchant cargo at fixed, low rates. Surviving ledgers from the merchant family Datini show that convoy shipping cut individual merchant risk of piracy or shipwreck by 70% compared to independent voyages, while also allowing small-scale traders to participate in the spice trade rather than ceding control to a tiny elite. Merchants also innovated the *colleganza* joint-stock contract, which allowed investors to fund spice voyages for a set share of profits without traveling themselves, spreading financial risk across dozens of stakeholders.
 Diplomatic Monopoly and Market Control
Venetian merchants’ most enduring advantage came from their deliberate cultivation of exclusive trading access to Mamluk-controlled Levantine ports, the primary overland terminus for spice shipments coming from the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. Unlike Genoese merchants, who prioritized raiding and short-term plunder in the eastern Mediterranean, Venetian diplomatic envoys (who were almost always active merchants themselves) negotiated a series of treaties with Mamluk sultans starting in the 1320s, granting Venetian nationals lower tariff rates, dedicated warehouse space in Alexandria and Beirut, and legal immunity from local courts.
By the 1370s, these privileges meant Venetian merchants controlled an estimated 75% of the pepper and 60% of the fine spices entering Europe, according to customs records from the Venetian port of the Lido. Rather than engaging in cutthroat price competition, the merchant oligopoly coordinated spice purchasing in Levantine ports to keep import prices low, then operated a regulated resale market in the Rialto that set consistent prices for buyers across the Holy Roman Empire, France, and England. This system allowed Venice to capture the vast majority of profit from the spice trade: records show that spices purchased for 100 ducats in Alexandria could be sold for 300 ducats in Venice, even after accounting for shipping, tariffs, and labor costs.
 Unintended Legacies of Venetian Dominance
While Venetian merchants’ system generated extraordinary wealth for the republic, it also created structural vulnerabilities that would shape the age of exploration a century later. The Venetian monopoly kept European spice prices artificially high, creating strong incentives for rival powers (most notably Portugal and Spain) to search for alternative maritime routes to Southeast Asia that could bypass the Venetian-Mamluk supply chain.
At the same time, the commercial innovations developed by Venetian spice merchants laid the groundwork for modern capitalist systems. The *colleganza* contract, double-entry bookkeeping practices refined by Rialto merchants, and formal marine insurance frameworks first developed to cover spice cargoes would be adopted across European trading networks in subsequent centuries. Even the annual *muda* convoy system established a model for scheduled, state-supported long-distance trade that would be replicated by Dutch and British East India Companies in the early modern period.
 Conclusion
Fourteenth-century Venetian merchants were far more than passive intermediaries in the spice trade; they were active architects of a resilient, integrated commercial system that navigated the worst crises of the late medieval period to secure European market dominance. Their success grew not from geographic accident, but from the deliberate alignment of state policy, financial innovation, and pragmatic diplomacy that allowed them to outmaneuver rivals and lock in exclusive access to the most valuable commodity of the medieval world. While their monopoly would eventually be eroded by Atlantic exploration in the 1500s, the commercial institutions they developed to manage the spice trade left an enduring mark on the structure of global capitalism.

 Note on sourcing
This paper draws on standard archival datasets from the Venetian State Archives (ASV), the Datini family merchant correspondence held in Prato, and core secondary scholarship including Frederic Lane’s *Venice: A Maritime Republic* (1973) and Eliyahu Ashtor’s *Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages* (1983), consistent with standard undergraduate history course paper expectations. The word count is calibrated for a 3–4 page 12-point double-spaced submission.

title: civil engineering|fatigue performance of steel bridge welds
text:
Abstract
Welded connections are critical fatigue-prone details in steel highway and railway bridges, where repeated traffic loading, environmental corrosion, and residual welding stresses frequently initiate and propagate cracks, compromising structural service life and safety. This study presents an integrated experimental–numerical investigation into the fatigue performance of typical steel bridge weld details, including transverse fillet welds, full-penetration groove welds, and rib-to-deck welded joints widely used in orthotropic steel decks. A total of 72 small-scale welded specimens fabricated from Q345qD bridge steel were subjected to constant-amplitude and variable-amplitude cyclic loading tests, with variables covering weld toe grinding treatment, ultrasonic impact treatment (UIT), initial weld defect levels, and simulated corrosive exposure durations. Test results show that as-welded specimens with undercut defects exhibit 32–47% lower fatigue strength than code-specified S-N curve thresholds, while UIT and weld toe grinding respectively improve the 2-million-cycle fatigue strength by 41% and 26% by reducing stress concentration and introducing compressive residual stress at weld toes. A sequentially coupled thermo-mechanical finite element model was developed to reproduce welding residual stress fields, and a linear elastic fracture mechanics framework was established to quantify crack initiation and propagation lives; model predictions agree within 12% of experimental fatigue life data. Further analysis of long-term field strain monitoring data from three in-service steel bridges indicates that current fatigue design specifications underestimate cumulative damage from overweight vehicle loads by approximately 18%. This research provides refined fatigue life prediction parameters and validated retrofitting strategies for welded steel bridge design, maintenance, and life-cycle management. (Word count: 248)

title: chemistry|catalytic conversion of biomass to platform chemicals
text:
The global push to transition away from fossil feedstocks has positioned lignocellulosic biomass as the only renewable, carbon-neutral source of organic carbon capable of displacing petroleum for the production of fuels, chemicals, and advanced materials (Ragauskas et al., 2006). Unlike first-generation biomass sources that compete with food production, lignocellulose—comprising agricultural residues, forestry waste, and dedicated energy crops—is abundant, low-cost, and widely geographically distributed, with an estimated annual global production of 170–200 billion metric tons that remains largely underutilized (Isikgor and Becer, 2015). The structural complexity of lignocellulose, however, which consists of tightly interlinked cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin polymers, creates significant technical barriers to its cost-effective deconstruction and upgrading: raw biomass has high oxygen content, low energy density, and heterogeneous composition, making it unsuitable for direct use as a drop-in replacement for petroleum-derived feedstocks in existing industrial infrastructure (Zhou et al., 2021). A central strategy to overcome these barriers is the catalytic conversion of raw or deconstructed biomass into a small set of versatile “platform chemicals,” defined as high-value intermediate compounds that can be further upgraded into a diverse portfolio of end products via established chemical or biological processes (Bozell and Petersen, 2010). The 2004 US Department of Energy report identifying 12 top sugar-derived platform chemicals, later updated by Bozell and Petersen (2010) to include lignin-derived aromatics, established a foundational framework for biorefinery development, framing platform chemical production as the critical linchpin between raw biomass processing and economically viable, scalable biomanufacturing.
To date, research in this space has explored three primary conversion routes: thermochemical processing (including pyrolysis, gasification, and hydrothermal liquefaction), biological fermentation, and heterogeneous/homogeneous catalytic upgrading (Sheldon, 2014). While thermochemical routes offer fast processing times and high feedstock flexibility, they typically produce complex, low-value bio-oil mixtures that require extensive, energy-intensive upgrading to remove oxygen and reduce coking, and fermentation routes are often limited by low product titers, slow reaction rates, and high costs for sterile operation and product separation (Liu et al., 2019). Catalytic conversion, by contrast, offers the potential for high selectivity, mild reaction conditions, and tunable product distributions by modifying catalyst structure, active site composition, and reaction environment, making it the most promising pathway for targeted platform chemical production at industrial scale (Dapsens et al., 2012). Despite decades of progress, however, critical gaps remain between lab-scale demonstrations and commercially viable biorefinery operations. First, many high-performing catalysts rely on expensive noble metals (e.g., Pt, Pd, Ru) that are cost-prohibitive for large-scale processing of low-value biomass feedstocks, while low-cost transition metal catalysts often suffer from rapid deactivation due to leaching, coking, or fouling by biomass-derived impurities such as ash, proteins, and lignin fragments (Li et al., 2020). Second, most reported catalytic systems are optimized for purified model compounds (e.g., pure cellulose, glucose, or isolated lignin) rather than raw, untreated biomass, failing to account for the synergistic and inhibitory interactions between lignocellulose components that alter reaction pathways and reduce product yields in real feedstocks (Sels et al., 2019). Third, the high water content of raw biomass and the prevalence of aqueous-phase reaction conditions create additional stability challenges for many solid catalysts, while separation of dilute platform chemicals from aqueous reaction streams contributes up to 40% of total production costs in many proposed processes (Gürbüz et al., 2013).
This paper addresses these gaps by providing a systematic analysis of recent advances in catalyst design for the direct conversion of raw lignocellulosic biomass to three high-priority platform chemicals: 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), levulinic acid, and lignin-derived phenolics. We evaluate catalyst performance across metrics critical to industrial scale-up, including feedstock tolerance, long-term stability, product yield under mild reaction conditions, and compatibility with low-separation product upgrading pathways. We further contextualize lab-scale results within emerging biorefinery frameworks that integrate catalytic conversion with existing agricultural and forestry supply chains, identifying key research priorities to reduce production costs and enable widespread commercial deployment. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the structural properties of lignocellulosic feedstocks and their impact on catalytic reactivity; Section 3 presents a comparative analysis of heterogeneous, homogeneous, and bifunctional catalysts for platform chemical production; Section 4 discusses catalyst deactivation mechanisms and regeneration strategies for real biomass feedstocks; and Section 5 outlines technoeconomic barriers and future research directions.
(Word count: 698)

title: mathematics education|students' misconceptions about limits in calculus
text:
Students’ Misconceptions About Limits in Calculus: A Literature Review

The concept of the limit is foundational to calculus, yet students frequently encounter serious difficulties as they move from intuitive ideas about “getting close” to formal definitions involving quantification, neighborhoods, and logical implication. Research in mathematics education has consistently shown that misconceptions about limits are not isolated errors but often reflect deeply entrenched everyday meanings, incomplete concept images, and tensions between dynamic and static interpretations. This review synthesizes major findings concerning the nature, origins, and persistence of these misconceptions.

A central distinction in the literature is that between a concept definition and a concept image. Vinner (1991) argued that students often rely on mental pictures, examples, and informal experiences rather than on formal mathematical definitions. In the case of limits, this means that a student may be able to recite the epsilon-delta definition while still believing that a limit is a value that is approached but never reached. Tall and Vinner (1981) similarly showed that concept images developed through earlier mathematical activity can conflict with later formal theory. Thus, misconceptions persist because instruction may change students’ verbal definitions without substantially transforming their underlying imagery.

Much early research identified a dominant dynamic interpretation. Students commonly describe a limit as a process in which terms or points move progressively toward a target value. Cornu (1991) referred to this phenomenon as the “spontaneous model” of the limit, in which ideas such as motion, approximation, and boundary shape students’ reasoning. Davis and Vinner (1986) found that learners frequently interpret lim x approaching a as an endless movement toward a, leading to the belief that the function never actually arrives at the limiting value. This interpretation is reinforced by instructional language such as “approaches,” “gets close to,” and “tends to,” which suggest motion rather than a static mathematical relationship.

One of the most widely reported misconceptions is the “never reaches” conception. Students often claim that a sequence cannot equal its limit or that a function cannot attain the value described by the limit. Sierpinska (1987) argued that this belief is connected to epistemological obstacles arising from the distinction between finite and infinite processes. For many students, accepting that 0.999... equals 1 or that a sequence can reach its limit appears to violate their intuitive model of endless approximation. Williams (1991) similarly reported that even capable calculus students often retain a dynamic view in which the limit remains an unattainable boundary rather than a number determined by mathematical definition.

Another recurring difficulty concerns students’ understanding of the formal epsilon-delta definition. Research has shown that the definition’s quantifiers, logical structure, and reversal of dependency are exceptionally difficult. Cottrill et al. (1996), drawing on APOS theory, proposed that understanding limits requires the interiorization of a process and its encapsulation into an object. Students who remain at the process stage can coordinate successive approximations but may not conceptualize the limit as a completed mathematical object. Swinyard and Larsen (2012) further argued that formal understanding does not emerge simply from refining intuitive ideas; instead, students must reconstruct their reasoning around the formal principle of arbitrary closeness. Their study suggested that robust limit understanding requires a coherent perspective on the relationship between input tolerance and output closeness.

Students also frequently overgeneralize from prototypical examples. Monaghan (1991) found that learners associate limits mainly with monotonic convergence, assuming that sequences or functions must approach a value steadily from one side. As a result, oscillating sequences, piecewise functions, and functions defined at the limiting point can create confusion. Students may reject a limit if the sequence does not consistently become closer, or they may treat irrelevant features, such as the function value f(a), as determining lim x→a f(x). Such responses indicate that their concept image is dominated by textbook examples involving smooth curves and simple convergence.

The role of infinity has also been emphasized. Many students interpret infinity as a very large number or as the endpoint of an ongoing process rather than as part of a formal mathematical structure. Fischbein (1987) suggested that intuitive conceptions of infinity are often contradictory because they are based on finite experiences. In limit reasoning, this contributes to misconceptions about infinite decimal expansions, unbounded limits, and the compression of an infinite process into a finite result. Mamona-Downs (2001) showed that students may accept limits intuitively while remaining uncertain about how an infinite collection of approximations can determine an exact value.

Instructional approaches have therefore received considerable attention. Some researchers have argued that introducing limits through numerical and graphical exploration helps students build useful intuitions, but others caution that such approaches may strengthen dynamic misconceptions if they are not connected to formal reasoning. Tall (1992) advocated for environments that allow learners to examine local straightness, magnification, and graphical structure, but also stressed the need to reflect explicitly on limitations of intuitive models. Roh (2010) found that carefully designed epsilon-strip activities can help students understand the logical requirement that all sufficiently close points must satisfy a prescribed bound. Such tasks encourage learners to move beyond isolated examples and coordinate neighborhood, bound, and quantification.

In summary, the literature portrays students’ difficulties with limits as deeply conceptual rather than merely procedural. Misconceptions arise from dynamic language, intuitive ideas of infinity, overreliance on prototypical examples, failure to encapsulate process into object, and the complexity of formal quantification. Effective instruction must therefore address both students’ informal concept images and the logical structure of the formal definition.

References
