title: art history|patronage and workshop practice in Ming dynasty court painting
text:
Methodology
This study adopts a mixed-methods art historical framework that integrates archival philology, technical art analysis, and social network mapping to disentangle the reciprocal dynamics of imperial patronage and workshop production in Ming dynasty (1368–1644) court painting, addressing longstanding gaps in scholarship that has either framed court painters as isolated, imperial-mandated “academic masters” or reduced workshop production to unskilled rote replication.

 Data Sources
Three interconnected corpora of primary sources form the study’s evidentiary base, selected to cut across the traditional divide between textual and object-centered analysis. First, textual archival records include 12 compendia of Ming court administrative documents: the *Ming Shilu* (Veritable Records of the Ming), *Neifu Gongcheng Zeli* (Imperial Household Workshop Regulations), *Wanli Yehuobian* (Unofficial Gleanings from the Wanli Reign), and the collected biji (brush notes) of 16 palace eunuchs and Hanlin Academy scholars who served as painting curators or patronage intermediaries between the 1420s and 1620s. These documents record painter recruitment, rank promotions, commission orders, material stipends, and disciplinary actions against workshop members. Second, the painting corpus comprises 214 works attributed to Ming court workshops held in four institutional collections: the Palace Museum (Beijing, 127 works), National Palace Museum (Taipei, 61 works), Shanghai Museum (17 works), and the Metropolitan Museum of Art (9 works), selected for their documented provenance traceable to Qing imperial collection inventories (the *Shiqu Baoji* and *Bidian Zhulin*) that confirm their origins as Ming court holdings rather than later forgeries or commercial works misattributed to court artists. Third, technical data is drawn from publicly available high-resolution multispectral imaging, X-radiography, and pigment analysis reports published by the three Chinese collecting institutions between 2015 and 2023, supplemented by first-hand examination of 28 hanging scrolls and handscrolls accessible at the Palace Museum Beijing during two 2022 fieldwork visits.

 Sample
The painting sample is stratified across three distinct phases of Ming court patronage to capture institutional change: the early Ming (Hongwu to Xuande reigns, 1368–1435, n=72), when court painting institutions were first formalized after the collapse of the Song imperial academy; the mid-Ming (Chenghong to Jiajing reigns, 1465–1566, n=89), when eunuch-managed workshops displaced Hanlin scholar oversight of court painting; and the late Ming (Longqing to Chongzhen reigns, 1567–1644, n=53), when commercial market pressures began to shape court production norms. The sample excludes works with contested attributions that cannot be linked to named court painters or documented workshop units, as well as works bearing later collector seals indicating they circulated outside the palace prior to the fall of the Ming. It deliberately includes both signed, iconic works by celebrated court masters (e.g., Bian Wenjin, Qiu Ying) and unsigned, workshop-produced didactic scrolls, imperial portrait sets, and seasonal decorative paintings, which have been largely excluded from prior studies focused on connoisseurship of masterworks.

 Analytical Procedures
Analysis proceeds in three sequential stages. First, textual records are coded using a structured qualitative coding scheme to map patronage networks: entries are tagged for patron identity (emperor, imperial consort, eunuch, Hanlin official), commission purpose (ritual, diplomatic gifting, private imperial enjoyment, court reward), workshop division (e.g., Figure Painting Office, Imperial Portrait Studio), and division of labor (design draftsman, colorist, inscriber, final validator). This coding is used to build a relational database tracking 276 named court painters and 49 patron intermediaries active across the three study phases. Second, object analysis pairs close visual formal analysis with technical data to identify workshop production signatures: repeated compositional templates, underdrawing patterns, pigment layer stratigraphy, and brushstroke idiosyncrasies are matched across works to distinguish works produced solely by a named master from collaborative workshop pieces, or works completed by junior apprentices to fulfill patron-mandated production quotas. Third, cross-correlation of textual and visual data tests two core hypotheses: that shifts in patron identity (from direct imperial oversight to eunuch management across the mid-Ming) coincided with increased workshop division of labor and standardized production, and that patron-mandated stylistic requirements (rather than individual painter choice) explain the long-observed shift from the bold, virtuosic ink-wash style of early Ming court painting to the polished, decorative style of mid- and late-Ming works. Triangulation across sources mitigates the bias inherent in connoisseurship-led studies that rely solely on stylistic attribution, while centering unsigned workshop works corrects for the historical erasure of junior artisans from formal archival records. (Word count: 598)

title: philosophy|moral luck and the limits of responsibility
text:
Abstract
The problem of moral luck stands as one of the most persistent paradoxes in contemporary ethical theory, arising from the apparent contradiction between two deeply entrenched commitments: the widespread intuition that moral responsibility is immune to factors beyond an agent’s control, and the equally pervasive practice of ascribing differential moral blame and praise based on outcomes shaped by luck. This article examines the four canonical categories of moral luck—resultant, circumstantial, constitutive, and causal—to argue that the standard debate between “luck skeptics” who defend the Control Principle and “moral luck realists” who endorse outcome-based responsibility rests on a shared failure to distinguish two distinct dimensions of moral assessment: accountability for action and aretaic evaluation of character.

Drawing on P.F. Strawson’s reactive attitudes framework and recent work on epistemic situationism, the article develops a bounded account of moral responsibility that acknowledges the ineliminable presence of luck in human life without collapsing moral assessment into mere fortune. It argues that resultant luck (e.g., the difference between a successful and attempted murder) properly affects the scope of harms for which agents must take remedial responsibility, but not the degree of their moral blameworthiness, while constitutive and circumstantial luck reveal that the Control Principle cannot serve as an absolute foundation for responsibility, but only as a regulative ideal embedded in our practices of holding one another responsible.

Against both hard-line rejection of moral luck and uncritical acceptance of outcome-based moral differences, the article concludes that the limits of moral responsibility are not fixed by a metaphysical line between what is and is not within an agent’s control, but are negotiated through our participatory practices of moral address, excuse, and reconciliation. This bounded view resolves the paradox of moral luck not by eliminating luck from the moral life, but by showing how responsibility can remain rational and fair even as it extends beyond the boundary of what agents fully control. (Word count: 252)

title: environmental science|wetland restoration and carbon sequestration
text:
Wetlands, covering just 6% of Earth’s terrestrial surface (Mitsch et al., 2013), represent one of the planet’s most effective natural carbon sinks, storing an estimated 20–30% of global soil carbon despite their limited geographic extent (Nahlik & Fennessy, 2016). This disproportionate carbon storage capacity stems from the unique biogeochemical conditions of wetland ecosystems: saturated soils limit oxygen diffusion, slowing microbial decomposition of organic matter and enabling the long-term accumulation of peat and organic-rich sediments over centuries to millennia (Kayranli et al., 2010). Yet, over the past three centuries, global wetland loss has exceeded 50% in many temperate and tropical regions, driven by agricultural conversion, urban development, hydrological modification, and resource extraction (Davidson, 2014). The drainage and degradation of wetlands not only eliminate a critical carbon sink but also transform these ecosystems into significant greenhouse gas (GHG) sources, releasing stored carbon as carbon dioxide (CO₂) and methane (CH₄) at rates that contribute an estimated 1.7 gigatons of CO₂-equivalent emissions annually, or roughly 5% of global anthropogenic GHG emissions (IPCC, 2019).
Against this backdrop, wetland restoration has emerged as a prominent nature-based solution (NbS) for climate change mitigation, with growing inclusion in national climate action plans, voluntary carbon markets, and global biodiversity frameworks such as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (UNEP, 2022). The core premise of restoration for carbon sequestration is that re-establishing natural hydrological regimes, native vegetation communities, and soil biogeochemical function can reverse degradation-driven carbon losses, enabling wetlands to resume long-term organic carbon accumulation in soils and biomass (Mitsch & Mander, 2023). However, despite widespread enthusiasm for wetland carbon projects, significant uncertainties remain regarding the magnitude, timing, and persistence of sequestration benefits across wetland types, restoration approaches, and climatic contexts. Early synthesis efforts reported average sequestration rates of 0.2–0.5 kilograms of carbon per square meter per year for restored freshwater marshes and peatlands, but these estimates often fail to account for context-dependent variability, including pre-restoration land use, soil legacy effects, and non-CO₂ GHG fluxes that can offset net climate benefits (Bridgham et al., 2013).
A key unresolved debate in the field centers on the tradeoffs between carbon sequestration and CH₄ emissions in restored wetlands. While hydrological rewetting is a foundational step for most wetland restoration projects, anaerobic soil conditions also stimulate methanogenesis, leading to elevated CH₄ emissions that can persist for decades after restoration is initiated (Petrescu et al., 2015). For example, restored peatlands in boreal regions have been found to take 20–30 years to achieve net cooling effects, as initial high CH₄ fluxes gradually decline while soil carbon accumulation rates rise (Wilson et al., 2016). In contrast, restored tidal salt marshes often exhibit more immediate net climate benefits, as sulfate in seawater suppresses methanogen activity, while high rates of root productivity drive rapid sediment carbon storage (McLeod et al., 2011). These divergent outcomes highlight the risk of overgeneralizing wetland carbon sequestration potential across ecosystem types, and underscore the need for site-specific assessments that account for both long-term carbon storage and short-lived climate forcer emissions.
Additional gaps persist in understanding the long-term persistence of sequestered carbon in restored wetlands. Many existing studies rely on short-term (5–15 year) monitoring datasets that capture initial carbon accumulation trajectories, but fail to account for disturbance events such as droughts, wildfires, storm surges, and sea level rise that can reverse decades of carbon gains (Moomaw et al., 2018). For instance, severe droughts in the southwestern United States have been shown to dry out restored freshwater marshes, triggering rapid soil carbon oxidation and CO₂ releases that erase 10+ years of sequestration gains in a single dry season (Moritsch et al., 2023). Furthermore, most carbon accounting frameworks for wetland restoration projects do not explicitly incorporate soil legacy carbon pools, which can make up 90% of total wetland carbon stocks, or account for albedo effects and hydrological feedbacks that modify net climate impacts at local to regional scales (Hemes et al., 2021).
This paper addresses these critical knowledge gaps by synthesizing 30 years of peer-reviewed data on carbon sequestration and GHG fluxes across 428 restored wetland sites spanning boreal, temperate, tropical, and coastal biomes. We first quantify variability in net ecosystem carbon balance across restoration types and age classes, identifying key biotic and abiotic drivers that explain differences in sequestration outcomes. We next develop a standardized framework for accounting for non-CO₂ GHG fluxes and disturbance risks to enable more robust carbon credit accounting for wetland restoration projects. Finally, we provide evidence-based guidance for restoration design that maximizes synergies between carbon sequestration, biodiversity conservation, and coastal or flood protection ecosystem services. As global efforts to scale up nature-based climate solutions accelerate, improving the scientific rigor of wetland carbon sequestration estimates is essential to ensure that restoration investments deliver measurable, long-term climate benefits without compromising other critical ecosystem functions. title: international relations|small-state hedging strategies in Southeast Asia
text:
Discussion

The findings presented above complicate prevailing accounts that treat Southeast Asian hedging as either a straightforward response to structural uncertainty or a largely uniform posture available to all small states. What the comparison of Singapore, Vietnam, and Malaysia suggests is that hedging is not a single strategy arrayed along a continuum from balancing to bandwagoning. Rather, it is an institutionalized practice through which ruling coalitions manage competing external dependencies while preserving domestic political space. Singapore’s combination of forward security engagement with the United States, economic embedding in China, and investment in regional multilateralism reflects the constraints faced by a city-state whose survival depends on the credibility of open markets and great-power access. Yet its hedging is not ambiguity for its own sake. The publicly visible dimensions of its security policy—access arrangements, joint exercises, defense technological cooperation—communicate reliability to Washington, while its repeated insistence that it does not take sides is calibrated to avoid compelling Beijing to define Singapore as an adversarial node.

Vietnam’s hedging follows a different rhythm. Its security cooperation with external powers has expanded, but Hanoi has retained strict limits on formal alignment and on the operational visibility of defense partnerships. The empirical pattern indicates that Vietnam hedges most intensively in domains where Chinese pressure is direct—maritime claims, coast guard coordination, energy security—and more cautiously in domains where ideological and regime-security considerations predominate. This distinction matters. It suggests that authoritarian small states do not simply balance against material threats; they also calculate whether external partnerships may introduce normative or political liabilities. Vietnam’s “ bamboo diplomacy” should therefore not be read merely as elegant rhetoric. It captures a real tension: resistance to Chinese coercion without producing the domestic political consequences associated with alliance-like dependence on the United States.

Malaysia, in turn, demonstrates how domestic political turnover alters the credibility and content of hedging. During the period examined, Kuala Lumpur moved between publicly assertive pushback against Chinese maritime presence and elite bargaining over infrastructure, investment, and ethnic and business linkages. Its hedging was less institutionally insulated than Singapore’s and less ideologically constrained than Vietnam’s. Consequently, shifts in partisan competition, leadership change, and bargains among domestic coalitions produced visible inconsistency. This does not mean that Malaysia abandoned hedging. Rather, its hedging operated through issue-specific recalibration: legal and diplomatic firmness on sovereignty, selective renegotiation of Chinese-backed projects, continued participation in US-led maritime exercises, and reliance on ASEAN frameworks to avoid bilateral isolation.

These cases also expose limits in the common claim that ASEAN centrality is the primary mechanism through which Southeast Asian states hedge. ASEAN provides a useful diplomatic platform, procedural cover, and normative vocabulary, but its value varies. For Singapore, regional institutions are one component within a denser strategy of economic and military diversification. For Vietnam, ASEAN helps multilateralize disputes, but cannot substitute for direct defense partnerships or coast-guard capacity. For Malaysia, ASEAN offers domestic political protection against accusations of alignment, yet consensus rules weaken its coercive bargaining power. In that sense, hedging is not primarily produced by ASEAN; states use ASEAN as one instrument among several.

The study has several limitations. First, the evidence relies heavily on publicly observable policy signals—joint statements, exercises, treaty participation, investment disputes, and elite rhetoric. Much of hedging occurs through private assurance, intelligence relationships, and informal bargaining, which cannot be fully assessed without classified materials. Second, the temporal focus on the post-2009 period captures intensified South China Sea competition but does not fully explain longer postcolonial trajectories, particularly the formation of Singapore’s security doctrine or Vietnam’s post-Cold War normalization. Third, although the comparison identifies domestic mechanisms, it does not develop a fully testable theory of coalition politics. A larger sample, including Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines, would help distinguish regime type, economic exposure, leadership turnover, and maritime vulnerability as separate causal factors. Finally, the paper treats China and the United States mainly as external pressures; future work should examine how great-power embassies, firms, and military commands actively attempt to narrow small-state choices.

 Conclusion

Hedging in Southeast Asia is best understood not as indecision, but as the deliberate maintenance of contradictory policy options under asymmetric pressure. The cases show that small states can preserve room for maneuver when they combine multiple partnerships, avoid irreversible alignment, and convert bilateral disputes into regional or institutionalized processes. But they also show that hedging is not equally available or similarly composed. Singapore’s strategy rests on administrative capacity, economic centrality, and credible defense signaling. Vietnam’s is shaped by maritime threat, socialist regime security, and suspicion of all formal alliances. Malaysia’s reflects more fluid elite coalitions and therefore greater issue-by-issue variability.

The principal contribution of this article is to move beyond the binary of balancing and bandwagoning without dissolving small-state behavior into an undifferentiated category of “hedging.” The strategy has observable components: economic diversification, limited security cooperation, rhetorical neutrality, institutional multilateralism, and selective confrontation. Which component dominates depends less on a state’s size alone than on its domestic institutions, vulnerability profiles, and the political coalitions that define acceptable dependence.

These findings also caution against expecting Southeast Asian states to align cleanly with the United States as China becomes more powerful. Even states directly challenged by Chinese maritime power seek calibrated cooperation with Beijing, while those with deep American security ties retain extensive Chinese economic interests. At the same time, hedging should not be romanticized. It can reduce immediate risk, but it also imposes costs: ambiguous commitments may weaken deterrence, domestic criticism can force sudden posturing, and reliance on ASEAN consensus may produce lowest-common-denominator outcomes. Under conditions of sustained great-power competition, the central question is therefore not whether Southeast Asian small states hedge, but how long their particular domestic bargains can sustain that posture without forcing choices they have spent decades trying to avoid.

title: geography|urban heat islands and green space distribution
text:
Urban Heat Islands and Green Space Distribution: Causal Links and Planning Implications
 Abstract
The urban heat island (UHI) effect, defined as the 2–8 °C temperature gap between dense built-up areas and surrounding rural zones, has emerged as a pressing climate justice risk for 21st-century cities, where 56% of the global population resides. This paper synthesizes remote sensing data, urban microclimate surveys, and equity-focused case studies to examine how inequitable green space distribution amplifies UHI intensity, and how targeted green infrastructure planning can deliver cooling co-benefits. Analysis of 12 mid-latitude megacities (including Beijing, Chicago, and Berlin) finds that neighborhoods with less than 10% tree canopy cover record 3.2 °C higher average summer peak temperatures than adjacent areas with 30%+ canopy cover, with low-income and racial minority groups 2.7 times more likely to live in heat-exposed, green-space-poor zones. The paper concludes that equity-centered green space distribution, rather than aggregate city-wide green cover targets, is critical to mitigating UHI-related health disparities. (Word count: 128)

 Introduction
In July 2023, Phoenix, Arizona recorded 31 consecutive days of temperatures above 43 °C, with inner-city neighborhoods registering 6 °C higher than outlying suburban areas—a stark example of UHI-related extreme heat that caused 425 confirmed heat-associated deaths that month. While UHI formation is driven by multiple factors, including impervious surface heat retention, anthropogenic waste heat from traffic and buildings, and blocked urban ventilation, a growing body of geographic scholarship identifies uneven green space access as the single most modifiable driver of intra-urban heat variation. Early UHI research in the 1970s treated temperature differences as a uniform city-wide phenomenon, but recent high-resolution Landsat thermal imaging reveals that heat exposure is deeply uneven at the neighborhood scale, shaped by decades of zoning and disinvestment. This paper first maps the biophysical mechanisms linking green space to local cooling, then analyzes distributional inequities in green space access, before evaluating evidence-based planning interventions to align green infrastructure with heat mitigation goals. (Word count: 149)

 Biophysical Links Between Green Space and UHI Mitigation
The cooling effect of urban green space operates through three interconnected biophysical pathways, with measurable impacts at scales ranging from individual street trees to 50-hectare urban parks. First, evapotranspiration: tree canopies and grassy surfaces release water vapor as plants photosynthesize, converting incoming solar radiation to latent heat rather than warming surrounding surfaces; a single mature deciduous tree can transpire up to 450 liters of water per day, delivering cooling equivalent to two 12,000 BTU air conditioners running for 24 hours. Second, shading: dense tree canopy blocks 90–95% of incoming solar radiation, reducing surface temperatures of asphalt and concrete by 15–20 °C compared to unshaded adjacent sites. Third, wind channeling: connected green corridors can draw cooler rural air into dense urban cores, reducing stagnant heat build-up in street canyons.
Crucially, geographic scale shapes cooling efficacy: a 2024 meta-analysis of 85 UHI studies finds that green spaces smaller than 0.5 hectares deliver localized cooling within a 100-meter radius, while parks larger than 10 hectares generate a "cool island spillover effect" that reduces temperatures for 300–500 meters beyond their boundaries. This scalar dynamic means that scattered, small-scale green patches distributed across high-density neighborhoods often deliver more equitable heat relief than a small number of large, concentrated urban parks on city peripheries. (Word count: 218)

 Distributional Inequities in Green Space and Heat Exposure
Geographic information system (GIS) mapping of 12 mid-latitude megacities conducted between 2018 and 2023 reveals a consistent, structurally driven mismatch between green space distribution and heat vulnerability, exacerbating UHI-related inequities. In Chicago, for example, neighborhoods with majority Black and Hispanic populations have 17% less tree canopy cover than majority white neighborhoods with identical population density, leading to a 2.9 °C average summer evening temperature gap between these areas. In Beijing, neighborhoods outside the 5th Ring Road, where 62% of the city’s low-income migrant population resides, have 22% less public green space per capita than central urban districts, recording 3.4 °C higher peak daytime temperatures.
These gaps are not accidental: they reflect historical zoning policies that prioritized green space investment in affluent residential areas, mid-20th century "redlining" practices that denied tree planting and park investment to marginalized neighborhoods, and market-driven green gentrification that often restricts access to new green amenities to high-income groups. Critically, the populations most exposed to UHI effects are also the most vulnerable to heat-related illness: elderly residents, unhoused populations, and low-income households without access to air conditioning face 4 times higher risk of heat exhaustion and mortality in green-space-poor neighborhoods. (Word count: 207)

 Planning Interventions for Equitable Cooling
To address these gaps, geographic scholarship points to three evidence-based green space planning strategies that prioritize UHI mitigation and equity, rather than cosmetic greening targets. First, cities should replace aggregate "per capita green space" metrics with canopy cover targets for high-heat, high-vulnerability neighborhoods: for example, Los Angeles’ 2019 Green New Deal set a mandatory target of 25% tree canopy cover in all neighborhoods with current summer peak temperatures above 38 °C, prioritizing street tree planting and pocket park development in previously redlined districts, with early monitoring showing a 1.7 °C temperature reduction in targeted zones after 4 years. Second, planners should prioritize connected green corridor networks along riparian zones and former industrial railway lines to facilitate cross-city ventilation, rather than building isolated park complexes. Third, cities must implement anti-displacement policies, such as community land trusts for new green spaces, to prevent green gentrification that pushes low-income residents out of newly cooled neighborhoods.
Notably, green space is not a universal solution: in arid cities such as Phoenix, water-intensive turf grass parks can increase urban water stress, so planners prioritize drought-tolerant native tree species and green roofs that deliver cooling without excessive resource use. (Word count: 162)

 Conclusion
The UHI effect is not an inevitable consequence of urbanization, but a geographically patterned phenomenon shaped by the distribution of green infrastructure across urban space. As extreme heat events become more frequent under climate change, green space planning must move beyond aesthetic and recreational goals to center heat mitigation and distributional equity. The evidence presented in this paper demonstrates that even modest increases in tree canopy cover in high-vulnerability neighborhoods can deliver measurable cooling benefits, reduce heat-related mortality, and narrow long-standing environmental justice gaps. Future geographic research should prioritize high-resolution, neighborhood-scale monitoring of green space cooling effects, to support context-specific planning that balances UHI mitigation, ecosystem health, and equitable access for all urban residents. (Word count: 102)

title: psychology|sleep deprivation and emotional regulation in adolescents
text:
Methodology

 Study Design and Participants

This cross-sectional study employed a quantitative, correlational design to examine associations between sleep deprivation and emotional regulation capacities among adolescents. Participants were recruited from four public secondary schools in urban and suburban districts of a mid-sized metropolitan area in the southeastern United States. Inclusion criteria required enrollment in grades 9–12 (ages 13–18 years), regular attendance at school during the assessment period, and ability to complete self-report questionnaires in English. Adolescents with diagnosed neurodevelopmental conditions (e.g., autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability) or those taking medications known to substantially alter sleep or affect (e.g., stimulants, sedatives) were excluded to reduce heterogeneity, although adolescents with treated, stable anxiety or depression were retained given their high prevalence in this population.

A priori power analysis using G*Power 3.1 indicated that a sample of 260 participants would provide 90% power to detect a small-to-medium bivariate association (r = .20) at α = .05, accounting for up to 15% missing data. Of 342 information packets distributed, 298 parental consent and adolescent assent forms were returned (87.1% response rate). Fourteen participants were excluded due to incomplete actigraphy data or questionnaire nonresponse, yielding a final analytic sample of 284 adolescents (51.4% female; 47.5% male; 1.1% nonbinary or not reported). The racial/ethnic composition was 54.9% White, 22.2% Black or African American, 12.7% Hispanic/Latino of any race, 4.9% Asian, and 5.3% multiracial or other, broadly approximating district demographics. Socioeconomic status, indexed by eligibility for free or reduced-price lunch, was 38.7%. All procedures were approved by the university Institutional Review Board and participating school boards prior to recruitment.

 Measures and Data Sources

Data were collected across one 7-day assessment period scheduled to avoid examination weeks and immediately followed school holidays. Sleep was measured using two complementary sources. First, adolescents wore Micro MotionLogger wrist actigraphs (Ambulatory Monitoring, Inc.) continuously for seven nights, except during bathing or contact sports. Actigraphic data were scored in 60-second epochs using the Sadeh algorithm, with nightly variables including total sleep time, sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, and sleep efficiency. Bedtimes and rise times were corroborated using daily sleep diaries completed each morning and evening. Sleep deprivation was operationalized both continuously (mean weekday total sleep time) and categorically using age-based recommendations: fewer than 8 hours per night on school nights was classified as insufficient sleep, consistent with consensus guidelines for adolescents.

Emotional regulation was assessed using the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale–Short Form (DERS-SF), an 18-item self-report measure yielding six subscales (nonacceptance, goals, impulse, awareness, strategies, clarity) and a total score, with higher scores indicating greater regulation difficulties. Internal consistency in the present sample was excellent (Cronbach’s α = .91 for total score; subscale α = .76–.88). To reduce common-method and state-response bias, participants also completed a 5-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA) via a study-provided smartphone. Four semi-random prompts per day asked adolescents to rate current positive and negative affect and the degree to which they had successfully managed recent emotions using 0–10 scales. EMA items were averaged within person to derive trait-like indicators of affective intensity and perceived regulation success.

Parents of a subset (n = 196) completed the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) emotion symptoms subscale as an external outcome measure. Participants additionally reported age, sex, race/ethnicity, grade, pubertal status using the Pubertal Development Scale, caffeine and energy drink use, screen time after 22:00, extracurricular employment, and self-reported depressive symptoms (PHQ-9). These variables were considered covariates based on established associations with both sleep and emotional functioning.

 Data Analysis

Analyses were conducted in R version 4.3.2, with an a priori two-tailed α of .05. Actigraphy and diary records were first aggregated across school nights; weekends were modeled separately in sensitivity analyses. Descriptive statistics and bivariate correlations were computed to characterize sleep, DERS-SF, and EMA variables. Primary hypotheses were tested using multiple linear regression in which DERS-SF total and subscale scores were regressed on mean weekday total sleep time, adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, pubertal status, free/reduced-price lunch, depressive symptoms, caffeine use, and nighttime screen time. Multilevel models evaluated EMA outcomes, with observations nested within persons; sleep duration from the preceding night predicted momentary negative affect and regulation success at Level 1, while between-person sleep differences and covariates were modeled at Level 2. Missing data, comprising less than 6% of questionnaire items and 9% of EMA prompts, were addressed using full information maximum likelihood under a missing-at-random assumption. Robust standard errors were used to account for clustering by school. Effect sizes were reported as standardized beta coefficients and semi-partial R² values, with sensitivity analyses comparing the <8-hour sleep-duration group to peers obtaining 8–10 hours.

title: agronomy|intercropping maize and soybean under drought stress
text:
Abstract
Drought stress is a leading constraint to rainfed maize-soybean intercropping productivity across semi-arid and sub-humid agroecosystems, where smallholder farmers rely on diversified cropping to buffer yield volatility under increasingly erratic rainfall. While intercropping is widely promoted for its resource use efficiency, the mechanisms underpinning drought resilience, and the tradeoffs between productivity, resource capture, and soil health, remain poorly quantified across stress intensities. This two-year (2022–2023) field experiment in the semi-arid North China Plain evaluated four cropping treatments (sole maize, sole soybean, 1:1 row maize-soybean intercropping, 2:2 row maize-soybean intercropping) under three water regimes (full irrigation, moderate drought (40% field capacity reduction at reproductive stage), severe drought (60% field capacity reduction)) to assess yield performance, interspecific interactions, water/nitrogen use efficiency, and rhizosphere soil enzyme activity. Results showed that relative to sole crops, intercropping systems achieved 18–27% higher land equivalent ratio (LER) across drought levels, with the 2:2 row configuration delivering the most stable performance: it maintained 23% higher system yield than weighted sole crop yields under severe drought, associated with 31% greater post-silking water uptake, 24% higher nitrogen fixation in soybean, and 19–28% higher activity of rhizosphere β-glucosidase and urease relative to sole crops under stress. Interspecific complementarity, rather than competition, dominated under drought, as maize accessed deeper soil water while soybean fixed additional N to support system productivity. These findings demonstrate that optimized row configuration of maize-soybean intercropping can mitigate drought-induced yield losses, providing a low-input, climate-resilient practice for rainfed smallholder systems facing increasing water scarcity. (Word count: 249)

title: psychology|sleep deprivation and emotional regulation in adolescents
text:
Adolescence is a developmental period marked by rapid changes in sleep physiology, emotion processing, social stress, and self-regulation. At the same time, many adolescents obtain insufficient sleep because of early school schedules, academic demands, technology use, and changing circadian preferences. Sleep deprivation is now common among teenagers and is associated with irritability, anxiety, depressed mood, impulsivity, and interpersonal conflict. One explanation for these associations is that inadequate sleep compromises the neural and cognitive systems needed to regulate emotion. Understanding how sleep deprivation affects emotional regulation in adolescents is therefore important because emotion regulation difficulties can affect academic functioning, peer relationships, risk behavior, and long-term mental health.

Emotional regulation refers to the processes through which individuals monitor, evaluate, and modify the intensity, duration, and expression of emotional responses (Gross, 2015). These processes include effortful strategies such as cognitive reappraisal and attentional deployment, as well as more automatic forms of control involving inhibition, conflict monitoring, and recovery from arousal. Adolescence is a key period for the maturation of these abilities. Prefrontal control networks continue to develop throughout the teenage years, while subcortical affective systems show heightened reactivity to social and rewarding stimuli (Casey et al., 2008). This developmental imbalance may make adolescents especially sensitive to conditions that reduce prefrontal control, including sleep loss.

Sleep supports multiple processes relevant to emotion regulation. Prefrontal cortex functioning, attentional control, working memory, and inhibitory control are vulnerable to sleep deprivation, while amygdala reactivity may increase after inadequate sleep. In adults, experimental sleep restriction is associated with stronger neural responses to negative stimuli and reduced connectivity between emotion-generating and emotion-regulating brain regions (Yoo et al., 2007). Sleep also contributes to habituation, extinction learning, and the overnight regulation of emotional memories (Walker & van der Helm, 2009). When sleep is shortened or fragmented, adolescents may therefore enter emotionally demanding situations with reduced control resources and heightened affective reactivity.

A large body of correlational research links poor sleep to emotional difficulties in adolescence. Short sleep duration, long sleep latency, and nighttime awakenings have been associated with higher symptoms of depression and anxiety, greater negative affect, and lower positive affect (Short et al., 2013; Raniti et al., 2017). Population studies indicate that adolescents sleeping fewer than the recommended hours often report more mood disturbance and difficulty managing daily stressors (Fitzgerald et al., 2019). However, observational designs cannot fully establish directionality. Emotion dysregulation, rumination, and heightened arousal may also delay sleep onset or reduce sleep quality, creating a reciprocal cycle. Adolescents who struggle to regulate emotions may lie awake ruminating, and the resulting sleep loss may make emotion regulation more difficult the following day.

Experimental and quasi-experimental studies provide stronger evidence that sleep plays a causal role. Studies using partial sleep restriction, total sleep deprivation, and sleep extension paradigms have found that restricted sleep worsens emotion recognition, impulse control, attentional bias to negative information, and self-reported mood (Talbot et al., 2010; Baum et al., 2014). For example, sleep-restricted adolescents often show smaller gains in positive affect and larger increases in irritability or hostility than when well rested. There is also evidence that sleep loss affects adolescents differently from adults. Developmental changes in circadian timing, homeostatic sleep pressure, brain maturation, and psychosocial environments may increase vulnerability during the teenage years (Carskadon, 2011).

Despite this evidence, several questions remain. First, many studies examine mood outcomes rather than regulation processes, making it unclear whether sleep loss primarily amplifies emotional reactions, weakens deliberate regulation, or impairs recovery. Second, the field uses many indicators of sleep, including duration, quality, timing, variability, and insomnia symptoms, and these dimensions may not have identical effects. Third, adolescents differ in vulnerability. Chronic sleep restriction, pre-existing anxiety or depressive symptoms, pubertal stage, family conflict, and genetic or cognitive differences may moderate the association. Finally, experimental studies often use small samples and brief manipulation periods, whereas most adolescents experience repeated, socially patterned sleep loss across school weeks rather than one night of total deprivation.

The present paper addresses these issues by integrating evidence on sleep deprivation and emotional regulation in adolescence. It considers experimental, longitudinal, and self-report research, with attention to developmental mechanisms and methodological limitations. Clarifying this relationship may inform school start-time policies, clinical interventions, and prevention programs aimed at improving adolescent mental health.

References cited in this introduction: Baum et al. (2014); Carskadon (2011); Casey et al. (2008); Fitzgerald et al. (2019); Gross (2015); Raniti et al. (2017); Short et al. (2013); Talbot et al. (2010); Walker & van der Helm (2009); Yoo et al. (2007).

title: history|grain prices and famine relief in eighteenth-century Qing China
text:
Literature Review: Grain Prices and Famine Relief in Eighteenth-Century Qing China
The study of grain prices and famine relief in eighteenth-century Qing China has evolved significantly over the past four decades, moving from early narratives of imperial administrative stagnation to nuanced analyses of market integration, state capacity, and the uneven impacts of relief interventions across regional and social divides. Early scholarship framed Qing famine governance as a largely symbolic, inefficient system, undermined by bureaucratic corruption and a failure to respond to the subsistence crises that rippled across the empire in the wake of droughts, floods, and harvest failures. In his foundational 1958 work on Chinese famine history, Ho argued that while the Qing state had established formal granary reserves and relief distribution protocols by the Kangxi reign, systemic underfunding and official graft rendered these mechanisms largely ineffective by the mid-eighteenth century, leaving peasant populations exposed to catastrophic mortality during major subsistence shocks. This narrative remained dominant until the 1980s, when archival research on granary records and grain price data prompted a major re-evaluation of Qing state capacity in the High Qing era.
Will and Wong’s 1991 landmark collaborative study Nourish the People marked a paradigmatic shift in the field, drawing on over a decade of work in central and provincial archives to demonstrate that the eighteenth-century Qing state operated one of the most sophisticated famine relief systems in the early modern world. Their analysis of grain price reports from 1740 to 1820 showed that the empire’s network of ever-normal granaries, charitable granaries, and community granaries held sufficient reserves to buffer localized harvest failures for up to two years in core provinces such as Jiangsu, Zhejiang, and Zhili, and that targeted price stabilization interventions—including grain sales at below-market rates, direct grain disbursements to affected households, and temporary tax waivers—reduced excess mortality during the 1743–1744 Zhili drought and 1755 Yangtze flood to a fraction of levels recorded in comparable crises in contemporary Europe. Will and Wong further documented that the Qing court’s requirement for provincial officials to submit monthly grain price reports allowed the central state to track regional supply gaps in near real time, facilitating the coordinated transfer of surplus grain from surplus-producing regions in the middle Yangtze to deficit regions at levels that would not be matched by most European states until the late nineteenth century.
Subsequent scholarship has built on this revisionist framework while highlighting key structural limits to the Qing relief system, particularly its uneven performance across core and peripheral regions, and its gradual erosion from the 1780s onward. Perdue’s 1992 study of grain logistics in the northwest border provinces of Gansu and Shaanxi found that relief interventions in frontier regions were 60 percent less effective than in core Yangtze and Yellow River provinces, due to higher transport costs, thinner grain markets, and lower granary reserves, leaving populations in these areas exposed to repeated high-mortality famines even during the High Qing peak of administrative capacity. Shiue’s 2002 quantitative analysis of 140 prefectural grain price series between 1742 and 1795 further refined this argument, showing that the Qing state’s price stabilization efforts were most effective when integrated with well-developed private grain markets: in prefectures with high levels of interregional trade, official granary releases worked in tandem with private merchant shipments to smooth price spikes within three to six months of a harvest failure, while in more isolated prefectures with limited market connectivity, even large official grain disbursements failed to prevent extreme price volatility and localized starvation.
More recent scholarship has turned to the social and distributional impacts of Qing relief policy, challenging the earlier revisionist framing of High Qing relief as a uniformly successful, inclusive system. Dunstan’s 2020 analysis of local relief records from 1760s Henan found that gentry households and large landowners were often able to manipulate relief registration lists to claim disproportionate shares of disbursed grain, while landless tenants and migrant agricultural laborers—groups most vulnerable to food price shocks—were frequently excluded from official support, forcing many to rely on informal charitable networks or migrate in search of subsistence even during officially “successful” relief campaigns. Further, Li’s 2022 analysis of granary audit records from the 1780s to 1790s confirmed that the system’s fiscal and administrative sustainability was eroded by the late Qianlong reign, as official embezzlement of granary reserves, rising population pressure, and the fiscal strains of the White Lotus Rebellion reduced national granary stocks by nearly 40 percent between 1770 and 1800, sharply reducing the state’s capacity to respond to the widespread famines of the early nineteenth century.
Across this body of scholarship, a key unresolved tension remains between assessments of Qing relief capacity as an exceptional early modern state achievement and critiques of its structural inequalities and long-term fragility. While existing work has mapped broad patterns of market integration and relief performance across macro-regions, gaps remain in understanding how marginalized groups including ethnic minorities, migrant populations, and rural women experienced grain price shocks and relief access, and how local informal institutions mediated the impacts of top-down state interventions. (Word count: 698)

title: public health|community health workers and childhood vaccination coverage
text:
Community Health Workers and Childhood Vaccination Coverage: Strengthening Equity in Public Health Delivery

 Abstract

Childhood vaccination remains one of the most cost-effective public health interventions, preventing millions of deaths annually from vaccine-preventable diseases. However, global and local coverage gaps persist, particularly among rural, low-income, marginalized, and conflict-affected populations. Community health workers (CHWs) play a critical role in addressing these gaps by connecting formal health systems with underserved communities. Through home visits, health education, reminder systems, trust-building, and referral support, CHWs improve vaccination initiation, timeliness, and completion. This paper examines how CHWs contribute to childhood vaccination coverage, the mechanisms through which they work, and the challenges affecting their effectiveness. It argues that CHW programs are most successful when integrated into national health systems, supported with adequate training and supervision, and equipped with fair compensation and digital tools. Investing in CHWs is therefore not only a strategy for immunization improvement but also a broader commitment to primary health care and health equity.

 Introduction

Vaccination is a cornerstone of child survival. Routine immunization protects children from diseases such as measles, polio, tuberculosis, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B, and pneumonia. Despite long-standing global immunization efforts, millions of children remain incompletely vaccinated or receive no vaccines at all. The World Health Organization estimates that substantial numbers of children, especially in low-resource settings, still miss essential doses each year. The COVID-19 pandemic further disrupted immunization services, highlighting weaknesses in health-system resilience.

Low coverage is rarely caused by a single factor. Physical distance from clinics, user fees, caregiver work burdens, limited health literacy, vaccine hesitancy, poor service availability, and social exclusion all contribute. Many of these barriers occur at the community or household level, where CHWs operate. As frontline members of the communities they serve, CHWs are uniquely positioned to identify unvaccinated children, communicate with caregivers, and support navigation of health services. This paper analyzes the role of CHWs in increasing childhood vaccination coverage and considers how public health programs can maximize their contribution.

 How CHWs Improve Vaccination Coverage

CHWs improve immunization outcomes through several interconnected mechanisms. First, they increase access to information. During home visits and community meetings, CHWs explain the vaccine schedule, disease risks, common side effects, and the importance of completing doses on time. This information is especially valuable in settings with low literacy or limited exposure to formal health education. Unlike external health professionals, CHWs often speak local languages and understand cultural beliefs, allowing them to frame messages in socially acceptable ways.

Second, CHWs reduce missed opportunities through reminders and tracking. They may maintain village registers, identify newborns, notify caregivers before scheduled vaccination sessions, and follow up with children who have dropped out of the schedule. Studies in multiple settings have shown that reminder and outreach interventions can significantly improve timely vaccination. CHWs are particularly effective in reaching families who live far from health facilities or who have irregular contact with clinical services.

Third, CHWs build trust. Vaccine hesitancy often arises from suspicion of medical institutions, rumors, religious concerns, or past negative experiences. A trusted community member can address fears, clarify misinformation, and model help-seeking behavior. In communities where health facilities are understaffed or perceived as unwelcoming, the relationship between CHWs and caregivers may be decisive in whether a child is vaccinated.

Fourth, CHWs support referrals and service coordination. They may accompany caregivers to clinics, help arrange transport, collaborate with nurses during mobile vaccination campaigns, or report supply shortages to health authorities. In this way, they bridge the gap between community demand and health-system supply.

 CHWs as Agents of Health Equity

One of the strongest arguments for CHW involvement is their potential to reduce inequities. Children in remote rural areas, informal urban settlements, migrant communities, and conflict-affected regions often have the lowest vaccination rates. CHWs live within or near these communities and can deliver services where clinic-based care is difficult to access.

CHWs also tend to reach caregivers who are socially disadvantaged, including mothers with limited education, low-income households, and ethnic minorities. By providing individualized counseling and practical support, they can reduce disparities associated with knowledge, mobility, and bargaining power. For example, CHWs may encourage fathers or other household decision-makers to support vaccination, or help mothers overcome transportation costs and clinic waiting times.

However, CHW programs do not automatically produce equity. If CHWs are assigned only to accessible villages, receive inadequate resources, or are expected to work without payment, programs may reproduce existing inequalities. Equity-focused design requires targeting underserved areas, selecting diverse CHWs, and ensuring that workers have the materials and authority needed to deliver results.

 Challenges Affecting Effectiveness

Despite their contributions, CHWs face significant constraints. Many workers receive short, intermittent training and limited supervision, which can weaken the accuracy of vaccination messages and data collection. Heavy workloads are another common problem. CHWs are often responsible for family planning, nutrition, malaria prevention, infectious disease surveillance, and maternal health in addition to immunization. Without realistic task allocation, vaccination outreach may become inconsistent.

Compensation and motivation are also central concerns. Some CHWs are volunteers who receive only small stipends or performance-based rewards. Unfair compensation can increase turnover, reduce time available for fieldwork, and weaken accountability. Digital tools, such as mobile registries and electronic reminders, can improve efficiency, but they may fail if networks are poor, devices are unavailable, or workers lack technical support.

Furthermore, CHWs cannot solve health-system failures alone. Vaccine stockouts, absent clinic staff, poor cold-chain management, and long travel distances can undermine even the most effective community outreach. Successful programs therefore combine demand generation with reliable service delivery. CHWs should be viewed as part of a functioning primary health-care team rather than as substitutes for investment in facilities, nurses, vaccines, and infrastructure.

 Policy and Program Implications

To maximize CHW impact on childhood vaccination, programs should adopt several strategies. First, CHWs need standardized, competency-based training that includes vaccine science, communication, hesitancy management, recordkeeping, and referral procedures. Training should be ongoing rather than limited to initial recruitment.

Second, supervision should be supportive and regular. Nurse supervisors or district health teams can conduct field observations, review registers, discuss difficult cases, and provide feedback. Supervision also creates a channel for CHWs to report vaccine shortages or community resistance.

Third, governments should formalize CHW roles and provide clear compensation. Fair remuneration improves retention and professionalism and recognizes that community health work is skilled labor. Where full employment is not immediately possible, programs should offer predictable stipends, transportation support, insurance, and career progression opportunities.

Fourth, vaccination data systems should be simple and integrated. CHWs should be able to identify defaulters, monitor coverage, and share information with facilities without duplicating paperwork. Mobile applications may help, but digital systems must fit local connectivity and literacy conditions.

Finally, community participation is essential. CHWs perform best when local leaders, women’s groups, religious leaders, and families view immunization as a shared responsibility. Public health programs should engage these actors in dialogue rather than treating communities merely as targets for intervention.

 Conclusion

Community health workers make essential contributions to childhood vaccination coverage by delivering information, tracking children, reminding caregivers, building trust, and linking communities with health facilities. Their proximity to underserved populations makes them powerful agents of equity, particularly in settings where formal services are inaccessible or underused. However, their effectiveness depends on stronger health-system support. Adequate training, supervision, compensation, data tools, and reliable vaccine supply are necessary conditions for success. Rather than replacing clinical services, CHWs extend the reach of primary health care into households and communities. As countries work to recover from pandemic-related disruptions and achieve universal immunization goals, sustained investment in CHWs should be a central public health priority.

title: philosophy|Zhu Xi's theory of principle and its reception in Joseon Korea
text:
Methodology
This study adopts a contextualist textual hermeneutics framework to examine Zhu Xi’s (1130–1200) theory of li (principle, 理) and its contested reception in Joseon Korea (1392–1910), rejecting anachronistic framing of Joseon Neo-Confucianism as a derivative appendage to Song Chinese thought. The approach is rooted in two methodological commitments: first, to reconstruct the internal logic of Zhu’s core claims about li as both ontological ground and ethical norm from his own corpus, rather than later orthodox readings; second, to trace how Joseon scholars adapted li theory to resolve local intellectual, political, and ritual crises, rather than measuring their interpretations against a putatively “authentic” Zhuist standard.

 Data Sources
Primary data is drawn from two curated corpora, selected to avoid the bias of focusing exclusively on canonical “master texts” at the expense of contextual debate. The first corpus comprises core Zhu Xi writings: the *Collected Commentaries on the Four Books* (Sishu zhangju jizhu), the 1175 *Reflections on Things at Hand* (Jinsi lu, co-edited with Lü Zuqian), the topically arranged *Classified Conversations of Master Zhu* (Zhuzi yulei, focusing on juan 1–6 addressing li, qi [vital force, 氣], and the Great Ultimate), and Zhu’s surviving letters debating li’s priority to qi with contemporaries including Lu Jiuyuan and Chen Liang. The second corpus is a purposive sample of Joseon primary sources, spanning the four key phases of Joseon Zhu reception: (1) early Joseon (1392–1550) foundational texts, including the canonized *Confucian Diagram of the Four Beginnings and Seven Feelings* (Sadan ch’ilchong to) by Kwon Kun (1352–1409), and official state ritual codes that anchored li in dynastic governance; (2) mid-Joseon (1550–1700) Four-Seven Debate texts, including selected letters between Yi Hwang (Toegye, 1501–1570) and Ki Taesŭng (Kobong, 1527–1572), and the competing Horak Debate texts of Yi I (Yulgok, 1536–1584) and Song Siyŏl (Uam, 1607–1689); (3) late Joseon (1700–1860) critical re-engagements, including works by Yi Kan (1677–1727), who defended a “li as active agency” reading against qi-monist critiques, and Jeong Yakyong (Tasan, 1762–1836), who repurposed li as practical administrative norm rather than ontological substance; (4) 20th-century secondary Joseon materials, including colonial-era (1910–1945) nationalist framing of Joseon Zhuism as a uniquely Korean moral system. All pre-modern texts are accessed in their original literary Chinese (hanmun) editions, cross-referenced with modern annotated Korean and Chinese translations to resolve lexical ambiguity, particularly around terms (e.g., li’s “manifestation” [fa, 發]) that carry divergent connotations in Song and Joseon usage.

 Sampling Strategy
Sampling is purposive and stratified to capture both consensus and contestation, rather than treating Joseon Zhu reception as a linear orthodox tradition. First, 12 core Zhu Xi passages on li are selected as the analytical baseline, chosen because they were repeatedly cited in Joseon debate (rather than selected for their prominence in modern Chinese Zhu scholarship): these include Zhu’s comment on the *Great Ultimate* as “li without form,” his claim that “li is one, its manifestations are many” (liyi fenshu, 理一分殊), and his ambiguous framing of whether li itself can issue moral feeling, or only qi carries activating force. For the Joseon corpus, 22 primary texts are selected to represent three competing interpretive lineages: the Toegye school (li as logically and ethically prior to qi, with its own motive force), the Yulgok school (li as immanent in qi, with no independent activity), and late Joseon critics of both schools. Official state civil service examination (gwageo) essays from 1400, 1550, 1650, and 1750 are also included to trace how li theory was institutionalized as state orthodoxy, rather than remaining a purely scholarly debate.

 Analytical Procedure
Analysis proceeds in three iterative stages. First, conceptual genealogy: we map Zhu Xi’s li discourse across his own writings, identifying unresolved ambiguities (e.g., the tension between li as transcendent ontological ground and li as immanent in concrete qi) that later Joseon scholars would exploit, rather than forcing Zhu’s thought into a single coherent system. Second, intertextual tracing: for each Joseon text, we identify how authors cite, paraphrase, or omit Zhu’s core claims, and map deviations to local contextual pressures: for example, Yi Hwang’s emphasis on li’s independent activity is linked to his need to defend moral autonomy against factional purges of scholar-officials, while Tasan’s rejection of li as ontological substance is tied to his advocacy for practical administrative reform after the 18th-century state collapse. Third, reception coding: we code each Joseon interpretation against three axes: (1) ontological framing of li (transcendent/immanent/regulative), (2) the li-qi relationship (li prior/qi prior/non-dual), and (3) the ethical-political function of li (personal moral cultivation/state ritual order/practical governance). This coding avoids binary “orthodox/heterodox” judgments, instead tracing how Joseon scholars transformed Zhu’s li theory into a distinct Korean philosophical tradition tied to local political and moral concerns. Reliability checks are conducted via cross-comparison with leading Korean and Chinese Neo-Confucian scholarship to resolve ambiguous readings of contested passages. (Word count: 598)

title: literary studies|landscape and exile in the poetry of Su Shi
text:
Landscape and Exile in the Poetry of Su Shi
This article examines the reciprocal constitution of landscape experience and exile subjectivity in the poetic oeuvre of Su Shi (1037–1101), the Northern Song literatus whose successive demotions to Huangzhou, Huizhou, and Danzhou redefined the expressive and philosophical possibilities of Chinese exile poetry. Moving beyond the dominant critical framing of Su’s landscape writing as a passive consolation for political displacement, the study traces how the poet’s embodied encounters with the marginal ecologies of the Song empire’s southern frontiers—from the tidal wetlands of the Yangtze River to the tropical monsoon forests of Hainan—actively reshaped his understanding of self, community, and cosmic belonging. Drawing on close formal readings of regulated verse, ancient-style poetry, and occasional ci lyrics alongside contextual analysis of Song bureaucratic exile institutions, literati garden culture, and Northern Song intellectual debates over self-cultivation, the article argues that Su’s poetics of “following along with things” (yu wu wei liu) does not mark a retreat from political engagement but a deliberate reconfiguration of ethical life outside the institutional spaces of the imperial court. The analysis is structured around three interconnected landscape motifs: the river as a figure of temporal flux that dissolves the distinction between displacement and home; the neglected garden plot as a site of material labor that forges new bonds of solidarity with local commoners and indigenous communities; and the distant mountain as a vantage point from which to reframe imperial center and peripheral margin as contingent positions within an unbounded natural order. By situating Su’s exile poetics against both the conventions of preceding “demotion poetry” (qianzhe shi) and the ideological constraints of Song literati bureaucratic culture, the study demonstrates how his landscape writing converts the coerced spatial displacement of exile into a radical form of existential freedom that would shape Chinese literary responses to displacement for centuries thereafter. (Word count: 252)

title: history|the role of Venetian merchants in the fourteenth-century spice trade
text:
The fourteenth century stands as a pivotal, understudied turning point in the history of the medieval spice trade, an era long framed by scholarship as a period of unbroken Venetian dominance preceding the Portuguese entry into Indian Ocean networks in the late fifteenth century. Traditional narratives of Mediterranean commerce, rooted in mid-twentieth-century works such as Lane’s (1973) foundational history of Venice, cast the city-state’s merchant class as the unchallenged brokers of global luxury goods between the eastern termini of overland and maritime Asian routes and the consumer markets of Latin Christendom. Yet this teleological framing, which reads fourteenth-century Venetian success backward from the city’s fifteenth-century territorial and commercial zenith, often obscures the structural vulnerabilities, adaptive innovations, and contested negotiations that defined Venetian merchants’ engagement with the spice trade across a century marked by pandemic, inter-state warfare, Mamluk fiscal centralization, and Mongol political collapse. As recent scholarship on medieval Eurasian connectivity has emphasized (Hunt 2018; Jacoby 2020), the fourteenth century was not a static interlude between the high medieval commercial revolution and the age of European maritime expansion, but a period of radical reconfiguration in which Venetian merchants reshaped their institutional, financial, and diplomatic practices to retain access to pepper, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, and mace—commodities that carried not only outsized economic value, but profound cultural, medical, and religious weight across Latin Europe. This paper argues that Venetian merchants did not hold a structural monopoly on the fourteenth-century spice trade, but rather constructed a fragile, contingent competitive advantage by blending coercive diplomatic pressure, flexible collective risk-mitigation institutions, and cross-cultural brokerage practices that allowed them to outmaneuver rival merchant communities from Genoa, Catalonia, and Provence even as the trans-Asian routes that had sustained high medieval spice flows contracted sharply.
To contextualize this argument, it is first necessary to disentangle the myth of perpetual Venetian dominance from the on-the-ground conditions of the early fourteenth century. As Lopez (1976) first documented, the Venetian position in the spice trade remained deeply precarious in the decades following the 1261 Byzantine recapture of Constantinople, which stripped the city of the privileged trade access it had held in the Black Sea and eastern Mediterranean under the Latin Empire. Genoese merchants, who had supported the Byzantine restoration, secured preferential tariffs in Mamluk Alexandria and Black Sea emporia such as Tana and Caffa through the 1280s, controlling an estimated 60 percent of pepper imports to Western Europe at the turn of the fourteenth century (Kedar 1976). The Venetian turn toward systematic state support for spice trade convoy routes, formalized in the 1294 establishment of the annual muda galley system, was not a marker of unchallenged power, but a deliberate response to Genoese competition, designed to reduce individual merchant risk, standardize cargo pricing, and leverage the Venetian state’s naval capacity to protect high-value spice cargoes from piracy and wartime seizure. The impact of the Black Death, which reached Venice in 1348 and killed an estimated 60 percent of the city’s population, further disrupted existing trade networks, creating labor shortages, collapsing consumer demand in some regional markets, and spurring inflation in spice prices as Mamluk authorities in Alexandria raised tariffs on transit goods to offset their own pandemic-related revenue losses (Ashtor 1983).
While prior scholarship has tended to frame Venetian success in this era as a product of superior state institutions, this paper centers the on-the-ground practices of individual and collective merchant networks, drawing on previously underutilized notarial records from the Venetian colonial outpost of Candia, merchant correspondence preserved in the Archivio di Stato di Venezia, and Mamluk administrative records to trace how merchants negotiated access to spice supplies at times when formal diplomatic treaties broke down. As Phillips (1998) notes, Venetian merchants were uniquely positioned to operate across religious and political boundaries, maintaining long-term commercial partnerships with Jewish and Muslim brokers in Alexandria and Beirut even during periods of formal papal ban on trade with Mamluk lands, a flexibility that allowed them to secure spice cargoes when Genoese and Catalan traders were expelled from Mamluk ports during the 1360s Alexandrian Crusade. This brokerage role, however, came with persistent costs: Venetian merchants faced repeated rounds of extortion, arbitrary cargo seizure, and price-gouging from Mamluk authorities, and were forced to develop innovative financial instruments, including early forms of marine insurance and commenda contracts that spread risk across multiple investors, to offset these vulnerabilities (Munro 2012). By the last quarter of the fourteenth century, these adaptations had allowed Venetian merchants to capture nearly 75 percent of spice imports to Western Europe, laying the institutional groundwork for the city’s fifteenth-century commercial empire, even as the seeds of later decline were sown in their growing dependence on Mamluk-controlled maritime routes, a vulnerability that would be exploited by Portuguese navigators a century later. In tracing these dynamics, this paper contributes to a growing body of scholarship that moves beyond state-centric narratives of medieval trade to center the contingent, negotiated work of merchant actors in shaping pre-modern global connectivity.
